## **Executive summary** 

Head and neck cancer is a general term that covers different cancers that start in the tissues in the head and neck area, including the oral cavity, pharynx and larynx. In England in 2022, there were 9,997 diagnoses of the cancers of cancers of the oral cavity, oropharynx, larynx, and hypopharynx. The disease, as well as the effects of treatment, have debilitating effect on patients' day-to-day general function and health-related quality of life. 

The standard of care for newly diagnosed locally advanced resectable head and neck cancer has not changed for the last 20 years and consists of surgical resection of the tumour and neck lymph node dissection, followed by radiotherapy alone or in combination with cisplatin. After such treatment the rates of tumour recurrence are high (up to 56% of patients with locally advanced disease experience recurrence usually within 2 years following initial treatment) and the proportion of patients surviving after 5 and 10 years are low (69% and 10%, respectively). This submission addresses the expected marketing authorisation for pembrolizumab *****. This covers the technology’s full expected marketing authorisation for this indication. 

The clinical effectiveness of pembrolizumab in this indication is demonstrated by the phase 3, multicentre, open-label, randomised, active-controlled KEYNOTE-689 trial. 

Participants with locally advanced HNSCC were randomised in a 1:1 ratio to receive 2 cycles of neoadjuvant pembrolizumab and 15 cycles of adjuvant pembrolizumab (both at a dose of 200 mg every 3 weeks) in addition to standard of care (pembrolizumab + SOC group) or standard of care alone (SOC group). Standard of care was surgery and adjuvant radiotherapy with or without concomitant cisplatin. 

The latest available results from this study are from the first interim analysis (IA1) with a database cut-off date of 25[th] July 2024, where the median actual follow-up time was 2.25 years (range 0.04 years to 5.54 years) in patients with baseline PD-L1 CPS ≥1. A total of 347 patients with baseline PD-L1 CPS of ≥1 were assigned to the pembrolizumab + SOC group and 335 patients to the SOC group. In these patients, a statistically significant and clinically meaningful improvement in event-free survival (EFS) was observed in the pembrolizumab + SOC group compared with the SOC group (hazard ratio [HR]: 0.70; 95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.55, 0.89; p=0.00140), reducing the risk of recurrence or progression by 30% among patients with resectable locally advanced HNSCC. The overall survival HR also favoured pembrolizumab + SOC versus SOC (HR:0.72; 95% CI: 0.56, 0.94; nominal p=0.00666). There was a statistically significant and clinically meaningful improvement in major pathological response (mPR) in the

pembrolizumab + SOC group compared with the SOC group with a difference in response rates of 9.8% (95% CI: 7.0, 13.3; p<0. 00001), and an improvement in pathological complete response (pCR) in the pembrolizumab + SOC group compared with the SOC group with a difference in response rates of 3.1% (95% CI: 1.6, 5.6; nominal p=0.0006). The benefit of pembrolizumab + SOC over SOC was largely consistent across prespecified subgroups across the efficacy endpoints. 

Health-related quality of life changes between the pembrolizumab + SOC and SOC groups were similar as measured by the European Organisation for Research and Treatment of Cancer (EORTC) QoL questionnaire (QLQ)-C30 and EuroQol 5-dimension 5-level questionnaire (EQ-5D-5L). The study showed that pembrolizumab had a manageable safety profile that was generally consistent with the well-established safety profile of pembrolizumab without any new safety concerns. 

To assess the cost-effectiveness of perioperative pembrolizumab + SOC compared to SOC alone (surgery followed by adjuvant radiotherapy with or without cisplatin) in patients with resectable locally advanced HNSCC with CPS≥1, a _de novo_ four-state Markov model was developed consisting of event-free (EF), local or salvageable recurrence (L/SR), incurable recurrence/progression (IRP), and death. Data from the most recent KEYNOTE-689 trial data cutoff (25 July 2024) were used to populate the model. Where model parameters were not available from KEYNOTE-689, systematic literature reviews were used to inform inputs. 

The model results demonstrated perioperative pembrolizumab + SOC to be a cost-effective use of NHS resources, and extensive sensitivity and scenario analyses show the results to be robust to alternative sets of assumptions. KEYNOTE-689 is a true step-change in the management of patients with resectable locally advanced HNSCC as the first clinical study to read positive in the perioperative space, demonstrating statistically significant improvement in event free survival and a positive trend in overall survival, allowing more patients to benefit from reduced risk of recurrence in the longer term. 

Pembrolizumab + SOC would be the first peri-operative treatment option available for these patients, enabling a greater proportion of patients to experience prolonged time without cancer and consequently reducing the overall burden of advanced disease treatment for the NHS. Introducing this technology to the NHS will result to significant benefits for the patients, their families, the health system and the wider society overall.

## **1 Decision problem, description of the technology and clinical care pathway** 

## **Summary of the decision problem, technology, and clinical care pathway** 

- This submission addresses the anticipated marketing authorisation for pembrolizumab *****. This covers the technology’s full expected marketing authorisation for this indication. 

- Pembrolizumab (KEYTRUDA®) is a monoclonal antibody (mAB) of the IgG4/kappa isotype designed to exert a dual ligand blockade of the PD-1 pathway by directly blocking the interaction between PD-1 and its associated ligands, PD-L1 and PD-L2 which appear on the antigen-presenting or tumour cells. By binding to the PD-1 receptor and blocking the interaction with the receptor ligands, pembrolizumab releases the PD-1 pathway-mediated inhibition of the immune response and reactivates both tumour-specific cytotoxic T lymphocytes in the tumour microenvironment and antitumour inactivity. 

- Head and neck cancer is a general term that covers a range of cancers that start in the tissues in the head and neck area, including the oral cavity, pharynx and larynx. It is a considerably burdensome disease with few treatment advances in the last 20 years, most of which were in the advanced disease stages. In England in 2020, there were a total of 7959 registrations of malignant neoplasm of the lip, oral cavity and pharynx (International classification of Diseases [ICD]-10 codes C00-C14). 

- The long-term survival of patients with HNSCC depends on several factors, mainly the origin/site of the cancer and the stage of the disease at diagnosis, with the 5- year survival rate being 69% for locally advanced HNSCC. Up to 56% of LA HNSCC patients experiencing disease recurrence following treatment, contributing to poor survival outcomes, including distant metastases. 

- There is considerable burden on patients living with HNSCC. The disease, as well as the effects of treatments (such as surgery and radiotherapy), can have severe impact on patients' ability to speak, swallow, breath, see, smell, and taste. These lead to a debilitating effect on patients' day-to-day general function and healthrelated quality of life.

• The current standard of care (SOC) treatment for patients with newly diagnosed Stage III-IV resectable LA HNSCC consists of surgical resection of the tumour and neck lymph node dissection, followed by either radiotherapy alone or in combination with cisplatin. Pembrolizumab as single agent monotherapy will be administered to patients with resectable locally advanced HNSCC with PD-L1 combined positive score (CPS) ≥1 as neoadjuvant treatment, then continued as adjuvant treatment in combination with radiation with or without platinum-containing chemotherapy followed by pembrolizumab as single agent. 

- Use of this technology is not anticipated to raise any equity or equality considerations.

## **1.3 Health condition and position of the technology in the treatment pathway** 

## **1.3.1 Health condition** 

Head and neck cancer is a general term that covers different cancers that start in the tissues in the head and neck area, including the oral cavity, pharynx (throat – includes nasopharynx, oropharynx and hypopharynx) and larynx (voice box) (Figure 1) (7, 8). Squamous cells are found in the outer layer of skin and in the mucous membranes, which are the moist tissues that line body cavities such as the airways and intestines. More than 90% of head and neck cancers are squamous cell carcinomas (HNSCC), originating from the epithelium of the mucosal lining of the upper aerodigestive tract. Head and neck cancers can also begin in the salivary glands, sinuses, or muscles or nerves in the head and neck, but these types of cancer are much less common than squamous cell carcinomas (9). HNSCC typically develops in the mucous membranes of the mouth, nose and throat (10). HNSCC is caused by a variety of factors that can alter the DNA in cells. The strongest risk factors for developing this form of cancer are tobacco use (including smoking or using chewing tobacco) and heavy alcohol consumption. In addition, studies have shown that infection with certain strains of human papillomavirus (HPV) is linked to the development of HNSCC. HPV infection accounts for the increasing incidence of HNSCC in younger people (10). HPV-positive and HPV-negative HNSCC represent two distinct biologies with different clinical presentations and prognosis (11). HPV infection is more specifically linked to oropharyngeal cancer, where HPV infection has been consistently associated with more favourable outcomes (12).

Head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) arises from the mucosal epithelium of the oral cavity (lips, buccal mucosa, hard palate, anterior tongue, floor of mouth and retromolar trigone), nasopharynx, oropharynx (palatine tonsils, lingual tonsils, base of tongue, soft palate, uvula and posterior pharyngeal wall), hypopharynx (the bottom part of the throat, extending from the hyoid bone to the cricoid cartilage) and larynx. Human papillomavirus-associated HNSCCs arise primarily from the palatine and lingual tonsils of the oropharynx, whereas tobacco-associated HNSCCs arise primarily in the oral cavity, hypopharynx and larynx (7). Source: Johnson et al. 2020 (7). 

In England in 2022, there were 9,997 diagnoses of the cancers of cancers of the oral cavity, oropharynx, larynx, and hypopharynx (13). Overall, malignant neoplasm of the lip, oral cavity or pharynx accounted for roughly 2.5% of cancer registrations for that year (14). In England in 2022-23, there were 30,516 finished consultant episodes (FCE), and 27,675 admissions with a primary diagnosis of malignant neoplasm of the lip, oral cavity or pharynx (ICD-10 codes C00-C14), resulting in 17,297 day cases and 79,575 FCE bed days (15). Head and neck cancer is the 8th most common cancer in the UK. Incidence rates in the UK for head and neck cancer are highest in people aged 70-74 (2016-2018). Over the last decade, incidence rates in the UK have increased by almost a sixth (16%) (16), and in the UK between 2017-2019, there were 4,143 deaths from head and neck cancer. The European age-standardised mortality rate per 100,000 of the population in the UK in 2017-2019 was 3.5 in females and 10.2 in males (16). 

The symptoms of HNSCC may include a lump in the neck or a sore in the mouth or throat that does not heal, a sore throat that does not go away, difficulty or pain in swallowing and a change or hoarseness in the voice. Other symptoms that may affect specific areas of the head and

neck include bleeding of the mouth, swelling of the jaw, ear pain, headaches, and paralysis of the muscles in the face, or pain in the face, chin or neck (17). Head and neck cancer is staged according to the American Joint Committee on Cancer/Union for International Cancer Control (AJCC/UICC) tumour, node, and metastasis (TNM) staging classification system v8 (Figure 2) (18). HNSCC tumour staging is complex and based on the location of the tumour, nodal involvement, and the degree of structural involvement at subsites. Classification considers local, regional, and distant characteristics of the disease; local disease includes the primary tumour (T 1-4); regional disease indicates the involvement of cervical lymph nodes (N 0-3); and distant metastasis (M 0-1) assesses spread of the primary tumour to sites beyond the cervical lymphatic system. 

The long-term survival of patients with HNSCC depends on several factors, mainly the origin/site of the cancer and the stage of the disease at diagnosis; the 5-year survival for localised HNSCC is 86%, decreasing to 69% for locally advanced and 40% for metastatic disease (16, 19). The 10-year survival rate of patients with advanced HNSCC can be as low as 10% (20). If the disease is diagnosed at an early stage the primary treatment is surgical resection of the tumour where possible, however recurrence of the tumour is a major driver of mortality and comorbidities in the management of HNSCC, posing a greater challenge than seen in many other types of cancer. Up to 56% of LA HNSCC patients experience disease recurrence following treatment, either locoregionally or as distant metastases, usually within 2 years following initial treatment, contributing to poor survival outcomes (21, 22). The recurrence rate for LA HNSCC is notably higher than in many other cancers, and is high even among patients who achieved a complete response after initial treatment (23, 24). Treatment of recurrent disease is often especially difficult due to factors such as prior therapies altering tumour cell biology, the infiltrative and multifocal nature of the disease, and the often significant morbidity and deteriorating performance status in patients who progress on initial therapy, further limiting treatment options (25). 

Locally advanced HNSCC is associated with considerable burden on patients daily living (26). Depending on the location and size of the tumour, the disease (as well as the effects of treatments, such as surgery and radiotherapy) can have a severe impact on a patient’s ability to speak, swallow, breath, see, smell, and taste (27, 28). These can therefore lead to a debilitating impact on patients' general function, including their ability to carry out day-to-day basic self-care, home roles, work, and leisure activities (26). 

The disease and its current treatments also often have considerable negative impact on patients' quality of life (29). Severe pain is linked to reduced overall 5-year survival rates in

oral cancer (31% in patients with severe pain vs. 52% in patients without) and pharyngeal cancer (33% in patients with severe pain vs. 52% without) (30). Head and neck cancer is also associated with a higher suicide rate: 37.9 compared to 11.8 per 100,000 person-years for the general population, this is the second highest rate among all cancer types and 3 times higher than the rate for the general population (31, 32). Due to the high likelihood of recurrence of the tumour, patients who have undergone treatment for HNSCC also experience a quality of life impact from the fear of recurrence (24, 33). In addition to the burden on the patients themselves, the caregivers of patients with HNSCC also experience a considerable burden in terms of psychological distress, physical and social functioning, and quality of life (34-36).

## **1.3.2 Treatment pathway and proposed positioning** 

The treatment pathway used for head and neck cancer in the UK is described in the “ _Head and Neck Cancer: United Kingdom National Multidisciplinary Guidelines, Sixth Edition_ ” and the “ _Squamous cell carcinoma of the oral cavity, larynx, oropharynx and hypopharynx: EHNSESMO-ESTRO Clinical Practice Guidelines for diagnosis, treatment and follow-up_ ” (1, 2). 

Recommendations on the management of LA HNSCC differ based on tumour site. However, across sites the first consideration is usually whether the tumour is surgically resectable; surgical resection is usually the recommended treatment for tumours in the oral cavity and larynx while organ-preserving approaches tend to be considered first for tumours of the oropharynx and hypopharynx, with surgical resection reserved for larger or more aggressive tumours. HNSCC tumours may be determined to be unresectable if they are too large or have invaded into nearby critical structures such that surgery to remove them is associated with unacceptable risk of severe and irreversible functional deficits (such as the loss of the ability to speak or swallow) or is technically impossible without causing death (such as in cases where the tumour is adjacent to the skull, spine or major blood vessels) (37). AJCC T4a HNSCC are often determined to be resectable while T4b are often determined to be unresectable (37). The standard of care for LA stage III and IV HNSCC cancers not treatable by surgery is concomitant definitive RT with cisplatin. 

The current SOC treatment for patients with newly diagnosed Stage III-IV resectable LA HNSCC consists of surgical resection of the tumour and neck lymph node dissection, followed by either RT alone or, for patients with post-surgical high-risk pathological features (extranodal extension and/or positive surgical margins), in combination with cisplatin. 

NICE guideline NG36 “ _Cancer of the upper aerodigestive tract: assessment and management in people aged 16 and over_ ” was last updated in June 2018 (38). In patients with locally advanced disease eligible for resection and who can tolerate chemotherapy, NG36 makes the recommendations described below for tumours of the larynx and hypopharynx, NG36 does not provide any recommendations for treatment of advanced tumours of the oral cavity or oropharynx. No immune-oncologic therapies are mentioned for these patients. 

- Squamous cell carcinoma of the larynx: 

   - Offer people with T3 squamous cell carcinoma of the larynx surgery with adjuvant radiotherapy, with or without concomitant chemotherapy.

NICE TA145 recommends cetuximab in combination with radiotherapy as a treatment option only for patients with locally advanced squamous cell cancer of the head and neck whose Karnofsky performance-status score is 90% or greater and for whom all forms of platinumbased chemoradiotherapy treatment are contraindicated. The clinical evidence base for TA145 was the Bonner et al. trial for which patients were ineligible if they had undergone surgery or had previously received radiotherapy for head and neck cancer (3). Subsequent clinical trials (e.g. RTOG 1016 and De-ESCaLATE HPV) have indicated that cetuximab in combination with radiotherapy is inferior to platinum-based chemoradiotherapy (5, 6), which further supports the TA145 restriction and is likely to increase clinician hesitancy to use this regimen. Accordingly, clinical expert advice to MSD is that use of cetuximab in this indication is now very rare and it is reserved only for unresectable patients with renal impairment who are not suitable for platinum chemotherapy. Therefore, as the indication under consideration in this appraisal is for patients who are receiving surgery (versus the non-surgical population for which cetuximab is available), and as the practical use of cetuximab in the LA HNSCC setting in UK clinical practice is very low, cetuximab plus radiotherapy is not a relevant comparator for the current decision problem.

The standard of care (SOC) for resectable locally advanced HNSCC has remained relatively constant since 2004, when two pivotal randomised trials (European Organization for Research and Treatment of Cancer [EORTC] #22931 and Radiation Therapy Oncology Group [RTOG] #9501 (39, 40)) first established the addition of cisplatin to postoperative radiotherapy as the recommended treatment regimen for high-risk disease, and recurrence rates remain high: approximately 50% of patients experience disease recurrence and the 5-year overall survival remains below 50% for high-risk patients. Over the intervening 20 years, the SOC for this patient population has not changed and there continues to be no approved adjuvant therapies that can be administered after completion of postoperative locoregional treatment (41). Several trials of adjuvant immunotherapies have been conducted in this this area with few showing meaningful benefit (42, 43). 

Furthermore, should the disease recur or progress, this frequently manifests as advanced inoperable or metastatic disease which is linked to complex disease management, and ultimately increased risk of death regardless of any subsequent treatment options. The median survival for recurrent or metastatic HNSCC is only approximately 12 months (21, 44). Accordingly, new treatment strategies to decrease rates of recurrence and distant metastases of HNSCC are needed to improve outcomes for this patient population. Owing to the limited progress in this area, there are currently no NICE-recommended neoadjuvant or adjuvant treatments for HNSCC for use in the NHS. The availability of pembrolizumab as an effective perioperative (neoadjuvant followed by adjuvant) therapy in this indication therefore presents the first meaningful advancement in this setting in over 20 years and represents a considerable step-change in the management of resectable locally advanced HNSCC. 

## **1.3.3 Treatment setting** 

Pembrolizumab as monotherapy will be administered to patients with resectable locally advanced head and neck squamous cell carcinoma as neoadjuvant treatment, continued as adjuvant treatment in combination with radiation therapy with or without concomitant cisplatin and then as monotherapy in adults *****. Pembrolizumab, both as neoadjuvant and adjuvant treatment, will be administered in the secondary care setting.

## **Summary of key clinical effectiveness information** 

## _**Randomised controlled trial:**_ 

- They KEYNOTE-689 study was identified in a SLR conducted with eligibility criteria aligned with the decision problem of this appraisal with a search date of 31-MAR2025. The SLR identified the KEYNOTE-689 study as the only study that investigated pembrolizumab in the indication of interest to this appraisal. 

- KEYNOTE-689 is a phase 3, multicentre, open-label, randomised, active-controlled trial conducted at 192 sites across three geographic regions. Participants were randomly assigned in a 1:1 ratio to receive neoadjuvant and adjuvant pembrolizumab in addition to standard care (pembrolizumab + SOC group) or to receive standard care alone (SOC group). Across the UK, there were six study sites which recruited 19 patients. 

- The latest available results from the KEYNOTE-689 study are from the first interim analysis (IA1) with a database cut-off date of 25-JUL-2024, which are reported in this submission. Median actual follow-up time was 2.26 years (range 0.04 years to 5.54 years) for all patients in the study and 2.25 years (range 0.04 years to 5.54 years) in patients with baseline PD-L1 CPS ≥1. The KEYNOTE-689 study is ongoing and may provide additional evidence in the next 12 months for the indication being appraised. Results for the subgroup of patients with PD-L1 ≥1 CPS are presented in this section. 

- A statistically significant and clinically meaningful improvement in EFS per RECIST 1.1 as assessed by BICR was observed in the pembrolizumab + SOC group compared with the SOC group (HR: 0.70; 95% CI: 0.55, 0.89; p=0.00140, which is below the p-value boundary of 0.0124). 

- The OS HR estimate favoured pembrolizumab + SOC versus SOC (HR:0.72; 95% CI: 0.56, 0.94; nominal p=0.00666) (per prespecified multiplicity strategy, OS was not formally tested in CPS ≥1 population at IA1). 

- There was a statistically significant and clinically meaningful improvement in mPR based on BIPR in the pembrolizumab + SOC group compared with the SOC group with a difference in response rates of 9.8% (95% CI: 7.0, 13.3; p<0. 00001).

- No indirect comparisons or mixed treatment comparisons were carried out as the KEYNOTE-689 study provides direct evidence for the treatment comparison of relevance to this appraisal. 

## _**Safety**_ 

- Pembrolizumab as neoadjuvant and continued as adjuvant treatment in combination with radiotherapy ± cisplatin followed by pembrolizumab monotherapy in participants with Stage IIII-VA resectable LA HNSCC has a manageable safety profile that is generally consistent with the well-established safety profile of pembrolizumab monotherapy and the individual safety profiles of RT and cisplatin. No new safety concerns for pembrolizumab are identified.

## **2.3.2 Baseline characteristics of trial participants** 

In participants with PD-L1 CPS≥1, demographic and baseline characteristics were generally similar in both treatment groups (Table 6). Most participants were male, white and of not Hispanic or Latino ethnicity. The overall median age was 60.0 (22 to 87) years. Most participants across both groups had an overall cancer staging at baseline of IVA, and 56.9% of participants across both groups had an ECOG-PS score of 0.

## **2.4.2 Analysis populations** 

## _**2.4.2.1 Efficacy analysis population**_ 

The Intention-to-Treat (ITT) population was the primary population for efficacy analyses in this study, which consists of all randomised participants. Participants were included in the treatment group to which they are randomised for the analysis of efficacy data using the ITT population. 

## _**2.4.2.2 Safety analysis population**_ 

Safety analyses were conducted in the All Participants as Treated (APaT) population, which consists of all randomised participants who received at least one dose of study intervention or surgery that is part of study treatment. Participants were included in the treatment group corresponding to the study treatment they actually received for the analysis of safety data using the APaT population. This was the treatment group to which they are randomised except for participants who take incorrect study treatment for the entire treatment period; such participants were included in the treatment group corresponding to the study treatment actually received.

Analyses of laboratory or vital sign measurements included only participants with at least one measurement obtained after at least one dose of study intervention. If the analysis assessed change from baseline, a baseline measurement was also required. 

## _**2.4.2.3 PRO analysis population**_ 

The PRO analyses are based on the PRO Full Analysis Set (FAS) population, defined as all randomised participants who have at least one PRO assessment available for the specific endpoint and have received treatment. Participants were analysed in the treatment group to which they are randomised.

## **2.5 Critical appraisal of the relevant clinical effectiveness evidence** 

A critical appraisal of the KEYNOTE-689 trial using the Cochrane Collaboration’s Risk of Bias tool (Version 2) is presented in Appendix B (section B3). 

## **2.6 Clinical effectiveness results of the relevant studies** 

## **Summary of key RCT clinical effectiveness results** 

- The latest available results from the KEYNOTE-689 study are from the first interim analysis (IA1) with a database cut-off date of 25-JUL-2024, which are reported in this submission. Median actual follow-up time was 117.8 weeks for all patients in the study and 117.4 weeks in patients with baseline PD-L1 CPS ≥1. The KEYNOTE-689 study is ongoing and may provide additional evidence in the next 12 months for the indication being appraised. Results for the subgroup of patients with PD-L1 ≥1 CPS are presented in this section.

© Merck Sharp & Dohme (UK) Limited (2025). All rights reserved 




<!-- page 53 -->

Confidential 

- A statistically significant and clinically meaningful improvement in EFS per RECIST 1.1 as assessed by BICR was observed in the pembrolizumab + SOC group compared with the SOC group (HR: 0.70; 95% CI: 0.55, 0.89; p=0.00140, which is below the p-value boundary of 0.0124). 

- The OS HR estimate favoured pembrolizumab + SOC versus SOC (HR:0.72; 95% CI: 0.56, 0.94; nominal p=0.00666) (per prespecified multiplicity strategy, OS was not formally tested in CPS ≥1 population at IA1, but these results showed a clinically meaningful trend towards significance). 

- There was a statistically significant and clinically meaningful improvement in mPR based on BIPR in the pembrolizumab + SOC group compared with the SOC group with a difference in response rates of 9.8% (95% CI: 7.0, 13.3; p<0. 00001). 

- There was an improvement in pCR rate based on BIPR in the pembrolizumab + SOC group compared with the SOC group with a difference in response rates of 3.1% (95% CI: 1.6, 5.6; nominal p=0.0006). 

The latest available results from the KEYNOTE-689 study are from the first interim analysis (IA1) with a database cut-off date of 25-JUL-2024, which are reported in this submission. Results for the subgroup of participants with PD-L1 CPS ≥1 are described in this section, results for the entire “all comer” overall KEYNOTE-689 participant population are provided in Appendix N. Patients with CPS ≥1 comprised 95.5% of the all comer overall trial population and the proportion of patients with CPS ≥1 was balanced between the two trial arms (95.4% in the SOC arm and 95.6% in the pembrolizumab + SOC arm). Note that PD-L1 status, measured using tumour proportion score (TPS), was a stratification factor at randomisation to ensure that the treatment groups were balanced with respect to this potential effect modifier. 

## **2.6.1 KEYNOTE-689 PD-L1 CPS ≥ 1 participants results** 

## _**2.6.1.1 Disposition of participants**_ 

The disposition of participants was similar in both treatment groups (Table 9). In the population of participants with PD-L1 CPS≥1, a total of 682 participants were randomised in the ITT population (347 in the pembrolizumab + SOC group, 335 in the SOC group). Median actual follow-up was 130.4 weeks (range 3.6 weeks to 282.1 weeks) in the pembrolizumab + SOC group and 101.8 weeks (range 2.1 weeks to 289.1 weeks) (Table 11).

## _**2.6.1.2 Event free survival (EFS) by BICR**_ 

A statistically significant and clinically meaningful improvement in EFS per RECIST 1.1 as assessed by BICR was observed in the pembrolizumab + SOC group compared with the SOC group (HR: 0.70; 95% CI: 0.55, 0.89; p=0.00140, which is below the p-value boundary of 0.0124), representing a 30% reduction in the risk of an EFS event in the pembrolizumab + SOC group versus the SOC group (Table 12).

Confidential 

Median EFS was 59.7 months in the pembrolizumab + SOC group compared with the median EFS of 29.6 months in the SOC group (Table 12). The EFS rate was higher in the pembrolizumab + SOC group than in the SOC group at all timepoints analysed (Table 12). 

The KM plot for EFS shows that the pembrolizumab + SOC curve separated from the SOC curve at approximately 3 months and remained separated over time (Figure 5).

## _**2.6.1.3 Overall survival**_ 

As per the prespecified multiplicity strategy, OS was not formally tested in the CPS≥1 population at IA1. Median actual follow-up time was 117.4 weeks in patients with baseline PDL1 CPS ≥1. The OS HR estimate favoured pembrolizumab versus SOC (HR:0.72; 95% CI: 0.56, 0.94; nominal p=0.00666) (Table 13). Median OS was not reached in the pembrolizumab + SOC group compared with a median OS of 61.8 months in the SOC group (Table 13).

## _**2.6.1.4 Major Pathological Response (mPR) by BIPR**_ 

There was a statistically significant and clinically meaningful improvement in mPR based on BIPR in the pembrolizumab + SOC group compared with the SOC group with a difference in response rates of 9.8% (95% CI: 7.0, 13.3; p<0. 00001), which was below the p-value boundary of 0.0005. The mPR rate was 9.8% for the pembrolizumab + SOC group; there were no participants in the SOC group with mPR (Table 14).

## **2.8 Subgroup analysis** 

Subgroup analyses of the efficacy endpoints of the KEYNOTE-689 study were conducted according to the subgroups pre-specified in the study protocol and analysis plan (as described in section 2.4). The results of subgroup analyses in the participants with baseline PD-L1 CPS≥1 are presented in this section. In general, the benefit of pembrolizumab over SOC was consistent across prespecified subgroups across the efficacy endpoints. Small sample sizes in some subgroups resulted in wide CIs and therefore the results of those analyses should be interpreted with caution.

## **2.9 Meta-analysis** 

Meta-analyses were not carried out as only one study (the KEYNOTE-689 study) reported clinical effectiveness data on pembrolizumab in the population of relevance to this appraisal. 

## **2.10 Indirect and mixed treatment comparisons** 

No indirect comparisons or mixed treatment comparisons were carried out as the KEYNOTE689 study provides direct evidence for the treatment comparison of relevance to this appraisal. Clinical opinion received (elicited as described in section 2.3.3) confirmed that the findings of the KEYNOTE-689 study are generalisable to UK clinical practice, including that the comparator arm of the study is reflective of current UK standard of care. 

## **2.11 Adverse reactions** 

## **Summary of adverse events information** 

- Pembrolizumab as neoadjuvant and continued as adjuvant treatment in combination with radiotherapy ± cisplatin followed by pembrolizumab monotherapy in participants with Stage IIII-VA resectable LA HNSCC has a manageable safety profile that is generally consistent with the well-established safety profile of pembrolizumab monotherapy and the individual safety profiles of RT and cisplatin. 

- No new safety concerns for pembrolizumab are identified. 

Based on the adverse events observed in the KEYNOTE-689 study, as described in this section, it can be seen that pembrolizumab as neoadjuvant and continued as adjuvant treatment in combination with radiotherapy ± cisplatin followed by pembrolizumab monotherapy in participants with Stage IIII-VA resectable LA HNSCC has a manageable safety profile that is generally consistent with the well-established safety profile of pembrolizumab monotherapy and the individual safety profiles of RT and cisplatin. 

Adverse events of special interest (AEOSI) in the pembrolizumab + SOC group are generally consistent with the established safety profile of pembrolizumab monotherapy in type and

## **2.11.1 KEYNOTE-689 all comer overall population** 

A summary of the adverse events of the KEYNOTE-689 study (at the 25-JUL-2024 database cut-off date) are provided below for the all comer overall population. Detailed adverse event information are provided in Appendix D. 

## _**2.11.1.1 Adverse Event Summary**_ 

The incidence and types of AEs, including drug-related AEs, AEs leading to death, and Grade 3 to 5 AEs in the pembrolizumab + SOC group were similar to the SOC group (<10% difference in incidence). The incidence of SAEs and AEs leading to treatment discontinuation was higher in the pembrolizumab + SOC group compared with the SOC group (≥10% difference in incidence). In the high-risk category, the incidence of SAEs was higher in the pembrolizumab + SOC group compared with the SOC group. In the low-risk category, SAEs, drug-related SAEs, drug-related Grade 3 to 5, discontinuation due to an AE, discontinuation due to a drugrelated AE, and discontinuation due to SAE was higher in the pembrolizumab + SOC group compared with the SOC group.

## **2.12 Ongoing studies** 

The KEYNOTE-689 study is ongoing and may provide additional evidence in the next 12 months for the indication being appraised (a subsequent interim analysis may be available based on a database lock date in ***** , however as the KEYNOTE-689 study is an eventdriven study the database lock date for predefined interim analyses cannot be definitively determined beforehand). 

## **2.13 Interpretation of clinical effectiveness and safety evidence** 

Efficacy results from KEYNOTE-689 at IA1 show that perioperative pembrolizumab provides a statistically significant and clinically meaningful improvement in EFS and a statistically significant improvement in mPR compared with adjuvant SOC RT ± cisplatin in treatmentnaïve participants with newly diagnosed Stage III-IVA resectable locoregionally advanced HNSCC. The point estimate of OS HR favours perioperative pembrolizumab versus SOC. The improvements in EFS and mPR, and favourable trend in OS, were consistent across the PDL1 CPS ≥1, and all participant populations. 

There ***** in the change from baseline in EORTC QLQ-C30 of EQ-5D VAS scores between the pembrolizumab and SOC groups in the CPS ≥1 population at post adjuvant RT ± cisplatin Week 25 and Week 51, indicating no negative effects of adding pembrolizumab treatment. 

The results of the KEYNOTE-689 study also showed that pembrolizumab as neoadjuvant and continued as adjuvant treatment in combination with RT ± cisplatin followed by pembrolizumab monotherapy in participants with Stage III-IVA resectable LA HNSCC has a manageable safety profile that is generally consistent with the well-established safety profile of pembrolizumab monotherapy and the individual safety profiles of RT and cisplatin. No new safety concerns for pembrolizumab are identified.

Standard care for resectable locally advanced HNSCC has remained relatively constant since 2004, when two pivotal randomized trials (European Organization for Research and Treatment of Cancer [EORTC] #22931 and Radiation Therapy Oncology Group [RTOG] #9501 (39, 40)) first established the addition of cisplatin to postoperative radiotherapy as the recommended treatment regimen for high-risk disease. The KEYNOTE-689 trial showed that the addition of neoadjuvant and adjuvant pembrolizumab to standard care conferred a significant improvement in event-free survival, reducing the risk of recurrence or progression by 30% among patients with resectable locally advanced HNSCC (41). The neoadjuvant pembrolizumab phase is a meaningful contributor to efficacy, potentiating early immune engagement to influence long-term outcomes, while the KEYNOTE-689 study also delivers positive results after previous trials in other adjuvant therapies in this indication have failed. This perioperative strategy increases immune system surveillance and demonstrably decreases the risk of disease recurrence The availability of pembrolizumab as an effective perioperative therapy in this indication therefore presents the first meaningful advancement in this setting in over 20 years, re-establish immunotherapy as a potential option in the curative setting, and represents a considerable step-change in the management of resectable locally advanced HNSCC.

## **3 Cost effectiveness** 

## **Summary of key cost effectiveness information** 

## **Objective:** 

- To model the cost-effectiveness of perioperative pembrolizumab plus standard of care (SOC; surgical resection followed by adjuvant radiotherapy ± chemotherapy) compared to SOC alone for patients with CPS≥1 resectable locally advanced head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (LA HNSCC), *****. 

## **Model structure:** 

- A systematic literature review (SLR) was conducted to identify cost-effectiveness analyses relevant to this decision problem. No previous studies or NICE technology appraisals were identified in the neoadjuvant or perioperative setting for LA HNSCC. 

- A _de novo_ four state Markov model was developed; event-free [EF], local/salvageable recurrence [L/SR], incurable recurrence/progression [IRP], and death. This structure captures the main elements of the disease course and heterogeneity in management of patients with LA HNSCC. 

## **Model inputs:** 

## _**Patient population inputs:**_ 

- The baseline characteristics were sourced from the KEYNOTE-689 trial. 

## _**Clinical efficacy inputs:**_ 

- Transition probabilities from the EF, L/SR, and IRP health states were derived from patient-level data from the KEYNOTE-689 trial. 

- Adverse event data were from the KEYNOTE-689 trial, pooled across both arms. 

## _**Utility inputs:**_ 

- The EQ-5D-5L was collected in the KEYNOTE-689 trial and mapped to EQ-5D-3L. 

- Measurements were pooled across treatment arms for the EF, L/SR and IRP preprogression health states, and a disutility for adverse events was applied. 

- Utility for the IRP state is split into pre-progression and post-progression to reflect the impact of progression on HRQoL. Due to limited events in the KEYNOTE-689 trial, utility for the IRP post-progression state was sourced from NICE TA473 (based on HRQoL data in the EXTREME trial).

## _**Costs and resource use inputs:**_ 

- Resource use associated with management in the EF state was obtained from UK clinical experts at an advisory board, meanwhile resource use in the downstream L/SR and IRP states was based on previous NICE appraisals in (recurrent/metastatic [R/M]) HNSCC. 

- Unit costs were sourced primarily from NHS reference costs, and drug acquisition costs were taken from the BNF and eMIT. 

## **Base-case results and sensitivity analyses:** 

- The base case incremental cost-effectiveness ratio (ICER) and ICERs in all one-way sensitivity and scenario analyses were below £20,000/QALY gained. 

- The probabilistic sensitivity analysis generated an ICER of *****, showing the model results to be robust, and indicated that there was a *****% probability that perioperative pembrolizumab is cost-effective at the £30,000/QALY threshold. 

## **Cost effectiveness conclusions:** 

- Treatment with perioperative pembrolizumab accrues quality-adjusted life years (QALYs) by increasing the number of years patients spend event-free. Similar to other (neo)adjuvant treatments, it is expected to increase the proportion of patients who achieve functional cure. The initial costs are offset to some degree by a reduction in the need for downstream care. 

- The model results demonstrate that perioperative pembrolizumab is a cost-effective addition to adjuvant standard of care for patients with resectable LA HNSCC. 

## **3.1 Published cost-effectiveness studies** 

A systematic literature review (SLR) was conducted on 9[th] April 2025. Searches were run from database inception, to identify economic evaluations in previously untreated, resectable patients with LA HNSCC. Full details on the methodology and findings are detailed in Appendix E. Three full-text publications met the inclusion criteria,(50-52) however none were from a UK perspective nor evaluated perioperative treatment regimens. No additional studies meeting the inclusion criteria were identified from the grey literature (bibliographic, conference, or HTA agency databases).

Of the six identified studies in Europe, two studies were in the overall head and neck cancer population, 3 across the oropharynx, hypopharynx, and larynx, and one study specific to the oropharynx only. ## **3.2 Economic analysis** 

No previous economic evaluations specific to the neoadjuvant or perioperative treatment setting in LA HNSCC have been identified (Appendix E), reflecting the lack of advancements and unmet need in this population. Only one previous technology, cetuximab in combination with RT for treatment of patients with LA HNSCC for whom all forms platinum-based chemotherapy are contraindicated, has previously been appraised by NICE in the LA setting (TA145).(4) As discussed in Section 1.1, the company does not consider TA145 to be applicable to the current decision problem as the population in the pivotal trial is based on patients who are not undergoing surgical resection; in addition, clinical experts expressed that cetuximab in LA HNSCC is very rarely used in practice and is reserved for patients with renal failure. 

In addition, pembrolizumab is the first perioperative (neoadjuvant followed by adjuvant) treatment for LA HNSCC to be evaluated by NICE in the UK. In the absence of published models in the perioperative setting, a _de novo_ economic model was developed to assess the cost-effectiveness of pembrolizumab as a neoadjuvant treatment followed by pembrolizumab and radiotherapy, plus or minus chemotherapy, as an adjuvant treatment for resectable LA HNSCC.

Figure 17 illustrates the specific health states and allowable transitions in the Markov model. The model consists of four mutually exclusive health states (i.e., event-free [EF], local or salvageable recurrence [L/SR], incurable recurrence/progression [IRP], and death) to track the disease course and survival of patients over time. 

The model structure differentiates health states by type of recurrence (either L/SR or IRP) depending on the site of recurrence (local or distant) and whether it is considered to be salvageable or not. The definition of the two recurrence health states is as follows: 

- **Local or salvageable recurrence (L/SR):** A patient has an EFS event of recurrence or progression and has received any subsequent surgery, or any subsequent oncological systemic therapy or radiation recorded as ‘with _Curative Intent’_ in the patient case report form, or none of the above and the EFS event is recorded as ‘Local PD/Recurrence’ confirmed with clinical approval 

- **Incurable recurrence/progression (IRP)** : A patient has an EFS event of recurrence or progression and received either subsequent oncological systemic therapy or oncological radiation recorded as ‘ _Recurrent/Metastatic/Incurable_ ’ in the patient case report form, or none of the above and EFS event is recorded as ‘ _Distant PD_ ’ or ‘ _Local and Distant PD_ ’ 

This definition of the recurrence health states reflects the management of patients in the KEYNOTE-689 trial post-recurrence or progression, differentiating patients who received subsequent treatment with ‘curative intent’. As such, patients in the IRP state are nonsalvageable and therefore would not be eligible for subsequent surgery. This structure allows the economic model to account for the heterogeneity in management of HNSCC patients, whilst retaining the principles of model parsimony and transparency. These two types of recurrence are expected to have different implications on patients’ prognosis and therefore result in different health outcomes and costs.

Note: Arrows indicate allowable transitions between health states 

All patients entered the model in the EF state following diagnosis of resectable stage III-IVa LA HNSCC, with characteristics consistent with the KEYNOTE-689 trial patient population at baseline (see Table 24). Neoadjuvant/adjuvant therapy affects patients’ risks of transitioning directly from EF to L/SR, IRP, or death. Patients who enter the L/SR state may receive salvage surgery, radiotherapy or systemic oncologic therapy, and are at risk of transitioning from L/SR to IRP or death. Following IRP, patients are assumed to receive first-line therapy for recurrent/metastatic HNSCC and may also receive second-line therapy in this setting. The distribution of individuals across health states is used in conjunction with state-specific costs and utility values to estimate life years (LYs), quality-adjusted life years (QALYs), and costs. 

The health states and allowable transitions were defined such that EFS and OS curves can be generated using the Markov trace. This facilitated validations of the model against observed Kaplan-Meier curves from the trial and external data sources, where available. 

The model uses a weekly cycle length to allow for precise calculation of drug acquisition and administration costs. Half cycle correction was applied to costs and effectiveness for additional precision. As an exception, half-cycle correction was not applied to cost components that are incurred at the beginning of a cycle, including neoadjuvant/adjuvant drug acquisition and administration costs (recurring costs starting from week 0) and AE-related costs in each model arm (applied as a lump-sum cost at week 0).

The cost-effectiveness analysis was conducted using a lifetime time horizon to comprehensively capture differences in costs and outcomes between perioperative pembrolizumab + SOC and its comparator arm, consistent with the _“NICE Guide to the Methods of Technology Appraisal_ ” which recommends that the time horizon should be long enough to reflect the differences in costs and outcomes between the technologies being considered.(63) The starting age of the patient cohort at model entry was based on the average age of the KEYNOTE-689 trial population at baseline. To approximate a lifetime horizon, the base-case model was run for 40.1 years (equal to 100 years minus the starting age), by which point virtually all patients *****) in the Markov cohort have reached the death state. 

The impact of alternative time horizons was explored via sensitivity analyses. 

## **3.2.3 Intervention technology and comparators** 

## _**3.2.3.1 Perioperative pembrolizumab + SOC**_ 

The intervention, perioperative pembrolizumab + SOC (adjuvant radiotherapy [RT] with or without cisplatin), is implemented in the economic model as per the KEYNOTE-689 trial, adjusted for the anticipated administration regimen in UK clinical practice. Of note, and in line with current SOC, the addition of cisplatin to radiotherapy in the adjuvant setting is determined by whether or not a patient has high-risk pathological features as assessed post-surgery. Highrisk pathological features as per KEYNOTE-689 include the presence of positive margins (<1mm in the primary resection specimen) or positive extranodal extension (ENE; defined as an extension of SCC from within a lymph node through the fibrous capsule and into the surrounding connective tissue). UK clinical experts confirm these are reflective of UK practice.(49) 

In KEYNOTE-689, the perioperative pembrolizumab + SOC regimen was administered as follows: 

- Neoadjuvant phase: 

      - Pembrolizumab 200 mg intravenous (IV) every three weeks (Q3W) for a maximum of 2 cycles 

- Adjuvant phase, following surgical resection: 

   - Patients with high-risk pathological features receive pembrolizumab 200 mg IV on day 1 of each Q3W cycle for up to fifteen cycles plus standard of care radiotherapy

© Merck Sharp & Dohme (UK) Limited (2025). All rights reserved 




<!-- page 93 -->

Confidential 

(see Section 3.2.3.2 below) and cisplatin 100 mg/m[2] intravenously on day 1 of each 3-week cycle for three cycles. 

- Patients without high-risk pathological features receive pembrolizumab 200 mg IV on day 1 of each Q3W cycle for fifteen cycles plus standard of care radiotherapy as adjuvant therapy 

Due to service capacity constraints, UK clinical experts indicated that in the adjuvant setting pembrolizumab is expected to be administered every 6 weeks (Q6W) at a flat dose of 400 mg. This is reflected in the base case economic model, whereby pembrolizumab administered in the adjuvant setting is assumed to be administered as 1 cycle of pembrolizumab 200 mg followed by up to 7 cycles of 400 mg Q6W. The initial dose was assumed to be 200 mg to reflect closer patient monitoring as they reinitiate treatment with pembrolizumab after surgery, and to prevent delivering a higher total dose of pembrolizumab over the full treatment schedule than is specified in the protocol. A scenario analysis is provided where adjuvant pembrolizumab is administered as 200 mg Q3W for up to 15 cycles as per the trial to evaluate the impact on model results. 

Some variation in cisplatin use is seen across clinical practice in the UK whereby cisplatin may be administered 40 mg/m[2] once weekly (QW). However, UK clinical experts advised that many centres use the Q3W regimen as this allows for better treatment persistence and flexibility in administration, therefore the dosing as per KEYNOTE-689 trial is considered generalisable to the UK.(49) 

## _**3.2.3.2 SOC**_ 

The comparator included in the economic model mirrors the KEYNOTE-689 trial, consisting of surgical resection followed by adjuvant radiotherapy plus a maximum of 3 cycles of cisplatin 100 mg/m[2] Q3W for patients with high-risk pathological features (as defined above) or radiotherapy alone for patients without high-risk pathological features. 

As part of SOC in both arms, radiotherapy consists of 2 Gy per day in 30 fractions (total of 60 Gy) for low-risk patients, 33 fractions (total of 66 Gy) for high-risk patients, and 35 fractions (total of 70 Gy) for patients with gross residual disease. Radiotherapy is costed based on the proportion of patients in both arms from KEYNOTE-689 who started RT and the mean number of fractions received in the adjuvant setting, pooled across both arms (further details of implementation in section 3.5.4).

## **3.3.2 Modelling transitions from the EF state** 

Transition probabilities starting from the EF state were estimated based on survival analyses of individual patient-level data from the KEYNOTE-689 trial, following the parametric multistate modelling approach described by Williams et al. (2017a & 2017b).(64, 65) Parametric models were used to estimate the cause-specific hazards of each transition (i.e., EF → L/SR, EF → IRP, and EF → death) over time within the perioperative pembrolizumab + SOC and SOC arms of the trial. Within each weekly cycle of the model, the probability of each of these transitions (as well as the composite probability of any EFS failure event) were calculated as a function of all three cause-specific hazards. 

## _**3.3.2.1 Estimation of cause-specific hazards for each individual transition starting from the EF state**_ 

In order to fit parametric models to each of the three health state transitions, standard survival analysis methods were used with one modification to account for competing risks: when analysing time to each specific type of EFS failure, the two competing failure types were treated as censoring events.(66) For example, to model the transition from EF to IRP, patients who experience a L/SR or death prior to IRP were censored at the time of the earlier competing event. After these additional censoring criteria were applied to the patient-level time-to-event data for each transition, parametric curve fitting was performed using the survival analysis package _flexsurvreg_ in R software. 

The following three parametric modelling approaches were used to explore uncertainty in the estimation of transition probabilities starting from the EF state: 

- Approach #1: Parametric models separately fitted to each treatment arm: Transition probabilities were estimated based on parametric models that were fitted individually to each treatment arm of the KEYNOTE-689 trial. Seven different parametric functions (exponential, Weibull, Gompertz, log-logistic, log-normal, gamma, and generalized gamma) were considered to model each transition from the EF state (i.e., EF → L/SR, EF → IRP, EF → death) in each treatment arm. 

- Approach #2: Parametric proportional hazards models with a time-constant treatment effect: Transition probabilities in the neoadjuvant pembrolizumab / adjuvant pembrolizumab + SOC and SOC arms were estimated based on jointly fitted models from the proportional hazards class (i.e., exponential, Weibull, or Gompertz) that incorporated a time-constant binary indicator equal to 1 in the perioperative

© Merck Sharp & Dohme (UK) Limited (2025). All rights reserved 




<!-- page 96 -->

Confidential 

pembrolizumab + SOC arm and 0 in the SOC arm of KEYNOTE-689. The models thus assumed a time-constant hazard ratio (HR) for perioperative pembrolizumab + SOC versus SOC in KEYNOTE-689. 

• Approach #3: Parametric proportional hazards models with a time-varying treatment effect (before and after year 1): Transition probabilities in the perioperative pembrolizumab + SOC and SOC arms of the model were estimated based on jointly fitted models from the proportional hazards class that used a time-varying HR for pembrolizumab versus observation in KEYNOTE-689. Specifically, the parametric models under Approach #3 incorporated a time-constant binary indicator equal to 1 in the perioperative pembrolizumab arm and 0 in the SOC arm of KEYNOTE-689. Beyond the first year follow up a time-varying binary indicator equal to 1 in the perioperative pembrolizumab + SOC arm and 0 for the SOC arm was applied. The models thereby allowed the treatment effect to differ during versus after the first year following initiation of adjuvant therapy. The allowance of a differing treatment effect during the first year versus following years is based on the protocol-defined maximum treatment duration of approximately 1 year. 

Parameter estimates associated with all parametric models under Approaches #1, 2, and 3 are reported in Appendix J1. 

For each of the two model arms, probabilities of each transition from the EF state were calculated based on all three cause-specific hazard functions. The predicted EFS curve over time in each treatment arm similarly depended upon all three cause-specific hazard functions. Therefore, in order to select base-case parametric functions, and across the three approaches described above, a total 397 (possible parametric functions combinations for EF → L/SR, EF → IRP, and EF → death were considered (Appendix J1). Criteria for the selection of basecase parametric functions are described below in Section 3.3.2.3.

## _**3.3.2.3 Selection of base-case parametric models for transitions from EF state**_ 

As noted by the NICE Decision Support Unit (DSU) Technical Support Document (TSD) 19, assessing model fit is more challenging in the context of multistate models than partitioned survival models, as the target outcomes of interest (e.g., the proportions of individuals experiencing the composite endpoint) are determined by a combination of survival models rather than by a single survival model.(66) 

Therefore, to select base case parametric functions, all 397 possible combinations of parametric functions for EF → L/SR, EF → IRP, and EF → death (across the 3 approaches, as described in section 3.3.2.1) were considered (see Appendix J1). In accordance with 

Company evidence submission template for Pembrolizumab before surgery (neoadjuvant) then with radiotherapy after surgery (adjuvant) for newly diagnosed resectable, locally advanced, squamous cell head and neck cancer [ID6477] 

© Merck Sharp & Dohme (UK) Limited (2025). All rights reserved

recommendations in the NICE DSU TSD 14 which states that unless there is clear and strong evidence against (i.e. pathophysiological, clinical or other rationale), base-case parametric functions should be selected such that the same functional form is used to model each health state transition in both the perioperative pembrolizumab + SOC and SOC arms. The rationale for this approach is to prevent the extrapolated portion of the EFS curves from following drastically different trajectories between these two model arms, as noted in NICE DSU TSD 14.(69) 

The appropriateness of the base case parametric functions was assessed using the following criteria: 

## • Statistical fit based on mean squared error (MSE) vs. observed EFS 

Akaike information criterion (AIC), a fit statistic commonly used in partitioned survival models, is not a suitable measure of fit with observed data when modelling competing risks.(64) MSE was therefore used as an alternative diagnostic test to assess fit of the predicted EFS curve versus the observed Kaplan-Meier curve during the within-trial period in each treatment arm. Specifically, MSE was calculated based on the average of the squared difference in predicted versus observed EFS at weekly intervals across the within-trial period, with weighting by number of patients at risk in each weekly interval. 

In addition, the assumption of proportional hazards was assessed through formal statistical tests to evaluate the potential suitability of Approach #2. Namely, for each transition, the function _cox.zph()_ in R was used to test for independence between time and the scaled Schoenfeld residuals from a Cox proportional hazards model with a timeconstant treatment covariate. The proportional hazard assumption is supported by a non-significant relationship between residuals and time. 

- Visual assessment of modelled vs. observed EFS 

Predictions generated by different combinations of parametric functions were visually verified against the observed data in each trial arm, following the approach used by Williams et al. (2017).(64) Specifically, predicted versus observed cumulative incidence curves were plotted for each of the three individual transitions starting from the EF state. The resulting predictions of EFS as a composite endpoint were also compared against the observed EFS Kaplan-Meier curve in each arm. Of note, the KEYNOTE-689 trial provided ~5 years of follow-up data which allowed for a robust assessment of modelled versus observed EFS during the trial period.

## • Clinical plausibility and external validity of long-term extrapolations 

A targeted literature review was used to identify real-world studies reporting long-term EFS and OS for SOC conducted in the resectable LA HNSCC population for external validation of modelled longer-term extrapolations from the economic model. A summary of identified studies is presented in Appendix J1.4. Due to the heterogeneity evident in head and neck cancer patients, none of the identified studies were considered generalisable to the KEYNOTE-689 population, in particular with regards to anatomical site which can be a strong determinant of prognosis. Regardless, these studies demonstrate the range of plausible outcomes for LA HNSCC to inform the long-term pattern of recurrence and survival. 

Due to the lack of previous neoadjuvant or perioperative treatment strategies in resectable LA HNSCC, identified studies reflect the adjuvant setting only and report disease-free survival (DFS), as is common practice in the adjuvant setting. This causes a discrepancy between the starting time (randomisation post-surgery for patients that have survived and are disease free at study entry) and the time at risk for a subsequent recurrence event, for the adjuvant studies vs the perioperative KEYNOTE-689 study. In adjuvant studies, early progressions precluding surgical resection, or deaths directly associated with surgery, are by definition excluded from the study population, and as such the trials may report improved survival outcomes compared with studies where follow-up starts prior to surgery as in KEYNOTE-689. No studies were identified reporting EFS to allow for external validation of SOC. As such no direct comparisons between DFS and EFS can be made. However, KEYNOTE-689 has substantial followup vs other early-stage studies (approximately 5 years) which enables a robust internal validation for EFS. 

With regards to OS, the extensive trial follow-up also enabled assessment of the internal validity of the OS extrapolations. As the primary censoring rules used in the EFS and OS analyses of the KEYNOTE-689 trial differed, it was necessary to reconcile the censoring rules used for EFS and OS to enable this validation – further details are provided in section 3.14 and Appendix J4. In addition, three studies (albeit with similar limitations as described above for EFS) reported long-term survival beyond the KEYNOTE-689 trial follow-up period to allow some validation of extrapolated long-term OS outcomes on SOC in current clinical practice.

## _**Curve selection process:**_ 

The distribution selection process first selected the distribution for the cause-specific hazards of EF → death, in line with the approach previously taken and accepted in NICE TA1017.(55) An assessment of summarised fit statistics led to the reduction of the number of candidate combinations from 397 to 67. Subsequent steps in the process identified the most suitable distributions for the cause-specific hazards of EF → L/SR and EF → IRP, based on a close inspection of statistical and visual fit in conjunction with clinical plausibility among the 67 remaining combinations. 

**1. Statistical fit of EF**  **death based on MSE:** The MSE for predicted versus observed EFS was computed for each of the 397 candidate combinations of distributions, and divided into thirteen sets defined by approach and EFdeath distribution (seven sets of 49 combinations under Approach #1 [combinations of models individually fitted to each arm], three sets of 9 combinations under Approach #2 [combinations of models that can be parameterised under proportional hazards], and three sets of 9 combinations under Approach #3 [combinations of models that can be parameterised under time-varying proportional hazards beyond year 1]). The average and minimum MSE was summarised across all combinations of distributions within each set (see Appendix J1.1 for further details) with the conclusions summarised below: 

   - Under Approach #1, MSE statistics for predicted vs. observed EFS supported the 49 combinations of distributions that used generalized gamma for EF→death. In both arms of KEYNOTE-689, these 49 combinations had the lowest average MSE and lowest minimum MSE out of the seven sets of 49 combinations using different EF→death distributions under Approach #1. 

   - Under Approach #2, MSE statistics supported the 9 combinations of distributions that used Gompertz for EF→death, which in both arms had the lowest average MSE and lowest minimum MSE out of the three sets of 9 combinations using different distributions for EF→death under Approach #2

2. **Visual assessment of fit vs observed EF failure events:** Cumulative incidence graphs were generated to compare observed versus predicted curves from the 67 different combinations of parametric functions remaining after Step 1 (see Appendix J1.2 for further details and associated figures). Visual inspection led to the exclusion of all but 16 combinations of parametric distributions under approaches #1-3: 

   - Under Approach #1, 12 combinations that use Gompertz or generalized gamma for EFIRP and that do not use exponential for EFL/SR 

   - Under Approach #2, 2 combinations that use Gompertz for EFIRP and that do not use exponential for EFL/SR 

   - Under Approach #3, 2 combinations that use Gompertz for EFIRP and that do not use exponential for EFL/SR 

3. **Statistical assessment of fit:** All 67 combinations of parametric functions that modelled EF death using generalized gamma under Approach #1 or Gompertz under Approach #2 or #3 were ranked for statistical fit based on MSE for predicted versus observed EFS (full details available in Appendix J1.3. Consistent with findings from the visual assessment, the corresponding 16 combinations identified all ranked in the top half for best statistical fit. 

Of note, the proportional hazards assumption could not be rejected for EFIRP or EFdeath, but was rejected for EFL/SR (p=0.0351). Schoenfeld residual plots, presented in Appendix J1.3, are non-horizontal suggesting potential violation of the proportional hazards assumption. Thus, the 2 combinations of parametric functions under Approach #2 were excluded from further consideration for the base case, but were assessed further in scenario analyses. 

MSE values were generally higher in magnitude in the SOC arm than the perioperative pembrolizumab + SOC arm, and therefore the choice of base case distributions prioritised statistical fit in SOC. Subsequent assessments of external validity and clinical plausibility therefore focused primarily on the 10 of the remaining 14

4. **Internal and external validations of predicted OS for SOC:** Predicted OS in the SOC arm for the remaining 10 best-fitting combinations was validated against observed OS data from KEYNOTE-689; all combinations provided an excellent fit to the observed OS data. OS data from published real-world cohort studies (see Appendix J1.4 for summary of real-world studies) among patients with resectable LA HNSCC, presented in Figure 18, were also used to assess external validity of extrapolations. 

As previously discussed, there is a wide heterogeneity amongst the LA HNSCC population that is reflected in the patient characteristics of the identified real-world studies, resulting in a wide range of long-term OS outcomes and limiting generalisability to the KEYNOTE-689 population (see Appendix J1.4). Specifically, Burbure et al and Chen et al included only hypopharyngeal patients who historically have a worse prognosis compared with other anatomical sites,(70, 71) whilst Leeman et al primarily included patients with oropharyngeal disease,(22) of which 48% were HPV-positive which is known to have better prognosis than HPV-independent disease. 

Consequently, no further exclusions could be concluded based on external validations of OS; however, the modelled OS for the SOC arm falls within the range of the external studies and is consistent with the comparative outcomes expected based on the differences in anatomical site described above, demonstrating that the predicted outcomes are within the range of plausible outcomes. Regardless of the magnitude of OS, all external studies demonstrate a consistent shape in the long-term survival curves, which are supportive of the modelled extrapolations for the SOC arm in the short-term and long-term OS prediction.

5. **Clinical plausibility of the predicted EFS and OS benefit:** The incremental EFS and OS benefit of perioperative pembrolizumab + SOC relative to SOC was assessed under the 10 finalist combinations of parametric distributions (see Appendix J1.5). 

All 10 combinations yielded reasonably close predictions of the observed incremental EFS and OS benefit during the available trial period. Beyond the trial period, at the 10year time point, all but 1 of the 10 finalist combinations predicted incremental EFS and OS benefits of ≥8 percentage points, and ≥9 percentage points under 8 of the 10 finalist combinations. The log-normal / Gompertz / generalized gamma combination under Approach #1 yielded outlying estimates of incremental EFS and OS benefits (6.7 and 6.8 percentage points, respectively) relative to the other combinations of distributions, in addition to a clinically implausible implied EFS HR that exceeds 1 by 4 years (contradicting the observed trial data); this combination was nevertheless retained for further consideration in a highly conservative scenario analysis to represent the lower bound of incremental effectiveness. 

Of note, clinical expert opinion to the company indicated that patients remaining EF at 5 years would be considered cured, and subsequently discharged, and an observed plateau in EFS would be expected in both arms. The EFS curve using Gompertz / Gompertz / Generalised gamma demonstrates a plateau in EFS in line with clinical experts’ expected cure pattern, however this same plateau is not observed in the lognormal / Gompertz / generalized gamma combination under Approach #1 (see Figure 22). 

## Base case 

Based on the findings described above, one of the 10 finalist combinations of distributions was chosen as the base case. 

The selected base case combination was Gompertz / Gompertz / generalized gamma under Approach #1, based on both visual and statistical fit, and clinical plausibility. The Gompertz function from EF → IRP was the preferred choice of distribution on the basis of visual inspection. Further, the combination of Gompertz / Gompertz / generalized gamma under Approach #1 had the best MSE ranking in the SOC arm among the combinations of distributions that used Gompertz for EF → IRP, and provides a mid-range incremental benefit amongst the finalist combinations. ## Cure point 

Clinical expert opinion to the company indicated that the majority of recurrences in LA HNSCC would occur in the first two years and that patients remaining EF at 5 years after the initiation of treatment would be considered functionally cured and subsequently discharged (although they noted that the risk of recurrence never becomes zero).(49) The modelled EFS, under the base case selection of curves for transitions from the EF health state, for both arms (Figure) demonstrates a plateau from approximately 5 years, in addition to the implied hazard rates of EFS failure in both arms showing a very low risk of recurrence or death by year 5 in the economic model (Figure 23). This suggests that potential for cure is already accounted for. Thus, in this instance the application of an additional cure assumption in the base case 

Company evidence submission template for Pembrolizumab before surgery (neoadjuvant) then with radiotherapy after surgery (adjuvant) for newly diagnosed resectable, locally advanced, squamous cell head and neck cancer [ID6477] 

© Merck Sharp & Dohme (UK) Limited (2025). All rights reserved 




<!-- page 109 -->

Confidential 

economic model may overestimate, and potentially double count, for the likelihood of cure. Therefore, and in contrast to several previous appraisals in early-stage cancer indications (TA569, TA632, TA746, TA837, TA1017, TA1037)(55, 57, 59, 72-74) no explicit cure assumption is applied in the base case economic model. A scenario analysis explores the impact of applying an instantaneous cure assumption at 5 years with a 95% risk reduction in recurrence or death on model results. 

Of note, the plateau in EFS and implied hazard rates of EFS failure seen in the base case are specific to the distributions selected for transitions from the EF health state. Therefore, the decision to apply a cure assumption is determined by the combination of curves selected in terms of hazard profile and predicted survival. This same profile is not seen across all the finalist combinations, such as those included in the scenario analysis (see Figure 22), and therefore under different distribution selections it may be appropriate to apply a cure assumption in order to capture the expected plateau in EFS across both arms.

## **3.3.3 Modelling transitions from the L/SR state** 

To estimate the cause-specific hazards of transitions from the L/SR state (L/SR  IRP and L/SR  death), exponential models were fitted to patient-level data from the KEYNOTE-689 CPS≥1 population for each arm. The exponential distribution is commonly assumed when estimating transition probabilities starting from intermediate health states in a Markov model, as the hazard rate does not depend on time since entry into the health state.(75) In the PDL1 CPS ≥1 population, the analytical sample included ***** who experienced L/SR as their first EFS failure event. Among these patients, exponential parametric functions were fitted to time (in weeks) from L/SR state entry until IRP to estimate the cause-specific hazard of L/SR → IRP, and similarly time from L/SR state entry until death for L/SR → death. Patients were censored at the last date that the patient was known to be alive or upon experiencing the competing event type (for example, when modelling the cause-specific hazards of L/SR → IRP, patients were censored at the earliest of death or date that the patient was last known to be alive). 

Within each model cycle, the transition probability from L/SR → death was set equal to the maximum of the estimated probability based on parametric modelling and background mortality.

## **3.3.4 Modelling transitions from the IRP state** 

Similar to the approach used to model transitions starting from L/SR (Section 3.3.3), exponential models fitted to patient-level data from KEYNOTE-689 were used to estimate the cause-specific hazard of the IRP → death transition in each trial arm. The analytical sample included a total of ***** patients who experienced IRP either as their first EFS failure event (*****; ***** in the perioperative pembrolizumab + SOC arm and ***** in the SOC arm) or who first experienced L/SR followed by IRP as a subsequent recurrence event *****; ***** in the perioperative pembrolizumab + SOC arm and ***** in the SOC arm). Among these patients, exponential parametric functions were fitted to time from IRP state entry until death (or until censoring at the end of data or loss of follow-up). The resulting hazard rates are presented in Table 31. 

As with other transitions to death, the transition probability from IRP → death in each weekly model cycle was set equal to the maximum of the estimated probability based on parametric modelling and background mortality. Of note, as with the transitions starting from the L/SR state, the transition from IRP to death was modelled using exponential distributions, as the memoryless property of Markov models prevents the use of transition probabilities that depend on time spent in an intermediate health state.(75) Internal validations of predicted versus observed cumulative incidences IRP → death are presented for each arm in Figure 26 and demonstrate that the exponential models provide a good fit to the observed data. 

The impact of varying the exponential rate for transitions from IRPDeath within the 95% confidence intervals is explored in the sensitivity analyses. In addition, the potential impact of using longer- or shorter-tailed distributions for this transition was explored in sensitivity analyses that varied the rates of OS and PFS failure associated with first-line treatments in the IRP state. As OS is modelled using trial data directly in the base case, this only impacts the ratio of OS and PFS which in turn determines costs and utilities based on pre- and postprogression in the IRP health state.
