As a scenario analysis, an alternative approach is considered in which the transition probabilities from IRP to death in each treatment arm are assumed to depend on the efficacy and market shares of subsequent treatments in the IRP state. Specifically, in each treatment arm, mean progression-free survival (PFS) and OS within the IRP state were estimated based on the market shares and efficacy of first-line treatments for recurrent/metastatic HNSCC received in that arm. The model included first-line treatment options that had relevant PFS and OS inputs available (Table 52 in Section 3.5.2.3) and that are recommended in UK clinical practice. Further details on this scenario analysis are provided in Appendix J2. Despite its complexities and data limitations, this is a common approach in previous NICE TA for earlystage indications due to immature trial data precluding estimation of this transition directly from the trial. However, the IA1 DBL of KEYNOTE-689 has sufficient follow-up and events to enable estimating transitions from IRP  death using trial data directly, which reduces the modelling complexity and reliance on external data. 

## **3.3.5 Adverse events** 

The inclusion of specific AEs within the economic model was based on a combination of the risk and severity of each event. The model considered AEs occurring in the neoadjuvant and adjuvant (i.e. perioperative) settings only; AEs associated with subsequent treatments in the metastatic setting were not considered due to their expected small impact on the costeffectiveness results. The model considered all-cause grade 3+ AEs that occurred with a frequency of ≥5% in either treatment arm. 

Risks of the included AEs for patients treated with perioperative pembrolizumab + SOC and SOC were obtained from KEYNOTE-689 (all comer population), based on the proportions of patients with all-cause grade 3-5 AEs reported for the all-participants-as-treated (APaT) population (Table 18). 

Mean duration per AE episode and mean number of episodes per patient with each included AE were collected from KEYNOTE-689 (pooling across both trial arms) and were used within the model to estimate the duration of the disutility impact from each AE regardless of treatment arm. The percent of AEs resulting in hospitalizations were also collected from KEYNOTE-689 (pooling across both trial arms) and used to calculate the cost per AE episode (see Section

## **3.4 Measurement and valuation of health effects** 

An SLR was conducted to identify published studies reporting health-related quality of life (HRQoL) or utility data for patients with LA HNSCC. Additional searches were conducted to identify utility data for the recurrent/metastatic setting to help inform the economic model. Full details on the methodology and findings of the SLR, including search terms, PRISMA diagram and outcomes are detailed in Appendix F, and a summary of identified studies is provided in 3.4.3. 

## **3.4.1 Health-related quality-of-life data from clinical trials** 

## _**3.4.1.1 KEYNOTE-689**_ 

HRQoL was measured in KEYNOTE-689 using the EORTC-QLQ-C30, EORTC-QLQ-H&N35 instrument, and the EuroQoL EQ-5D-5L instruments. The NICE STA guidelines state that the EQ-5D is the preferred tool to measure HRQoL and that the economic model should consider HRQoL data collected directly from patients in the relevant clinical study to inform the utility weights,(63) therefore the EQ-5D trial data were analysed for use in the economic evaluation. 

In KEYNOTE-689, the EQ-5D-5L questionnaire was completed by participants at various time points, including the pre-surgery and post-surgery periods. During the pre-surgery period, the EQ-5D-5L questionnaire was administered on weeks 1 and 4 (± 3 days) and then again in week 6 (± 10 days) in the perioperative pembrolizumab + SOC arm. The EQ-5D-5L questionnaire was administered once before surgery in the SOC arm. During the post-surgery treatment period, the EQ-5D-5L questionnaire was completed in conjunction with radiotherapy ± cisplatin treatment prior to treatment administration. During post-treatment follow-up period, the EQ-5D-5L questionnaire was completed 30 days (± 14 days) from the last dose, and then every three months from last scan (± 7 days) for up to end of year 3 and every 12 months (± 14 days) in years 4 and 5. 

Aligned with the economic model, utility values were calculated for the following states based on the average across all patient visits with an EQ-5D-5L measurement within that state, within the all comer population: 

- EF (without grade 3+ AEs; which includes patient-visits in the EF state while patients had no AEs or solely grade 1-2 AEs); 

- EF (with grade 3+ AEs; which includes patient-visits in the EF state while patients had grade 3+ AEs);

Utility values were estimated via descriptive analyses of patient-level EQ-5D-5L data from the IA1 data cut of KEYNOTE-689 and consisted of the PRO full analysis set (PRO-FAS), defined as all randomized participants who received at least one dose of study treatment and have at least one valid EQ-5D endpoint assessment. Each EQ-5D response from KEYNOTE-689 was categorised into one of these health states (based on a determination of the patient’s health state at the time of collection of each response) and included in the utility analysis accordingly. At each available patient-visit, the corresponding EQ-5D-5L score was used to characterize utility. Baseline measurements were excluded from the analysis, along with patient-visits with missing EQ-5D-5L responses. Compliance to the EQ-5D assessments was very good and remained over *****% in both treatment arms for all timepoints up to week 129 (see Appendix K). Summary statistics were computed based on multiple records per participant, which were treated as independent observations. 

The analyses were pooled across treatment arms to estimate the average utility for all patients in the trial, as there was no clinically meaningful difference in HRQoL observed between the treatment arms in either the neoadjuvant or adjuvant phases of the KEYNOTE-689 trial (section 2.6.1.6 and 2.6.1.7). Any differences in HRQoL as a result of adverse events of treatment were captured by the application of treatment-specific adverse event disutilities (section 3.4.4). It is therefore assumed that any HRQoL impact of a reduction in adjuvant cisplatin use in the pembrolizumab arm is captured by the adverse event disutility, however this may not fully capture the HRQoL benefit of avoiding of adjuvant chemotherapy. This approach also maximises the available data and is consistent with previous appraisals of early-stage cancers (e.g. NICE TA766, TA830, TA837, TA851, TA1017).(54-58) To reflect health preferences in the general UK population, patient responses to the EQ-5D-5L questionnaire were mapped onto the UK EQ-5D-3L value set using the crosswalk developed by Hernández Alava et al. (2023) in accordance with Section 4.3.16 of NICE's updated manual for health technology evaluations.(61, 63) 

It was not possible to generate utility values for pre- versus post-progression in the IRP health state as the available follow-up data from KEYNOTE-689 required to inform such analysis to date were too limited, and related to too few patients, to reliably capture the average utility over the entire post-progression disease course until death. ## **3.4.2 Mapping** 

As per NICE’s manual for reference case analyses, the EQ-5D-3L value set is preferred for the reference case analysis.(63) Therefore, the EQ-5D-5L measurements collected in KEYNOTE-689 were mapped to the EQ-5D-3L tool from which utilities from derived, using the mapping function and UK value set developed by the Decision Support Unit,(Hernández Alava et al. 2023) as recommended in the NICE methods guide.(61, 63) 

## **3.4.3 Health-related quality-of-life studies** 

## _**3.4.3.1 LA HNSCC**_ 

The SLR described in Appendix F was conducted to identify studies reporting utility values for patients with previously untreated LA HNSCC. No studies were identified that reported utility data specifically for resectable/resected LA HNSCC (i.e. aligned with the KEYNOTE-689 population); however, four publications reporting utilities for LA HNSCC, irrespective of resection status, were included. 

Of these, only one study was fully aligned with the NICE reference case. Smith et al, 2017 reported an EQ-5D utility value (disease-free: 0.7 [SD 0.03], n=564) for UK patients with N23 M0 HNSCC (including oropharyngeal, laryngeal, oral, hypopharyngeal or occult) within the PET-Neck pragmatic trial who had planned neck dissection either before or after primary chemoradiotherapy, or chemoradiotherapy with PET-CT management.(76) A range of utility values were available from the M-TAG utility study conducted to inform the NICE TA145 appraisal,(4) however whilst these were measured using the EQ-5D, the population surveyed

was nursing staff in oncology centres rather than HNSCC patients, and therefore the resulting values, while informative, are not aligned with the reference case. One additional study, TAX323/EORTC-24971 (Parthan et al, 2009), reported utility values collected via EORTC-QLQC30 and mapped to EQ-5D, from patients with unresectable LA HNSCC (stable, 0.7; progressive, 0.67; response, 0.79);(77) whilst not specified, as a UK CEA it is assumed to use the UK value set. 

## _**3.4.3.2 Progressed, recurrent HNSCC**_ 

As noted in section 3.4.1, it was not possible to generate utility values specifically for preversus post-progression in the IRP health state as the available follow-up from KEYNOTE689 trial was too limited to capture the average utility over the entire post-progression disease course until death. Therefore, external sources were considered to inform the IRP postprogression health state. 

A range of potential sources were identified via the utility SLR, targeted searches and internal MSD datasets. These are summarised in Table 34, and additional details are provided in Appendix F. Utility data available to MSD from KEYNOTE-048, a Phase 3 RCT of pembrolizumab ± chemotherapy versus cetuximab + chemotherapy in patients with incurable untreated R/M HNSCC, report a pooled post-progression utility that is higher than the IRP preprogression utility in KEYNOTE-689 (*****). Whilst this may seem counterintuitive, feedback from clinical experts to MSD was that whilst they would expect HRQoL to decrease on progression, in this specific case this observation is plausible as they would expect patients with _de novo_ metastatic disease to have better HRQoL than patients who recurred or progressed from LA disease, as a result of high morbidity following major surgery and CRT in the LA-recurrent group.(49) Only 27-32% of patients in KEYNOTE-048 had recurrent disease,(78) therefore a higher HRQoL in this study versus KEYNOTE-689 is not unexpected. However, consequently KEYNOTE-048 is not a useful source to inform the IRP postprogression utility in the current economic model. 

In NICE TA172/TA473, which assessed cetuximab for treating recurrent or metastatic HNSCC, EQ-5D-3L utility values obtained by mapping EORTC QLQ-C30 data collected from patients in the EXTREME trial were used.(62) For the post-progression state, the estimated utility value was 0.52; this could represent a suitable source to inform the IRP post-progression state, as it is logically consistent with the KEYNOTE-689 utility data and adequately captures the limited effective treatment options for patients at that stage of the treatment pathway.

## **3.4.5 Health-related quality-of-life data used in the cost-effectiveness analysis** 

As stated in the NICE methods guide, the preferred approach for incorporating HRQoL into the economic model is to collect health state measurements from patients relevant to the decision problem using the EQ-5D-3L tool, and the utility weights should be elicited from the UK general population.(63) Accordingly, for the EF, L/SR, and pre-progression IRP health states the base case analysis used utility values derived from the analyses of patient-level EQ-5D-5L data collected from the KEYNOTE-689 trial. The EQ-5D-5L measurements were mapped back to the EQ-5D-3L version of the tool using the NICE DSU algorithm(61) and utilities derived using the UK value set. A disutility for AEs was also estimated from the KEYNOTE-689 trial and applied as a one-off decrement in the first model cycle (Table 36). 

In line with the model structure, the IRP health state was comprised of two sub-states (preprogression and post-progression) to capture differences in outcomes and costs of patients who develop incurable recurrent/metastatic disease. As discussed in 3.4.1, EQ-5D data corresponding to post-progression were not available from KEYNOTE-689 as the available follow-up from the trial was too limited to enable a robust analysis of post-progression utility. Alternate sources were therefore reviewed for suitability to inform this parameter (see section

The utility value for progressive disease estimated based on EORTC-QLQ-C30 data collected in the EXTREME trial and mapped to EQ-5D (used in NICE TA172/TA473) was deemed the most appropriate source to inform the IRP post-progression health state, based on good general alignment with the NICE reference case and health state definition, and face validity with respect to the utilities from KEYNOTE-689 used to model the other health states. 

In each treatment arm, utility for the IRP state was then calculated as a weighted average of utility values in the pre- and post-progression IRP sub-states, based on the expected proportion of time spent pre- versus post-progression estimated using PFS and OS failure rates of first-line treatments as outlined in Appendix J2. ## _**3.4.5.1 Age-related disutility**_ 

The economic model accounted for disutility related to aging of the cohort over time, based on expected EQ-5D-3L by age and sex in the UK, as derived from Health Survey for England

(HSE) 2014 data.(80) Age-related disutility is applied starting from the end of the available within-trial period (i.e., 2.6 years, based on mean actual follow-up in KEYNOTE-689 at IA1), as the health state utilities derived from KEYNOTE-689 data already reflect the mean age of participants during the trial period. In each cycle _i_ thereafter, age-related disutility was computed as the utility corresponding to patients' age and gender distribution in cycle _i_ (as estimated using the general population utilities from HSE) minus the utility corresponding to patients' age and gender distribution at the end of the trial period (also estimated using the general population utilities from HSE).

## **3.5 Cost and healthcare resource use identification, measurement and valuation** 

An SLR was conducted to identify healthcare resource use and costs associated with treatment of LA HNSCC. All relevant search strategies, search identification, and methodology are presented in Appendix G. 

In line with the NICE reference case, the model took a UK National Health Service (NHS) and Personal Social Services (PSS) perspective and therefore only direct healthcare costs related to the treatment and management of LA HNSCC were considered. Evidence on resources used by patients in the treatment pathway were sourced from the KEYNOTE-689 trial and the published literature. Where trial data are used to inform inputs, the APaT population is used to account for the open-label nature of the KEYNOTE-689 trial and better reflect expected outcomes of patients receiving the respective treatment regimen. Healthcare costs were obtained from publicly available sources which primarily included the British National Formulary (BNF),(81) NHS Reference Costs,(82) and the Personal Social Services Research Unit (PSSRU) to ensure the model used the most up to date costs relevant to UK practice. These were supplemented by costs from published studies where relevant inputs from the public sources were not available. All costs are reported in 2024 GBP. 

## **3.5.1 Intervention and comparators’ costs and resource use** 

Drug acquisition and administration costs per infusion of neoadjuvant/adjuvant treatments were calculated in the model as a function of the list price per drug unit, defined dosing schedule and unit cost of drug administration. The proportions of patients remaining on each neoadjuvant/adjuvant drug component over time were based on observed data from KEYNOTE-689. 

## _**3.5.1.1 Drug acquisition costs**_ 

In the perioperative pembrolizumab + SOC and SOC treatment arms, the defined dosing schedules of drug components reflected the KEYNOTE-689 trial and anticipated licence (Table 37): 

- In the perioperative pembrolizumab + SOC arm, pembrolizumab is administered as a flat dose of 200 mg IV Q3W for up to 2 cycles in the neoadjuvant setting before surgery. In the adjuvant setting, to reflect clinical expert opinion that Q6W administration would be preferred to manage capacity,(49) pembrolizumab was assumed to be administered

However, to reflect closer patient monitoring as they reinitiate treatment with pembrolizumab after surgery, and to prevent delivering a higher total dose of pembrolizumab over the full treatment schedule than is specified in the protocol, it is assumed that the first dose in this setting will be 200 mg with the first 400 mg dose administered 3 weeks later. A scenario assuming only 200 mg Q3W dosing in the adjuvant phase for up to 15 cycles was also explored. 

- In both arms, high-risk patients received adjuvant cisplatin administered IV as a dose of 100 mg/m[2] Q3W for up to 3 cycles.

Unit drug prices were retrieved from the British National Formulary (BNF) for branded drugs and the electronic market information tool (eMIT) for generically available drugs.(81, 83) For generic drugs with multiple eMIT price listings for the same strength, the minimum price per unit was used. Additionally, price listings for a given strength were not used if a higher strength was available at a lower price per unit. A PAS with a simple discount is currently in place for pembrolizumab, reported in Appendix I; list prices are used for all other drugs, as any discounts in place are unavailable to MSD. 

For IV-administered drugs with weight-, AUC-, or BSA-based dosing, the base-case analysis assumed that vial-sharing is allowed. Under this assumption, the number of vials required per infusion was calculated based on average body weight, GFR, or BSA of patients in the model cohort. ## _**3.5.1.2 Drug administration costs**_ 

Unit costs of drug administration for both neoadjuvant/adjuvant and subsequent treatments were obtained from the NHS Reference Costs (Table 39),(82) and were applied according to the following principles: 

- For IV drug component(s) delivered on the first day of a treatment cycle, the unit cost for SB12Z (simple parenteral chemotherapy) in the outpatient setting was applied once if only one drug component (other than 5-FU) is delivered on that day. If multiple drug components are delivered on that day and 5-FU is not one of the drug components, the unit cost for SB13Z (complex parenteral chemotherapy) in the outpatient setting was applied once (covering the administration of all IV drug components delivered on that

© Merck Sharp & Dohme (UK) Limited (2025). All rights reserved

day). If multiple drug components are delivered on that day and 5-FU is one of the drug components, the unit cost for SB14Z (complex parenteral chemotherapy, including prolonged infusional treatment) in the outpatient setting was applied once (covering the administration of all IV drug components delivered on that day, as well as the prolonged administration of 5-FU spanning multiple days via a device such as a take-home pump). This approach is in line with the approach advised by the Cancer Drugs Fund lead in a recent pembrolizumab submission (TA983).(84) 

- For IV drug component(s) other than 5-FU that are delivered on subsequent days of a treatment cycle, the unit cost for SB15Z (subsequent elements of a chemotherapy cycle) in the outpatient setting was applied once per each subsequent day of the treatment cycle in which ≥1 IV drug component(s) are administered.

## _**3.5.1.4 Initial surgery and adjuvant radiotherapy costs**_ 

Costs associated with the initial surgery following neoadjuvant therapy and any post-surgery adjuvant radiotherapy were calculated based on the observed proportions of patients who underwent surgery as planned and who received post-surgery radiotherapy in KEYNOTE-689 (Table 42). Unit costs per surgery and per radiotherapy regimen were based on NHS Reference Costs. The cost per radiotherapy regimen was calculated as a fixed cost of initiating a radiotherapy regimen, plus an additional cost per week of radiotherapy multiplied by the observed average duration of a radiotherapy regimen (~6.4 weeks) among patients in KEYNOTE-689 who received adjuvant radiotherapy. The additional cost per week of radiotherapy was calculated as the cost per fraction of radiation multiplied by the planned number of fractions per week (i.e., 5 fractions/week, based on the KEYNOTE-689 trial protocol). 

Within the model, the timing of the costs of the initial surgery and any post-surgery radiotherapy was based on their average observed timing in KEYNOTE-689.

## **3.5.2 Health-state unit costs and resource use** 

## _**3.5.2.1 Disease management costs by health state**_ 

Medical resource use in the EF, L/SR, and IRP states includes outpatient provider visits, laboratory tests, and imaging procedures. Unit costs of medical resources were obtained from NHS Reference Costs (Table 45).(82) 

In the EF state, weekly frequencies of routine outpatient visits, laboratory tests, and CT scans were initially informed by clinical guidelines in head and neck cancer (UK National Multidisciplinary Guidelines)(1) and then refined based on clinical expert opinion obtained by 

Company evidence submission template for Pembrolizumab before surgery (neoadjuvant) then with radiotherapy after surgery (adjuvant) for newly diagnosed resectable, locally advanced, squamous cell head and neck cancer [ID6477] 

© Merck Sharp & Dohme (UK) Limited (2025). All rights reserved 




<!-- page 133 -->

Confidential 

MSD.(49, 85) Resource use in this state was modelled separately by treatment arm to capture the expected additional resource use associated with delivering and managing perioperative pembrolizumab. Other resources, such as dieticians and speech and language therapists, were not expected to differ by treatment and were therefore not included in the model. Frequencies were time-varying to account for the recommended change in the frequency of monitoring over time; monitoring would decrease after completion of adjuvant therapy (i.e. approximately year 2 onwards) and clinicians agreed that patients who remained event-free after 5 years would be discharged (Table 44). 

The IRP state encompasses both pre- and post-progression IRP. Therefore, in each model arm, disease management costs per week in the IRP state were computed as a weighted average of resource use associated with pre- versus post-progression IRP, based on the estimated proportion of time spent progression-free within the IRP state. Medical resource use frequencies per week before and after progression within the IRP state were based on sources and assumptions used in previous NICE submissions in the recurrent/metastatic HNSCC setting (including NICE TA490 and TA661) (Table 35).(86, 87) Specifically, TA490 assumed a monthly frequency of 1 oncologist visit, 1 cell blood count test, and 1 CT scan during initial therapy for recurrent/metastatic disease, and a monthly frequency of 0.33 oncologist visits and 0.33 cell blood count tests after discontinuation of initial therapy. These frequencies during and after initial therapy in NICE TA490 were applied to pre-progression and post-progression IRP, respectively, in the present model. Monthly frequencies were converted to weekly by dividing by (365.25/12/7). For other outpatient services, the percentages of patients using each service before and after progression were based on a medical chart review among UK patients with metastatic HNSCC who received ≥3 lines of systemic therapy (Nash Smyth et al. 2015),(88) the same source used to inform these inputs in TA490. As in TA490, the healthcare resource utilization results from Nash Smyth et al. were assumed to represent the monthly probability of using each service. ## _**3.5.2.2 L/SR health state**_ 

Patients who entered the L/SR health state were eligible for a range of treatment options including radiotherapy, salvage surgery or systemic therapies, as per the health state definition (section 3.2.2). As such, treatment in the L/SR state included one-time costs of radiotherapy, salvage surgery and/or systemic therapy for a proportion of patients who entered this state, based on the proportions of patients who received each of these therapies within this health state in the KEYNOTE-689 trial. 

## Subsequent radiotherapy and salvage surgery costs in the L/SR state 

Frequencies of radiotherapy and salvage surgery were based on observed percentages of patients with each type of treatment in the KEYNOTE-689 trial. The percentages of patients with salvage surgery and radiotherapy in the L/SR state were calculated using as the denominator the number of patients in KEYNOTE-689 who experienced L/SR as their first EFS failure event, pooling across both treatment arms (Table 46). 

Unit costs per salvage surgery and per radiotherapy course in the L/SR state were based on the same sources as those used to inform the unit costs of initial surgery and adjuvant radiotherapy, respectively, with the exception that the duration of salvage radiotherapy was conservatively assumed to be half that of the primary treatment course to reflect increased morbidity after recurrence (Table 46).

## Subsequent systemic therapy in the L/SR state 

Drug acquisition and administration costs associated with systemic therapies in the L/SR state were applied as a one-time cost upon entry into the state. Treatment options in the L/SR state and their dosing schedules were assumed to be the same as in the first-line IRP setting (see section 3.5.2.3). 

For systemic treatment regimens in the L/SR state, mean treatment durations were based on the observed mean durations of systemic treatments received in the L/SR state among patients in KEYNOTE-689 who experienced L/SR as their first EFS failure type (pooling across both treatment arms) (Table 47). Based on the estimated mean duration of each drug component in a regimen, the model estimated the mean total cost of the entire treatment regimen. 

In the base case analysis, in both arms the mix of systemic treatments in the L/SR state was based on observed subsequent treatment data among patients in KEYNOTE-689 who experienced L/SR as their first EFS failure event (Table 48), to ensure costs were aligned with the efficacy of drugs received by patients in the trial. As pembrolizumab + chemotherapy is not available in England, the observed market share of this regimen in the L/SR state in KEYNOTE-689 was redistributed to the other included regimens. 

However, UK clinical experts advised that the approach to managing patients with _nonsalvageable_ local recurrence in practice may not fully align with the approaches observed in the trial, as often these patients would be treated as per patients in the IRP state (i.e. systemic therapy without curative intent) and as such the degree of systemic therapy use in the L/SR state may underestimate what would be expected in UK clinical practice. Therefore, a scenario analysis was conducted in which the costs of systemic therapy in the L/SR state were assumed to equal the costs of systemic therapy in the IRP state.

## _**3.5.2.3 IRP health state**_ 

Within the model, drug acquisition and administration costs associated with subsequent therapies (including both first-line and second-line subsequent therapies) were applied as a one-time cost upon entry into the IRP state. A proportion of patients who entered the IRP state were assumed to receive an active first-line treatment for recurrent/metastatic HNSCC. The costs of second-line treatments for recurrent/metastatic HNSCC were also considered. Additional details are provided in the sub-sections below. 

## Unit drug costs and dosing schedules 

Drug acquisition cost per administration or pharmacy dispensing was calculated for drugs in the recurrent/metastatic HNSCC setting based on unit drug costs (Table 38) and defined dosing schedules (Table 49). The dosing schedules were based on prescribing information, treatment protocols in pivotal clinical trials, or clinical guidelines. 

Drug administration costs were applied according to the sources and principles described in section 3.5.1.2 (Table 39).

## Time on treatment of subsequent therapies 

First- and second-line treatments were selected for inclusion in the model based on available treatment options in the UK, verified by clinical experts,(49) and the second-line treatments observed in KEYNOTE-048 following ‘progressed disease’ state entry. 

The model estimated the mean total cost of each first- and second-line treatment regimen over the expected duration of each therapy. Durations of first-line treatment regimens for recurrent/metastatic HNSCC were modelled using the exponential rates of PFS failure to approximate treatment discontinuation rates for each treatment. Exponential rates of PFS failure for three reference treatments (including cetuximab + platinum + 5-FU from KEYNOTE048) were sourced from clinical trials and rates for all other treatments were estimated by applying HRs sourced from a network meta-analysis (NMA) of clinical trials to one of these reference regimens (Table 50).(97) See appendix J4 for further details of the NMA. Some regimens or components of regimens were subject to a maximum treatment duration based on recommended dosing schedules (Table 49). For second-line treatments, mean treatment durations were based on the observed mean durations of specific treatments received in the next line of therapy among patients in the KEYNOTE-048 trial (database cutoff date: 21-Feb2022)(Table 51).

## Mix of subsequent therapies 

The mean costs of first- and second-line treatments were then calculated for each perioperative treatment arm as a weighted average based on the first- and second-line treatment mix within each arm. In the base case, first-line treatment mix reflected observed first subsequent treatment use amongst patients who experienced IRP as their first EFS failure event in KEYNOTE-689. The model included first-line treatment options that had relevant PFS and OS inputs available, that are recommended by EHNS–ESMO–ESTRO clinical guidelines,(2) and may be used in the UK. The treatment mix of other first-line regimens (as observed in KEYNOTE-689) were distributed among the selected regimens in proportion to their observed usage as patients' first systemic treatment in the IRP state. Additionally, because pembrolizumab + chemotherapy is not recommended by NICE for this indication, the observed share of this regimen as first-line treatment in the IRP state in KEYNOTE-689 was also redistributed to the other included first-line regimens (note that the share was redistributed across all regimens rather than specifically pembrolizumab monotherapy, as patients who would receive the pembrolizumab + chemotherapy regimen are typically those with more aggressive disease who require rapid treatment, and may not be able to wait for the benefits of single-agent immunotherapy to kick in). 

The subsequent treatment use observed in the trial, and used in the base case model, was validated with UK clinical experts to ensure it was suitably reflective of clinical practice in the UK.(49) The experts advised that: 

- Approximately 70% of patients with IRP receive systemic first-line therapy, which is broadly aligned with patterns observed in the trial

- Of those receiving systemic therapy in current practice (i.e. after adjuvant SOC only), most patients (approximately 80%) would get anti-PD-1 treatment at first-line, which would usually be pembrolizumab monotherapy, but may be nivolumab in a few cases (and only if they had previously received adjuvant cisplatin) 

   - The overall pattern of anti-PD-1 use amongst treated patients with IRP in the trial (*****) was reasonably well aligned with UK practice, although it was slightly underestimated vs clinical opinion. However, nivolumab use may be overestimated in the trial vs UK practice, therefore a scenario reallocating nivolumab use to pembrolizumab was explored 

- Rechallenge with anti-PD-1 therapy may be permitted if the recurrence occurred at least 6 months after completing adjuvant treatment with pembrolizumab 

   - Patients who recurred within the first 18 months of the model start were therefore assumed to be ineligible for further anti-PD-1 therapy – the proportions of pembrolizumab and nivolumab use in the pembrolizumab arm were set to 0% for this period and proportionally redistributed. After 18 months, treatment mix proportions were set as per observed use in the pembrolizumab arm of the trial. As it is plausible that the trial subsequent treatment use disproportionately reflects early recurrences, a scenario assuming a treatment mix as per the SOC arm applied for recurrences after 18 months was conducted to explore the impact of higher pembrolizumab and cetuximab use in patients with later recurrence. 

- Approximately 20-35% of patients would get active therapy at second-line, but there are few suitable options once at that stage. This aligned well with patterns observed in the trial. However, as pembrolizumab is not approved for second-line use in the UK, any pembrolizumab shares were redistributed to nivolumab.

## **3.5.3 Adverse reaction unit costs and resource use** 

Costs associated with the management of AEs were applied as a lump-sum cost at model entry. In each model arm, this lump-sum cost was calculated as the sum-product of AE risks, mean number of episodes per patient with the AE (Table 32), and mean cost per episode of the AE (Table 54). For a given AE, the mean cost per episode was based on the proportion of patients with hospitalization due to this AE and AE-specific hospitalization and outpatient visit costs. 

For each AE, the mean cost per episode resulting in hospitalization was obtained from NHS Reference Costs. For AEs that do not result in hospitalization, the cost of an outpatient visit was assigned.

## **3.5.4 Miscellaneous unit costs and resource use** 

## _**3.5.4.1 PD-L1 testing costs**_ 

***** . Therefore, at model entry in the perioperative pembrolizumab + SOC arm, the model applied the cost of the expected number of PD-L1 tests needed to identify one patient with PD-L1 CPS ≥1 (i.e.,1.05 = 1 / proportion of patients with PD-L1 CPS ≥1 in the KEYNOTE-689 trial population, 95.5%). Given the transient nature of the PD-L1 biomarker and uncertainty regarding the prevalence of CPS ≥1 in UK practice, a scenario assuming the proportion of patients with PD-L1 CPS ≥1 is equal to the prevalence in the KEYNOTE-048 trial (72%, expected number of tests = 1.39) was also conducted. 

Additionally, in both arms, the model applied the cost of one PD-L1 test upon entry into the IRP state to determine patients’ eligibility for subsequent PD-L1 treatments in that state. Clinical experts at the advisory board stated that a repeat test would still be required for patients in the pembrolizumab arm as anti-PD-L1 treatment rechallenge is permitted for recurrences that occur at least 6 months after completing adjuvant treatment, and it is possible for the disease pathology of recurrent tumours to differ to the primary tumour.(49) 

The unit cost per PD-L1 test was based on the weighted average of NHS Reference Costs with currency code PATH02 (histopathology and histology). PD-L1 testing assumptions are presented in Table 55.

## _**3.5.4.2 Terminal care costs**_ 

Patients who transitioned to death were assumed to incur a one-time cost associated with palliative/terminal care in the last ~90 days of life. Terminal care costs (£8,498.27 after inflation-adjustment) were obtained from Georghiou & Bardsley (2014),(98) and inflated to the current cost year. 

## **3.6 Severity** 

MSD considers that pembrolizumab does not qualify for a severity modifier in this indication as the expected QALY loss for standard of care versus the general population does not meet any severity modifier threshold. 

## **3.7 Uncertainty** 

MSD considers that key areas of uncertainty relating to this indication have been adequately captured in the economic model and explored through sensitivity and scenario analyses.

## **3.8 Managed access proposal** 

MSD considers that this intervention is a candidate for baseline NHS funding. However, MSD remains committed to patient access as a priority and are willing to discuss options for managed access should it prove necessary. 

The later interim analyses and final analysis of the ongoing KEYNOTE-689 trial may allow for additional data collection to further reduce uncertainties identified during the technology appraisal, although it should be noted that the study follow up is already extensive.

## **3.9.2 Assumptions** 

A summary of the key assumptions used in the economic evaluation is provided in Table 57. 

**Table 57. Assumptions used in the economic evaluation** 

|**Parameter**|**Assumption**|**Justification**|
|---|---|---|
|Comparator|SOC; surgery followed by<br>adjuvant radiotherapy with<br>or without chemotherapy|The population in this decision problem is patients<br>with resectable LA HNSCC who have a CPS≥1. In<br>current practice, these patients are treated by<br>surgery followed by adjuvant radiotherapy with or<br>without cisplatin. This was validated with UK clinical<br>experts as the current SOC for this patient<br>population, and thus the appropriate comparator for<br>this appraisal.<br>To date, the only previous NICE Technology<br>Appraisal in LA HNSCC is TA145, cetuximab in<br>addition to primary/definitive RT for patients in whom<br>platinum-based chemotherapy is contraindicated.<br>The use of cetuximab is specific to the _unresected_<br>LA HNSCC population, as per its pivotal trial, and<br>thus is not relevant to the current decision problem.<br>In addition, clinical experts advised that the use of<br>cetuximab in the LA setting is limited to the small<br>subset of patients with unresectable tumours and<br>renal impairment making them ineligible for platinum-<br>based chemotherapy.|
|Cure|No cure assumption<br>applied|Due to the length of follow-up data available from<br>KEYNOTE-689 (DCO: 25 July 2024), when fitting<br>parametric distributions to transition from the EF<br>state a clear plateau is already evident in the EFS<br>curve in the base case model and the implied hazard<br>of a recurrence or death event is close to 0 from ~5<br>years. This suggests that the probability of cure is<br>already captured in the model and therefore no<br>further application of a cure assumption is applied.|
|Transitions<br>from the IRP<br>state|Estimated using patient<br>level data from<br>KEYNOTE-689 (CPS≥1<br>population)|Due to immature trial data, a common approach to<br>estimating transitions for the later health state in<br>early-stage cancer indications is to use an NMA<br>based on the efficacy and market shares of 1L<br>subsequent treatments. ## **3.11 Exploring uncertainty** 

A series of sensitivity and scenario analyses were conducted to explore the uncertainty around the parameters and assumptions used in the economic model. 

## **3.11.1 Probabilistic sensitivity analysis** 

To explore the uncertainty around the variables included in the economic model, probabilistic sensitivity analysis (PSA) was performed by running the analysis over 1,000 simulations. The distributions used to vary model parameters are presented in section 3.9.1 (Table 56). Whenever available, the standard error of the selected distribution was based on the same data source that informed the mean value. In the absence of data on the variability around health state cost values, the standard error for each cost parameter was assumed to be equal to 20% of the mean value. 

The cost-effectiveness results obtained from the PSA are shown in Table 60; the corresponding scatterplots of PSA results and cost-effectiveness acceptability curves (CEAC) are shown in Figure 27 and Figure 28, respectively. The probabilistic results are very similar to those in the deterministic base case. The PSA results demonstrate that, under base case assumptions, there is a ***** probability that perioperative treatment with pembrolizumab is a cost-effective treatment strategy SOC at a threshold of £30,000/QALY gained and ***** at £20,000/QALY gained.

## **3.11.2 Deterministic sensitivity analysis** 

To further assess the robustness of the model results, deterministic sensitivity analyses (DSAs) were conducted by individually varying modelling inputs between the upper and lower limits of their plausible range. Parameters were varied by their 95% confidence intervals, or by ±20% if measures of variance were not available. The following variables were explored in the DSA: 

- Exponential rates of transitions from L/SR and IRP health states 

- Exponential rates of OS and PFS failure with first-line treatments for metastatic HNSCC indications using the 1L metastatic NMA 

- Unit costs of drug administration 

- Patient weight, body surface area and GFR 

- Initial surgery and adjuvant radiotherapy costs in the EF state 

- Medical management costs in the EF state 

- Chemotherapy, salvage surgery and radiotherapy costs on L/SR state entry 

- Medical management costs in the L/SR state 

- Medical management costs in the IRP state (upon entry, pre-progression and postprogression) 

- Terminal care costs 

- Adverse event costs 

- Health state utilities and disutilities from adverse events 

The results of the DSA are presented in a tornado diagram (Figure 29) which illustrates the 10 parameters that had the most impact on the ICER. 

The parameters which had the greatest impact on the ICER were the post-progression IRP utility value and the rate of transitions from the L/SR to IRP health state in the SOC arm. The post-progression IRP utility value was sourced from TA473 identified through a targeted literature review, in the absence of mature data from the KEYNOTE-689 trial. The impact in this one-way sensitivity analysis is a reflection of the wide reported confidence intervals informed by a small sample size contributing to the utility value calculation. ## **3.11.3 Scenario analysis** 

A series of scenario analyses was conducted to explore the uncertainty around key structural and methodological assumptions, and sources of data used to inform model inputs. The results of all scenarios are presented in Table 61 . 

The combination of parametric distributions used to estimate transitions from the EF state had the biggest impact on the ICER. Out of the 10 best fitting combinations using Approach #1, based on the selection process detailed in Section 3.3.2.3, the distributions resulting in the greatest and least incremental EFS and OS benefit at 10 years (see Table 65 in Appendix J1.5), are presented as a scenario analysis to demonstrate the range of outcomes on the model results (*****/QALY to *****/QALY). All scenarios of alternative long-term extrapolations are within the range of cost-effectiveness as per the £20,000 per QALY willingness-to-pay threshold, and it should be noted that the base case selection of extrapolations falls in the middle of this range. 

As discussed in section 3.3.2.3, no cure assumption was applied in the base case based on the implied hazard rate for EFS in both arms and the presence of a plateau in the EFS curve which aligned with clinical expert feedback received. However, alternative distributions of curve for transition from the EF state do not resemble the same patterns of recurrence and application of a cure assumption should be considered based on the hazard rates and modelled EFS. Therefore, two additional scenarios (scenarios 3 and 4) include a cure assumption applied at 5 years in addition to the alternative curve selections using Approach #1. 

The scenarios with the next greatest impact on the model results are using an alternative censoring rule for transitions from the EF health state and using a shorter time horizon of 20 years. The base case model reflects transitions from the EF health state based on the per protocol censoring criteria for EFS (censored at date of last disease assessment), to reflect the KEYNOTE-689 trial and the expected patient follow-up in real world practice. To help validate the modelled outcomes, an alternative approach to censoring for EF events, based on the OS analysis, is presented in Section 3.14.1.1. As per the NICE methods guide, the time horizon used in the economic model should reflect a lifetime time horizon to sufficiently capture all relevant benefits and costs. In the base case, there are *****% of patients alive at the end of the model time horizon and therefore 40.1 years reflects the NICE reference case. 

All scenario analyses produced ICERs under £20,000/QALY, showing the economic model outputs to be very robust to changes in the model assumptions and inputs.

## **3.12 Subgroup analysis**

## **3.13 Benefits not captured in the QALY calculation** 

MSD consider that wider patient, family and societal benefits of pembrolizumab in this indication exist that are not strictly captured within the NICE reference case and the formal QALY framework. Nonetheless these remain relevant for the purposes of decision making and are summarised below. MSD urges the NICE committee to account for these wider benefits in its decision making. 

## **Innovation in a disease that has had few advancements and limited treatment options** 

The KEYNOTE-689 trial of perioperative pembrolizumab is the first study to demonstrate a statistically significant EFS benefit and a strong positive trend for OS in a therapeutic area that has seen limited advances in the last 20 years. Clinical experts have highlighted the clinical significance of the results, with the inclusion of the neoadjuvant phase considered a clear differentiator.(49) It should be noted that the current SOC requires extensive surgery in complex anatomical areas which can affect daily functional activities (e.g. speaking, swallowing), all of which directly or indirectly negatively impact patients, families and their caregivers. 

Resectable LA HNSCC patients are prone to high rates of recurrence even after aggressive surgery and radiotherapy (± cisplatin), and any such recurrences are very aggressive in nature. The limited number of effective treatment options downstream (primarily IO monotherapies) mean that long-term survival post recurrence beyond 5 and 10 years remains low when compared to many other cancers. In England and Wales, pembrolizumab + chemotherapy is not recommended for advanced/metastatic disease, in contrast to Scotland where Scottish clinicians note its use in patients with urgent clinical need. This often includes patients who experience early recurrences from LA disease which is typically indicative of more aggressive disease that would benefit from combined treatment with immunotherapy and fast-acting chemotherapy. This highlights the need for more effective treatments to delay or prevent patients developing recurrent disease. 

## **Potential benefits of neoadjuvant component of treatment** 

The neoadjuvant component of the pembrolizumab treatment ensures patients receive an active and effective treatment whilst their surgery is being scheduled. This can reduce the tumour burden (i.e. downstaging of the tumour) which may in turn reduce the complexity of

the surgery and enable it to be more organ-sparing in nature (i.e. de-escalation of surgery). Consequently, the impact of surgery on morbidity and psychosocial factors may be reduced, resulting in HRQoL improvements versus SOC.(49) However, this de-escalation of surgery was not permitted according to the KEYNOTE-689 trial protocol, and therefore any cost or HRQoL benefits of this are not factored into the economic model. In addition, the active neoadjuvant treatment may also reduce the fear of disease progression whilst the surgery is being scheduled. 

## **Reduced fear of recurrence** 

The aggressive nature of HNSCC, and the invasiveness of treatment, means that there is frequently a substantial psychological impact at the point of diagnosis as well as throughout and post-treatment. Compared with other cancer types, patients with HNSCC are disproportionally affected by issues related to psychological distress, frequently reporting particularly high rates of anxiety, depression, and substance abuse.(33, 36) Amongst cancer patients and survivors, fear of recurrence is widely seen as a key concern resulting from, and contributing to, psychological distress, and one which appears to be especially prevalent in HNSCC;(33) patients with LA HNSCC are therefore particularly vulnerable to fears relating to recurrence risk. Patients having to endure the fear of developing a new HNSCC and the regular follow-up examinations may (re)activate and contribute to these fears. The availability of an active treatment option, such as perioperative pembrolizumab, which has been shown to significantly reduce the risk of recurrence may contribute to lessening the psychological impact of a new cancer diagnosis and a wider value of hope for these patients. 

## **Impact on families and caregivers** 

Beyond the patient, a cancer diagnosis also often has a negative impact on the HRQoL of families and carers of patients due to the additional caring responsibilities as well as anxieties relating to the fear of recurrence and understanding downstream implications of advanced disease.(99) Therefore, any benefits of pembrolizumab that result in a longer time spent eventfree and a reduced fear of recurrence for the patient are likely to extend to the family and other informal caregivers. 

## **Impact on indirect and societal factors** 

Recurrences from early-stage disease often have a negative impact to both patients and carers in terms of work productivity, employment, finances and increases in out-of-pocket expenditure, in addition to the captured health care utilisation. This negative impact is observed in both patients and caregivers and is regardless of the recurrence type (local or

distant), although its magnitude could vary.(100) These parameters are not captured in the NICE reference case, but the reduction in the incidence of recurrence events expected with the use of perioperative pembrolizumab is likely to reduce the impact of the disease on these factors. 

## **Bereavement QALY due to increased suicide rates of HNSCC** 

The need to perform extensive surgery in complex anatomical areas which may be visible and affect daily functioning activities such as speech, chewing and swallowing, can result in stigma, isolation and lower levels of community engagement. Some patient testimonies relating to these issues are presented extensively in “The Swallows” charity organisation website.(101) Such aspects associate head and neck cancer with a higher suicide rate: 37.9 per 100,000 compared to 11.8 per 100,000 person-years for the general population. This is the second highest rate among all cancer types and 3 times higher than the rate for the general population.(31, 32) This is more likely to take place within the first 5 years since diagnosis and younger or middle-aged patient cohorts are more likely to be affected. Indirect effects of this such as a bereavement QALY due to sudden family loss and family spill over are long term effects not factored in the economic evaluation.(102) 

## **Impact of reduced adjuvant cisplatin use on HRQoL** 

Whilst the study was not formally powered to ascertain cisplatin utilisation differences in the adjuvant setting, a lower proportion of patients requiring adjuvant cisplatin after surgery in the pembrolizumab arm, as a result of reducing the proportion of patients with high-risk pathological features, may reduce the negative impact of treatment on HRQoL due to reduced toxicity. Due to the open-label trial design, the trial not being powered for cisplatin use, and the application of pooled utilities, any HRQoL impact of reduced cisplatin use in the pembrolizumab arm is not captured in the economic model. 

## **Severity modifier thresholds across the head and neck pathway** 

To date, all other NICE STAs for inoperable or metastatic disease (i.e. TA661, TA736)(86, 87) have been appraised and approved under end of life criteria (pre-2022 STA process). Whilst this indication using the strict NICE criteria does not qualify for a severity modifier, the downstream head and neck patient pathway itself qualifies for severity weighting to account for the end of life nature of all downstream treatments. As such the decision ICER for this technology could be argued to exceed that of a standard technology without end-of-life given the aggressive nature of recurrent disease.

## **3.14 Validation** 

## **3.14.1 Validation of cost-effectiveness analysis** 

To verify the results of the cost-effectiveness model, quality control procedures were undertaken to ensure that the mathematical calculations are performed correctly and are consistent with the model's specifications, and that parameter input values are correctly populated throughout the model. Additionally, internal and external validation was also assessed comparing modelled outcomes with the observed trial data and data from external sources, respectively. 

## _**3.14.1.1 Internal validation**_ 

The internal validity of the model was assessed by comparing modelled efficacy outcomes against the original sources that informed the efficacy inputs. The present economic model was developed using data from the first interim analysis of KEYNOTE-689 (data cutoff date: 25-Jul-2024), representing 3.2 years of median follow-up (defined as the time between the date of randomization until the database cutoff date) in the all comer population. Comparison of the predicted and observed cumulative incidence curves for each individual transition from the EF state (i.e., EF to L/SR, EF to IRP, and EF to death; Figure 19), the L/SR state (i.e., L/SR to IRP and L/SR to death; Figure 24 and Figure 25), and IRP state (i.e., IRP to death; Figure 26) showed an excellent fit for all transitions in both trial arms. In addition, the EFS and OS curves predicted for the two arms of KEYNOTE-689 were plotted alongside the observed Kaplan-Meier curves for EFS and OS to ensure that the curves are well-aligned during the trial period (Figure 20 and Figure 21). These demonstrated that the modelled curves for both EFS and OS had excellent alignment with the observed trial data. 

It should be noted however that, per the protocol of KEYNOTE-689 trial, differing censoring rules for EFS and OS were specified whereby EFS was censored at the date of last disease assessment and OS was censored at the last date known alive. The date of the patient’s last disease assessment is typically earlier than the last date that the patient was known to be alive. In other words, for patients who are censored with respect to both EFS and OS (i.e., those without any disease recurrence or death), the censoring date in the per-protocol KaplanMeier analysis of EFS is typically earlier than the censoring date in the per-protocol KaplanMeier analysis of OS. As of the 25-Jul-2024 DBL, in the all-comer population, a total of ***** patients (***** patients in the KEYNOTE-689 CPS≥1 population) were censored in the KaplanMeier analysis of OS, and ***** of these patients (***** in the CPS≥1 population) were also

censored in the Kaplan-Meier analysis of EFS. Among those ***** patients, the date of the last disease assessment was, on average, ***** days before the last date that the patient was known to be alive. 

It is necessary for validation purposes to reconcile the two censoring rules as they are structurally linked in the economic model. When estimating the transition probabilities from the EF state, the per protocol censoring rule for EFS is used, and the resulting EFS endpoint is jointly determined by the three transition probabilities from the EF state (i.e., EF → L/SR, EF → IRP, and EF → death). Meanwhile, the OS endpoint is jointly determined by all transition probabilities in the model (i.e., EF → L/SR, EF → IRP, EF → death, L/SR → IRP, L/SR → death, and IRP → death). Therefore, if the ***** patients without any disease recurrence or death are censored at the last disease assessment when fitting the transition probabilities for EF → L/SR, EF → IRP, and EF → death, they are effectively also censored at the last disease assessment with respect to OS. This would result in a discrepancy between the modelled and observed curves for OS whereby modelled OS is censored at the date of last disease assessment whereas observed OS is censored at the last date known to be alive (Figure 30). 

## **Figure 30. Discrepancy in modelled vs observed OS resulting from differing per protocol censoring rules used for EFS and OS** ***** 

Abbreviations: EFS, event-free survival; OS, overall survival; SOC, standard of care. Modelled base case OS is a function of all modelled transitions, based on the per protocol censoring rule for EFS (censored at date of last disease assessment). 

Whilst the discrepancy is relatively small and affects both treatment arms, to enable internal validation of the modelled OS curves in the base case analysis versus the observed KaplanMeier OS curves from KEYNOTE-689, it was necessary to align the censoring rule used in the OS analysis with that used in the EFS analysis by censoring patients at: 

- Last disease assessment for patients who are censored with respect to both EFS and OS 

- Last date known to be alive for patients who are censored with respect to OS but not EFS 

Alternatively, the censoring rules could instead be reconciled by applying the censoring rules used in the OS analysis (i.e. censor at last date known alive) to the EFS analysis, and recalculating the transitions from the EF health state, enabling the modelled OS to be validated against the per protocol observed OS. To test the impact of this approach, an alternative scenario is presented whereby EFS is censored at the last date known to be alive, in line with the per protocol censoring rule for OS (see Appendix J3 for full details). ## _**3.14.1.2 External validation**_ 

Model predictions were also compared against observed long-term data from three identified external studies. As this is the first treatment in the perioperative setting for LA HNSCC, no real-world data were identified to validate EFS in this population. As discussed in Section 3.3.2.3, external real-world studies contained a range of patients across anatomical sites in HNSCC, with two studies in hypopharyngeal SCC only and one by Leeman et al., 2017 with a high proportion of HPV-positive oropharyngeal SCC (~48% HPV+ve and 43% of the sample with HPV status “unknown”). Anatomical site is an important prognostic indicator of outcomes and thus differences in the populations limits the usefulness of these studies to validate numerical modelled OS outcomes. In addition, all three real world studies with long-term outcomes were in the adjuvant setting, post-resection, which further impacts the generalisability to KEYNOTE-689. However, the shape of the long-term OS curves supported modelled predictions in both the SOC and intervention arm of the model.

Additionally, a total of 8 clinical experts treating LA HNSCC within the UK NHS were consulted via an advisory board and individual follow-up engagements to validate and inform the key model assumptions from a clinical perspective. 

## **3.15 Interpretation and conclusions of economic evidence** 

To date, NICE have only conducted one Technology Appraisal in the locally advanced HNSCC setting, which was in the unresected population and therefore is not relevant to this decision problem. Perioperative pembrolizumab in addition to current SOC (surgery followed by adjuvant radiotherapy with or without cisplatin) will be the first Technology Appraisal in the perioperative setting for patients with resectable disease. This represents a step change in the current treatment pathway and offers an innovative treatment option that addresses the high unmet need in this population.

A four-state Markov model was used to assess the cost-effectiveness of perioperative pembrolizumab. The four-state structure has been used in many previous NICE Technology Appraisals for early-stage cancers as it allows flexibility in modelling in the disease pathway to account for heterogeneity, whilst maintaining transparency and model parsimony. The KEYNOTE-689 pivotal trial provided randomised evidence to inform the primary treatment effect in the model, as well as other key model parameters. A key strength in the economic evaluation is the availability of approximately 5 years of follow-up data from the trial, which substantially reduces any uncertainty regarding the long-term outcomes. Where RCT evidence was not available, inputs were sourced through systematic literature reviews and clinical expert opinion. Both model inputs and outcomes were validated with clinical experts at an advisory board. 

Perioperative pembrolizumab is modelled to impact QALYs by delaying recurrence and by increasing the proportion of patients who are functionally cured. The increase in upfront costs of perioperative treatment is partially offset by reducing the proportion of patients with highrisk pathological features following surgery and subsequently requiring adjuvant chemotherapy, in addition to the large downstream savings in the management of incurable recurrence/progression. 

A limitation in this appraisal is the lack of real-world evidence to allow for external validation of modelled outcomes in the SOC arm. This is a reflection of the heterogeneity in HNSCC and pembrolizumab being the first perioperative treatment, that limits the generalisability of the external literature to the population in this decision problem. This was accounted for through extensive scenario testing to explore the impact of model extrapolations on long-term outcomes and model results. In addition, the availability of follow-up data from KEYNOTE-689 is extensive compared to previous early-stage indications and provides increased confidence in long-term OS modelled outcomes. 

The value of perioperative pembrolizumab was demonstrated in a robust economic analysis where the addition of perioperative pembrolizumab to current SOC was shown to be costeffective at a willingness-to-pay threshold of £20,000/QALY compared to current SOC alone. The sensitivity and scenario analyses conducted indicated that perioperative pembrolizumab 

plus SOC is cost-effective when tested against a range of inputs and assumptions. Incremental QALY gains were in the range of ***** to *****, with ICERs in the range of ***** to ***** per QALY. All sensitivity or scenario analyses were under the £20,000/QALY threshold, with a ***** probability of perioperative pembrolizumab being a cost-effective treatment in addition to SOC for patients with resectable LA HNSCC at the £30,000/QALY threshold.

## **Summary of Information for Patients (SIP):** 

## **The pharmaceutical company perspective** 

## **What is the SIP?** 

The Summary of Information for Patients (SIP) is written by the company who is seeking approval from NICE for their treatment to be sold to the NHS for use in England.  It is a plain English summary of their submission written for patients participating in the evaluation.  It is not independently checked, although members of the public involvement team at NICE will have read it to double-check for marketing and promotional content before it is sent to you. 

The **Summary of Information for Patients** template has been adapted for use at NICE from the Health – Technology Assessment International Patient & Citizens Involvement Group (HTAi PCIG). Information about the development is available in an open-access IJTAHC journal article 

## **SECTION 1: Submission summary** 

**1a) Name of the medicine** (generic and brand name): 

**Generic name:** Pembrolizumab **Brand name:** KEYTRUDA 

**1b) Population this treatment will be used by.** Please outline the main patient population that is being appraised by NICE: 

Pembrolizumab is being appraised as neoadjuvant treatment and then continued as adjuvant treatment for patients with newly diagnosed locally advanced head and neck cancer tumours which can be surgically removed. A neoadjuvant treatment is used before surgery, and an adjuvant treatment is used after surgery. 

In the neoadjuvant treatment phase, two cycles of pembrolizumab are used. In the adjuvant phase 15 cycles of pembrolizumab are used in combination with the current standard of care, which is radiotherapy with or without chemotherapy given at the same time (in this case cisplatin). Use of chemotherapy (cisplatin) would depend as to whether evidence of high-risk features are identified based on local clinical guidelines and an assessment after the surgery. 

The goal of adding treatments to surgery and radiotherapy (with or/without chemotherapy) is to reduce the risk of the cancer coming back. Even if all the tumour is removed during surgery, there might be some cancerous cells left behind, which might move through the body to other sites. The body has something called an immune response, which is a reaction to protect the body against anything unusual that enters the body. Drugs called immunotherapies act by triggering the immune response and helping the immune system to fight, amongst other things, cancer. Pembrolizumab is an immunotherapy drug. Giving pembrolizumab before and after surgery (also known as ‘perioperative’ treatment) helps the body to target and kill any cells that are there before the surgery and that might be released during the surgery. Pembrolizumab may also shrink the tumour and keep it from spreading, which can make surgery easier and less complicated. By doing this, there is a better chance that surgery will remove all the cancer, and patients may be less likely to need extra treatments like chemotherapy afterwards.

## **SECTION 2: Current landscape** 

## **2a) The condition – clinical presentation and impact** 

Please provide a few sentences to describe the condition that is being assessed by NICE and the number of people who are currently living with this condition in England. 

Please outline in general terms how the condition affects the quality of life of patients and their families/caregivers. Please highlight any mortality/morbidity data relating to the condition if available. If the company is making a case for the impact of the treatment on carers this should be clearly stated and explained. 

Head and neck cancer is a term used for several different cancers that start in the tissues in the head and neck area. This includes the oral cavity (the lips, mouth, tongue, gums), pharynx (throat, nasopharynx, oropharynx and hypopharynx) and larynx (the voice box) (1, 2). 

Like other cancers, head and neck cancer happen when cells in these areas start to grow out of control. These abnormal cells can form lumps, called tumours.  Head and neck cancers can be divided into two main groups: squamous cell cancers (which affect the surface of tissues) and nonsquamous cell cancers. Around 9 out of 10 head and neck cancers are squamous cell cancers (3). 

Doctors describe cancer by its stage, which shows how advanced it is (4). 

- Stage I cancer is small and has not spread to other parts of the body. 

- Stage IV is the most advanced stage, where the cancer has spread to other areas or organs (known as secondary or metastatic cancer). 

- Stages II and III are in-between, where the cancer may be bigger or have spread to nearby tissues or lymph nodes. 

Some head and neck cancers are linked to infection with the human papilloma virus (HPV), especially cancers in the oropharynx (the part of the throat just behind the mouth). These HPVrelated cancers are often linked to better outcomes compared to those not caused by HPV (5, 6). 

Head and neck cancer is the 8th most common cancer in the UK. It is more likely to be diagnosed in people aged 70-74 years (2016-2018) (7). Over the past 10 years, the number of people diagnosed with head and neck cancer has increased by almost 16%. Between 2017-2019, there were 4,143 deaths from head and neck cancer in the UK (7). 

The main risk factors for developing this cancer are (8): 

- Tobacco use (smoking or chewing tobacco) 

- Heavy alcohol use 

- Infection with HPV 

Cancers linked to HPV may have better survival rates, but they can still cause serious health problems and affect quality of life (6). 

When head and neck cancer is found at an early stage, the chances of living for many years after diagnosis are much higher. However, the 10-year survival rate of patients with advanced HNSCC can be as low as 10% (9). The disease often comes back, and this a major reason for poor outcomes. Up to 56% of people with locally advanced head and neck cancer have their cancer return after treatment, sometimes spreading to other areas of the body (10, 11). 



<!-- page 188 -->

**Confidential** 

The treatments for head and neck cancer include surgery, radiotherapy and chemotherapy (12-14). These can all affect a person’s ability to speak, swallow, breathe, see, smell and taste (15). This can have a big impact on daily life, making it harder to eat, talk, work and enjoy social activities, alongside their ability to carry out day-to-day basic self-care, home roles, work, and leisure activities (16). 

People who have head and neck cancer also face a higher risk of suicide - about three times higher than the general population (17). Many also live with a constant fear that the cancer will return, which can affect their wellbeing (18, 19). 

Common symptoms may include a lump in the neck or a sore in the mouth or throat that does not heal, a sore throat that does not go away, difficulty or pain in swallowing and a change or hoarseness in the voice. Other symptoms that may affect specific areas of the head and neck include bleeding of the mouth, swelling of the jaw, ear pain, headaches and, paralysis of the muscles in the face, or pain in the face, chin or neck {National Cancer Institute, 2021 #66. 

## **2b) Diagnosis of the condition (in relation to the medicine being evaluated)** 

Please briefly explain how the condition is currently diagnosed and how this impacts patients. Are there any additional diagnostic tests required with the new treatment? 

In the UK, if a GP or dentist suspects head and neck cancer based on the above-mentioned symptoms, the patient will usually be referred urgently to a specialist within two weeks. This will often be an ear, nose and throat (ENT) surgeon or an oral and maxillofacial surgeon (OMFS), depending on where the symptoms are. 

The specialist will examine the head and neck area, including the lymph nodes, and may arrange further test to confirm the diagnosis and see how advanced the cancer is. These tests may include: 

- Imaging scans - such as CT, MRI, PET-CT, or ultrasound, to assess the size of the tumour and whether it has spread. 

- Biopsy - taking a small tissue sample to confirm cancer under the microscope. 

Once the cancer is confirmed, further tests help doctors decide on the most suitable treatment. For some treatments, including certain immunotherapies like pembrolizumab, the biopsy sample may be tested for a protein called PD-L1, which can help guide treatment decisions. 

For the specific use of pembrolizumab being considered here, before and after surgery for head and neck cancer, PD-L1 testing is expected to be required before starting treatment.

## **2d) Patient-based evidence (PBE) about living with the condition** 

**Context:** 

- **Patient-based evidence (PBE)** is when patients input into scientific research, specifically to provide experiences of their symptoms, needs, perceptions, quality of life issues or experiences of the medicine they are currently taking. PBE might also include carer burden and outputs from patient preference studies, when conducted in order to show what matters most to patients and carers and where their greatest needs are. Such research can inform the selection of patient-relevant endpoints in clinical trials. 

In this section, please provide a summary of any PBE that has been collected or published to demonstrate what is understood about **patient needs and disease experiences** . Please include the methods used for collecting this evidence. Any such evidence included in the SIP should be formally referenced wherever possible and references included. 

Locally advanced HNSCC poses a considerable burden on patients daily living (15). Depending on the location and size of the tumour, the disease (as well as the effects of treatments, such as surgery and radiotherapy) can have a severe impact on a patient’s ability to speak, swallow, breath, see, smell, and taste (20, 21). These can have a debilitating impact on patients' ability to carry out dayto-day basic self-care, home roles, work, and leisure activities (15). 

The disease and its current treatments also often have considerable negative impact on patients' quality of life (16). Severe pain is linked to reduced overall 5-year survival rates in oral cancer (31% in patients with severe pain vs. 52% in patients without) and pharyngeal cancer (33% in patients with severe pain vs. 52% without) (22). Head and neck cancer is also associated with a higher suicide rate: 37.9 compared to 11.8 per 100,000 person-years for the general population, this is the second highest rate among all cancer types and 3 times higher than the rate for the general population (17, 23). Due to the high likelihood of recurrence of the tumour, patients who have undergone treatment for HNSCC also experience a quality of life impact from the fear of recurrence (18, 19). In addition to the burden on the patients themselves, the caregivers of patients with HNSCC also experience a considerable burden in terms of psychological distress, physical and social functioning, and quality of life (24-26).

|Our immune system is designed to protect us by recognising and attacking things that don’t belong|
|in the body, such as bacteria, viruses or abnormal (cancer) cells. Immune cells called T cells play a|
|key role in this defence.|
|Cancer cells can sometimes hide from the immune system. One way they do this is by using a|
