## **3b) Combinations with other medicines** 

Is the medicine intended to be used in combination with any other medicines? • Yes / No If yes, please explain why and how the medicines work together. Please outline the mechanism of action of those other medicines so it is clear to patients why they are used together. If yes, please also provide information on the availability of the other medicine(s) as well as the main side effects. **If this submission is for a combination treatment, please ensure the sections on efficacy (3e), quality of life (3f) and safety/side effects (3g) focus on data that relate to the combination, rather than the individual treatments.** In the UK, treatment for locally advanced head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (LA HNSCC) is planned by a multidisciplinary team (MDT). This is a group of specialists including surgeons, cancer doctors (oncologists), radiologists, pathologists, dietitians, and speech and language therapists, who work together to decide the best treatment for each patient. The treatment approach depends on: 

- The exact location of the cancer 

- How far it has spread 

- The patient’s overall health and preferences 

In this treatment approach, pembrolizumab is given together with the current standard treatments for patients with locally advanced head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (LA HNSCC) that can be removed by surgery. 

The standard treatment is surgery followed by radiotherapy, sometimes combined with chemotherapy (often a drug called cisplatin), depending on the risk of the cancer coming back. Why are these medicines used together? 

- Pembrolizumab is an immunotherapy. It works by helping the body’s own immune system to recognise and attack cancer cells by blocking the PD-1 “brake” on immune cells. 

- Radiotherapy uses targeted high-energy X-rays to kill any cancer cells left behind after surgery. 

- • Chemotherapy (when given) works by damaging the cancer cells’ ability to grow and divide, making them more likely to die. Chemotherapy can also make radiotherapy work better. 

By combining pembrolizumab with radiotherapy (and chemotherapy if needed), the aim is to attack the cancer in different ways: • Surgery removes the main tumour. 



<!-- page 192 -->

**Confidential** 

- Pembrolizumab boosts the immune system to find and destroy any cancer cells that might remain in the body. 

- Radiotherapy (and chemotherapy, if given) targets any cancer cells left at the original site or nearby lymph nodes. 

Availability of the other medicines: 

- Radiotherapy and cisplatin chemotherapy are standard NHS treatments for LA HNSCC. These treatments are already widely available in specialist cancer centres across the UK. 

Main side effects: 

- Pembrolizumab: Can cause tiredness, skin rash, itching, diarrhoea, and effects linked to increased immune activity (such as inflammation of the lungs, liver, or thyroid). 

- Radiotherapy to the head and neck: Can cause sore mouth/throat, dry mouth, changes in taste, difficulty swallowing, and skin redness in the treated area. 

- Cisplatin chemotherapy: Can cause nausea, vomiting, loss of appetite, hearing changes, kidney effects, and changes in blood counts. 

Patients will be closely monitored throughout treatment to manage any side effects quickly. 

## **3c) Administration and dosing** 

How and where is the treatment given or taken? Please include the dose, how often the treatment should be given/taken, and how long the treatment should be given/taken for. How will this administration method or dosing potentially affect patients and caregivers? How does this differ to existing treatments? In the UK, treatment for locally advanced head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (LA HNSCC) is planned by a multidisciplinary team (MDT). This is a group of specialists including surgeons, cancer doctors (oncologists), radiologists, pathologists, dietitians, and speech and language therapists, who work together to decide the best treatment for each patient. The treatment approach depends on: • The exact location of the cancer 

- How far it has spread 

- The patient’s overall health and preferences 

In this treatment approach, pembrolizumab is given together with the current standard treatments for patients with locally advanced head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (LA HNSCC) that can be removed by surgery. 

This treatment is given in two phases: one before surgery and one after surgery and is usually provided in a hospital cancer centre. Phase 1: Before surgery (neoadjuvant treatment): 

- Two cycles (or treatment sessions) of pembrolizumab are given every 3 weeks by a drip into a vein (intravenous infusion). 

- Each cycle takes around 30–60 minutes for pembrolizumab. 

- The aim of giving pembrolizumab before surgery is to help the immune system attack the cancer early, possibly shrinking the tumour and lowering the risk of it coming back. 



<!-- page 193 -->

**Confidential** 

Surgery: 

- The tumour is removed, often with some surrounding tissue and lymph nodes, by an ENT surgeon or oral and maxillofacial surgeon (OMFS). 

## Phase 2: After surgery (adjuvant treatment): 

- Pembrolizumab is given again by intravenous drip for up to 15 cycles. 

- Patients also receive radiotherapy to the area where the tumour was, sometimes combined with cisplatin chemotherapy if there is a higher risk of the cancer returning. 

- The aim is to kill any cancer cells that may be left behind and to boost the immune system’s ability to keep the cancer away long term. 

## Treatment schedule: 

- Pembrolizumab is typically given once every 3 weeks. 

- Patients are monitored closely throughout for side effects and to check how well the treatment is working. 

How this differs from current standard treatment: 

- Standard treatment for resectable LA HNSCC usually involves surgery followed by radiotherapy with or without chemotherapy. 

- In this new approach, pembrolizumab is added both before and after surgery, aiming to improve long-term cure rates by using the immune system as well as standard treatments to fight the cancer. 

## **3d) Current clinical trials** 

Please provide a list of completed or ongoing clinical trials for the treatment. Please provide a brief top-level summary for each trial, such as title/name, location, population, patient group size, comparators, key inclusion and exclusion criteria and completion dates etc. Please provide references to further information about the trials or publications from the trials. 

The KEYNOTE-689 study is currently ongoing for the treatment for this indication (27). The KEYNOTE-689 study is ongoing Phase III, randomised, active-controlled, multi-site, open-label study of pembrolizumab given as a perioperative treatment in treatment naïve participants with newly diagnosed Stage III/IVA, resectable, locoregionally advanced, head and neck squamous cell carcinoma. The study evaluated pembrolizumab as neoadjuvant therapy, then continued after surgery in combination with standard-of-care radiotherapy (with or without cisplatin) as adjuvant therapy, followed by pembrolizumab as maintenance therapy, compared to adjuvant radiotherapy (with or without cisplatin) alone. The primary end point is event-free survival. Key secondary end points are major pathological response (≤10% residual viable invasive squamous-cell carcinoma) assessed by blinded independent pathological review and overall survival in the CPS-10 population, the CPS-1 population, and the total population. Other secondary end points include pathological complete response as assessed by blinded independent pathological review and safety and sideeffect profile. 

Results from the KEYNOTE-689 study are available from the first interim analysis, with a database cut-off date of 25-JUL-2024 (27, 28).

## **3e) Efficacy** 

Efficacy is the measure of how well a treatment works in treating a specific condition. 

In this section, please summarise all data that demonstrate how effective the treatment is compared with current treatments at treating the condition outlined in section 2a. Are any of the outcomes more important to patients than others and why? Are there any limitations to the data which may affect how to interpret the results? Please do not include academic or commercial in confidence information but where necessary reference the section of the company submission where this can be found. 

The KEYNOTE-689 study tested whether adding the immunotherapy pembrolizumab before and after surgery, alongside the usual standard of care of radiotherapy with or without chemotherapy, could help people with newly diagnosed locally advanced head and neck cancers that can be surgically removed, stay cancer-free for longer than the standard treatment alone (27). 

## **Efficacy: How well does the treatment work?** 

In the UK, most people with resectable locally advanced head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (LA HNSCC) are treated with surgery to remove the cancer, followed by radiotherapy (RT) to the head and neck area. If there is a higher risk of the cancer returning, chemotherapy (usually cisplatin) is also given with the radiotherapy. This is called “risk-adapted” treatment. 

The KEYNOTE-689 study looked at whether adding pembrolizumab (an immunotherapy that helps the body’s immune system attack cancer cells) to this standard approach could improve outcomes. People in the study either: 

- Had pembrolizumab before and after surgery, along with the usual radiotherapy (and chemotherapy if needed), then continued pembrolizumab for up to a year. 

- Or had the usual NHS treatment only. 

## **What did the study find?** 

The main measure the researchers looked at was event-free survival (EFS) – how long people live without their cancer coming back, growing, spreading, or causing death. 

- Pembrolizumab helped people stay cancer-free for longer than standard care alone. 

- In all patients, the chance of the cancer returning or causing death was reduced by 27%. 

- In patients whose tumours had a PD-L1 score (CPS) of 1 or more (something that is tested in the NHS), the chance was reduced by 30%. 

- In those with a PD-L1 CPS of 10 or more, the chance was reduced by 34%. 

- For people with PD-L1 CPS ≥1, the average time without cancer problems more than doubled (around 60 months with pembrolizumab vs 30 months with standard care). 

## **Other important results** 

- Tumour shrinkage before surgery: More people given pembrolizumab had a “major pathological response”, meaning most of the cancer was already destroyed by the time of surgery. 

- Getting to surgery: Almost everyone in both groups went ahead with surgery as planned, meaning pembrolizumab given before surgery did not delay or prevent operations. 

- Overall survival: At the time the results were first reported, it was too early to say for certain whether people lived longer overall. Follow-up is ongoing. 

## **What this means for patients in the UK** 

This is the first large study to show that adding pembrolizumab before and after surgery can significantly increase the time people with resectable LA HNSCC stay cancer-free, especially if their tumour is PD-L1 positive. It did not stop people from having surgery and did not add unexpected side effects. The biggest benefits were seen in those whose cancers expressed PD-L1, so testing for PD-L1 is an important step when considering this treatment.

## **3f) Quality of life impact of the medicine and patient preference information** 

What is the clinical evidence for a potential impact of this medicine on the quality of life of patients and their families/caregivers? What quality of life instrument was used? If the EuroQol-5D (EQ-5D) was used does it sufficiently capture quality of life for this condition? Are there other disease specific quality of life measures that should also be considered as supplementary information? 

Please outline in plain language any quality of life related data such as **patient reported outcomes (PROs).** Please include any **patient preference information (PPI)** relating to the drug profile, for instance research to understand willingness to accept the risk of side effects given the added benefit of treatment. Please include all references as required. 

Quality of life data such as patient reported outcomes (PROs) were collected in the KEYNOTE-689 study by using three types of questionnaire, the EORTC QLQ-C30, that looks specifically at the quality of life of cancer patients, the EORTC QLQ-H&N35, that looks specifically at the quality of life in head and neck cancer patients, and the EQ-5D, that looks at the general health status of a patient (28). 

The EQ-5D consists of 2 sections: the EQ-5D descriptive system and the EQ visual analogue scale (EQ VAS). The EQ-5D descriptive system has five questions on mobility, self-care, pain, usual activities, and psychological status with the latest version of the questionnaire enabling five possible answers for each item (1=no problem, 2=slight problem, 3=moderate problem, 4=severe problem and 5=extreme problem). Results from these questions can then be combined and scaled to produce a single score with a maximum score of 1. Scores can vary from 0, which represents death, to 1 which represents the best possible health state. The EORTC QLQ-C30 uses different questions, however, it also produces a score that is meant to represent a patient’s quality of life. The EORTC QLQ-H&N35 focuses specifically on the impact on patients ability to swallow and to speak as well as the impact of pain. The EQ VAS records the patient’s self-rated health on a vertical visual analogue scale, where the endpoints are labelled ‘The best health you can imagine’ and ‘The worst health you can imagine’. From this we can gather three scores (from the EQ-5D questionnaire, the EQ-5D VAS and the EORTC questionnaire) that can assess how a patient feels throughout their treatment. 

In the KEYNOTE-689 study these outcomes were collected before the study patients received the treatment (baseline), at post-adjuvant treatment week 25, and at post-adjuvant treatment week 51. In terms of the change from baseline to post-adjuvant treatment week 25 and post-adjuvant treatment week 51 in each of these PROs, no significant differences between the patients treated with pembrolizumab in addition to standard of care and the patients treated with standard of care without pembrolizumab were observed, indicating no negative effects of adding pembrolizumab treatment.

## **3g) Safety of the medicine and side effects** 

When NICE appraises a treatment, it will pay close attention to the balance of the benefits of the treatment in relation to its potential risks and any side effects. Therefore, please outline the main side effects (as opposed to a complete list) of this treatment and include details of a benefit/risk assessment where possible. This will support patient reviewers to consider the potential overall benefits and side effects that the medicine can offer. 

Based on available data, please outline the most common side effects, how frequently they happen compared with standard treatment, how they could potentially be managed and how many people had treatment adjustments or stopped treatment. Where it will add value or context for patient readers, please include references to the Summary of Product Characteristics from regulatory agencies etc. 

The side effects of neoadjuvant and adjuvant pembrolizumab in addition to standard of care were observed in the KEYNOTE-689 study (27). The overall number of patients with adverse events (side effects) was generally similar in the pembrolizumab group (96.4%) and standard of care group (96.8%). The most frequently side effects were stomatitis, radiation skin injury, weight decreased, anaemia, dysphagia, and constipation in the pembrolizumab group and stomatitis, radiation skin injury, anaemia, dysphagia, nausea, weight decreased, and dry mouth in the standard of care group. These side effects are known risks of radiotherapy or cisplatin. 

Potentially immune-mediated side effects occurred in 43.2% of the patients in the pembrolizumab group and 10.2% of those in the standard of care group. In both groups, the most common such event was hypothyroidism (24.7% in the pembrolizumab group and 5.4% in the control group). Potentially immune-mediated side effects of grade 3 or higher occurred in 10.0% of the patients in the pembrolizumab group and 0.6% of those in the standard of care group. 

Pembrolizumab as neoadjuvant and continued as adjuvant treatment in combination with radiotherapy with to without cisplatin has a manageable safety profile that is consistent with the well-established safety profile of pembrolizumab monotherapy and the individual safety profiles of radiotherapy and cisplatin. No new safety concerns for pembrolizumab were identified in the study.

## **3i) Summary of key disadvantages of treatment for patients** 

## Issues to consider in your response: 

- Please outline what you feel are the key disadvantages of the treatment for patients, caregivers and their communities when compared with current treatments. Which disadvantages are most important to patients and carers? 

- Please include disadvantages related to the mode of action, effectiveness, side effects and mode of administration 

- What is the impact of any disadvantages highlighted compared with current treatments 

## **Mode of Action - Immune System Activation:** 

- Pembrolizumab “switches on” the immune system to attack cancer, but this can also result in the immune system harming healthy organs. Immune-related side effects can be unpredictable, occur during or long after treatment, and may require ongoing immunesuppressing drugs, adding further risk and complexity for patients and carers. Please note there is clear guidance provided in the SmPC that instructs healthcare providers on how to manage these side effects. 

## **Side Effects - Added Burden and Risks:** 

- Pembrolizumab does bring risks of immune-related side effects (e.g., affecting skin, bowels, liver, lungs, hormone glands, kidneys, nerves, heart, or pancreas), which are not typical with current standard treatments. These complications may prolong recovery, require further treatment and increase the care burden. 

## **Mode of Administration and Treatment Disruption:** 

- Immune activation around surgery or radiotherapy may worsen inflammation and, rarely, complicate recovery by delaying wound healing or causing breaks in treatment. This can extend the physical and emotional strain on patients and caregivers and disrupt planned care schedules. 

## **Most Important Disadvantages for Patients and Carers:** 

- These are: `o` Potential for unpredictable immune side effects 

   - Possible delays in recovery or interruptions to planned treatments 

## **Community Impact:** 

- Greater need for complex care, additional monitoring, and support resources, with potential for increased strain on healthcare services compared to standard treatments.

## **3i) Value and economic considerations** 

## **Introduction for patients:** 

Health services want to get the most value from their budget and therefore need to decide whether a new treatment provides good value compared with other treatments. To do this they consider the costs of treating patients and how patients’ health will improve, from feeling better and/or living longer, compared with the treatments already in use. The drug manufacturer provides this information, often presented using a health economic model. 

In completing your input to the NICE appraisal process for the medicine, you may wish to reflect on: 

- The extent to which you agree/disagree with the value arguments presented below (e.g., whether you feel these are the relevant health outcomes, addressing the unmet needs and issues faced by patients; were any improvements that would be important to you missed out, not tested or not proven?) 

- If you feel the benefits or side effects of the medicine, including how and when it is given or taken, would have positive or negative financial implications for patients or their families (e.g., travel costs, time-off work)? 

- How the condition, taking the new treatment compared with current treatments affects your quality of life. 

Cost-effectiveness relates to how much new health (or quality-adjusted life years [QALYs]) the new medicine produces compared to its additional cost (vs. current care), for a typical/average patient and whether the new health is worth the extra cost required to pay for it. 

The cost-effectiveness of perioperative pembrolizumab in addition to standard of care compared to standard of care alone (radiotherapy with or without chemotherapy after surgery) is evaluated for the typical/average patient via modelling that uses trial data from KEYNOTE-689 to predict clinical effectiveness (efficacy) and costs over 40.1 years. The model comprises of four-health states: eventfree, local and/or salvageable recurrence, incurable recurrent or progression, and death. 

In early-stage appraisals, the efficacy and costs of downstream or subsequent treatments are an important consideration and were therefore captured in the KEYNOTE-689 model. Due to length of follow-up in the KEYNOTE-689 trial, the efficacy of treatments in recurrence/progression health state was modelled based on trial data directly. 

Quality-of-life data (event-free and local and/or salvageable recurrence, and pre-progression incurable recurrence or progression health states and adverse events) were available from the KEYNOTE-689 trial of pembrolizumab. The utility for the post-progression incurable recurrence or progression health state was informed by data from a previous NICE appraisal of cetuximab in recurrent/metastatic HNSCC (TA473). 

Differences in costs in the model are driven by the cost of pembrolizumab, which is offset by lower subsequent treatment and disease management costs in the recurrence health state compared with radiotherapy with or without chemotherapy alone. Differences in QALYs gained are largely driven by greater QALYs in the pembrolizumab arm in the event-free health state. This is because of pembrolizumab increasing the number of years patients spend event free, and the number of patients cured. 

MSD does not believe this indication qualifies for a Severity Modifier as expected QALY loss on SoC vs. the general population does not meet any Severity Modifier threshold. 

The results of the economic analysis show that pembrolizumab given before and after surgery, in addition to the current standard of care after surgery, is cost-effective compared with radiotherapy with or without cisplatin after surgery. The base-case results cannot be shared due to 



<!-- page 199 -->

**Confidential** 

confidentiality, but pembrolizumab is cost-effective compared to NICE’s normal threshold of £20,000-£30,000 per QALY gained. Additional scenario analyses were all under the normal threshold. The results demonstrate that pembrolizumab is clinically effective and, based on the modelling results, highly likely to be a cost-effective addition to standard care. 

## **3j) Innovation** 

NICE considers how innovative a new treatment is when making its recommendations. 

If the company considers the new treatment to be innovative please explain how it represents a ‘step change’ in treatment and/ or effectiveness compared with current treatments. Are there any QALY benefits that have not been captured in the economic model that also need to be considered (see section 3f) 

As explained in sections 1b and 2c, there are no perioperative treatments in established clinical practice available for the treatment of locally advanced HNSCC. This means that there is still a high chance for the disease to progress to stages where curative treatments are no longer possible. Pembrolizumab would represent a ‘step-change’ in the management of the condition for this population, by providing HNSCC patients with locally advanced disease with a treatment plan that reduces the risk of the cancer coming back. 

Implementation of an immunotherapy would allow shifting of treatment pathways towards earlier preventative treatment enabling more patients to remain disease-free. 

## **3k) Equalities** 

Are there any potential equality issues that should be taken into account when considering this condition and this treatment? Please explain if you think any groups of people with this condition are particularly disadvantaged. 

Equality legislation includes people of a particular age, disability, gender reassignment, marriage and civil partnership, pregnancy and maternity, race, religion or belief, sex, and sexual orientation or people with any other shared characteristics 

More information on how NICE deals with equalities issues can be found in the NICE equality scheme Find more general information about the Equality Act and equalities issues here 

Socioeconomic, sex-based, and racial/ethnic disparities in head and neck cancer have been documented in the UK (7, 29, 30), including: 

- The incidence rate of head and neck cancers in males is more than double that of females. 

- Incidence rates for head and neck cancer are lower in the Asian and Black ethnic groups, and in people of mixed or multiple ethnicity, compared with the White ethnic group, in England (however, incidence rates in females are higher in the Asian ethnic group than in the White ethnic group). 

- People living in the most deprived areas have almost double the incidence rate of head and neck cancer compared to those living in the least deprived areas. 

- People living in the most deprived areas were more likely to be diagnosed with head and neck cancer at a late stage than those living in the least deprived areas. 

- There is significant geographic variation in mortality rates. People living in the most deprived areas have more than double the mortality rate of those living in the least deprived areas.

## **Section A: Clarification on effectiveness data** 

## _**Literature searches**_ 

**A1.** Appendix B, section B1.1.1: The submission states that searches were conducted of clinicaltrials.gov and clinicaltrialsregister.eu. Was the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform (ICTRP) also searched? 

## **MSD response:** 

No, the WHO ICTRP was not searched. Clinicaltrials.gov and clinicaltrialsregister.eu are the largest contributors to ICTRP and index the majority of trials globally. Therefore, searching these two platforms is very likely to capture the same core data that ICTRP would provide, with minimal risk of missing relevant studies. 

**A2.** Appendix B, section B1.1.1 and Table 1, Table 2, Table 3. Please clarify which platforms or interfaces were used to search Embase, MEDLINE and CENTRAL, as this information is not stated in either section B1.1.1 or the tables reporting the individual search strategies. 

## **MSD response:** 

As noted in Appendix B, section B.1.1.1, Embase, MEDLINE, and CENTRAL were searched using the Ovid portal. The portal is accessible via https://ovidsp.ovid.com/. 

**A3.** Appendix B, section B1.1.1 and section B1.1.2. Please clarify whether hand searching of the bibliographies of relevant systematic reviews or meta-analyses took place and how this was conducted. The search strategy section B1.1.1 does not explicitly mention that this was done, but in the study eligibility criteria section, the submission states that ‘ _Relevant SLRs and meta-analyses of clinical trials were included at the abstract screening stage for the purpose of cross-checking’_ . 

## **MSD response:** 

Yes, hand searching of bibliographies from relevant systematic reviews and meta-analyses was conducted. Systematic reviews and meta-analyses identified through database searches (Embase, MEDLINE, and CENTRAL) and meeting the PICOTS eligibility criteria were included at the abstract screening stage. Full-text publications of these reviews were retrieved, and their reference lists were screened to identify any additional studies that may not have been 

Clarification questions 




<!-- page 205 -->

Confidential 

captured by the primary database searches. Any citation that was identified (and included) via this approach was counted under the “Hand searches” category of the PRISMA flow diagram. 

**A4.** Appendix E, section E1.3, Table 22. This search appears to have been performed simultaneously for two databases (MEDLINE and Embase) but without changing the subject headings (MeSH or Emtree as appropriate) to suit each database. Please comment on the possible implications for retrieval. 

The Embase.com platform contains both (a) native Embase citations (unique Embase citations that are not in MEDLINE and common citations that are available in both Embase and MEDLINE), as well as (b) imported MEDLINE citations that are not initially available in Embase. 

The native Embase citations (unique Embase citations and common MEDLINE citations) are directly indexed in Embase, with Emtree terms, in alignment with the Embase indexing guide. For MEDLINE citations that are licensed or imported from the National Library of Medicine (NLM), their index terms assigned by the NLM from the MeSH thesaurus are automatically mapped to Emtree. This automated mapping process ensures consistency in searching across all citations in the Embase.com interface, regardless of their original source. The Embase platform handles the mapping from MeSH to Emtree. Further details can be found on the Mendeley Support Center (1). 

A single search on the Embase platform therefore enables both databases to be searched comprehensively without the need to manually adapt the search terms and subsequently remove duplicate citations. 

**A5.** Appendix B, Table1, Table 2, Table 3; Appendix E, Table 23; Appendix F, Table 33. These database searches from both the clinical and economic systematic 

literature reviews (SLRs) have been conducted with an English language limit. Given the dangers of language bias, please provide a justification for the decision to apply this limit and, in particular, for doing so at the searching rather than 

screening/reviewing stage. Please also clarify why some of the database searches (listed above) had an English language limit applied and others (Appendix B, Table 4; Appendix E, Table 22, Table 24; Appendix F, Table 32, Table 34) did not. **MSD response:** 

With regard to Appendix B, Table 1, Table 2, Table 3, and Table 4 (the SLR to identify relevant - studies reporting clinical effectiveness data relevant to the decision problem of this appraisal): 

Clarification questions 




<!-- page 206 -->

Confidential 

The effective primary objective of this review was to identify the KEYNOTE-689 study as this is the only clinical trial that has investigated pembrolizumab in the context/indication of this decision problem. We know this with certainty as KEYNOTE-689 is an MSD study, pembrolizumab is an MSD medicine, and MSD is necessarily aware of all clinical trials using pembrolizumab especially those in indications for which regulatory approval had not been granted at the time of the trial. KEYNOTE-689 is also the most recent and only perioperative study to date which offers recent and transferable data for SoC. As stated in section 2.10 of the company evidence submission, no indirect comparisons or mixed treatment comparisons were required as the KEYNOTE-689 study provides direct evidence for the treatment comparison of relevance to this appraisal. Clinical opinion received confirmed that the findings of the KEYNOTE-689 study are generalisable to UK clinical practice, including that the comparator arm of the study is reflective of current UK standard of care. Consequently there is no need to explore/identify any other SoC studies, and English language filter was applied to balance specificity with sensitivity, to help contain the number of citations to screen. 

We were aware that the conference abstract on the KEYNOTE-689 results that had been published at the time of the searches was published in the English language (Uppaluri et al. American Association for Cancer Research 2025 [https://doi.org/10.1158/15387445.AM2025-CT001]). Accordingly, in the case of this review for this appraisal, there is no real risk of missing the relevant clinical evidence by including an English language limit in the database search strategies. 

The search strategy for the Northern Light database (Northern Light Life Sciences Conference Abstracts 2010 – 2025 Week 12) (i.e. that shown in Appendix B, Table 4, of the company evidence submission) did not include an English language limit as the final search results to screen from that search were already modest enough in number so no additional restriction to increase the specificity of the search was required. 

## With regard to Appendix E, Table 23 and Table 24; Appendix F, Table 32, Table 33, and Table 34 (the SLRs for economic and HRQoL/utility evidence): 

For the economic and HRQoL/utility SLRs, the English language filter was not applied to the main Embase and MEDLINE searches to ensure comprehensive coverage and maximise search sensitivity. For these specific SLRs, the language filter was only applied to the PubMed searches used to search MEDLINE In Process. The searches of this database supplemented the SLRs to identify the most recent citations not yet indexed in the main MEDLINE database. However, the overwhelming majority of citations identified by the PubMed search strategies in each SLR were indexed with the English language filter (Economic SLR, 1,586/1,593; 

Clarification questions 




<!-- page 207 -->

Confidential 

HRQoL SLR, 2,239/2,636) therefore the impact of the filter was minimal. MEDLINE In Process citations primarily consist of English language publications and for the purposes of informing the economic model, studies that are most relevant to the UK healthcare setting are most likely to be those published in English. 

**A6.** Appendix, E section E1.1; Appendix F, section F1.1. In the database searches for these reviews, search terms have been used to identify studies of the types eligible for inclusion (economic evaluations and cost and resource use data sources; studies reporting health related quality of life (HRQoL) data and health state utility values (HSUVs) respectively); however there is no indication that these are based on published filters which have been validated for sensitivity/precision in identifying eligible studies. Please indicate whether this was the case (providing a supporting citation to relevant validation studies). 

The search filters used for identifying economic and HRQoL studies were based on the search terms from Scottish Intercollegiate Guideline Network (SIGN; https://www.sign.ac.uk/what-wedo/methodology/search-filters/) and the Canadian Agency for Drugs and Technologies in Health (CADTH; https://www.cadth.ca/resources/finding-evidence/strings-attached-cadthsdatabase-search-filters#health/), accessed on 15[th] April 2024. The filters applied to the economic, cost/HCRU and HRQoL SLRs included all the key terms from these sources, adapted slightly to align with the objective of the SLRs.

## _**Literature review methods**_ 

**A9.** Please clarify why the principal KEYNOTE-689 publication (Uppaluri et al 2025) is not listed in the included studies (Appendix B, Table 7). Its publication appears to post-date the searches (31st March 2025), but the publication is cited (#41) in

section B.1.3.2 on treatment pathways. Please also clarify why the SLR was not updated to include this publication. 

## **MSD response:** 

The Uppaluri et al. 2025 full journal publication was first published in the New England Journal of Medicine on 18-JUN-2025 (https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa2415434) and does indeed post-date the searches of the SLR. 

The SLR conducted to identify studies reporting clinical-effectiveness data relevant to the decision problem of this appraisal (i.e. that described in section 2.1 and Appendix B of the company evidence submission) had its searches last executed on 31-MAR-2025 (as described in section 2.1 and Appendix B section B.1.1.1), which is within 6 months of the company evidence submission date of 01-SEP-2025. The SLR was not updated post 18-JUN2025 as the current SLR already fulfils NICE’s requirements of it being conducted using searches execute no earlier than 6 months from the time of company evidence submission. 

The KEYNOTE-689 study is MSD’s own trial, and so all the relevant data on this trial (including trial results from the 25-JUL-2024 data cut-off date) has been in MSD’s possession, data presented on/from the KEYNOTE-689 trial used in the submission are taken from MSD’s own protocol, statistical analysis plan, and clinical study report (CSR). The Uppaluri et al 2025 publication (which also report results from the 25-JUL-2024 data cut-off date) does not include any information that MSD did not already possess at the time of submission. Consequently, there was no need to update the SLR specifically to include this publication.

The KEYNOTE-689 is MSD’s own trial, data presented on/from the KEYNOTE-689 trial used in the submission are taken from MSD’s own protocol, statistical analysis plan, and clinical study report (CSR). The source of all methodological and clinical effectiveness data from the 25-JUL-2024 data cut-off date of the KEYNOTE-689 study (i.e. in sections 2.2 to 2.11 and Appendices C, D, L, M, N, and O of the company evidence submission) is directly from MSD, including from the referenced CSR.

**A11.** The clinical effectiveness review presented in the company submission (CS) identified for inclusion 85 reports covering 49 studies (CS, Appendix B, p.14, Figure 1 and Table 7). However, only evidence from one trial was presented in the clinical effectiveness section of the CS: KEYNOTE-689. Please clarify – for each study – the reason for its exclusion from the review in CS, Section 2 with specific reference to the Decision problem in CS, Section 1.1. 

## **MSD response:** 

As stated in section 1.1 of the company evidence submission, the decision problem for this appraisal covers the full anticipated marketing authorisation of for this indication in the UK which is: 

• ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ 

The decision problem is not restricted to patients with tumours in specific sites of the head and neck. 

The systematic literature review to identify relevant clinical effectiveness evidence for this appraisal was conducted initially with an objective to identify randomised controlled trials (RCTs) evaluating the efficacy, safety, and health-related quality of life (HRQoL) outcomes of surgery with neoadjuvant and/or adjuvant treatments in newly diagnosed patients with resectable LA-HNSCC (as described in Appendix B section B1 of the company evidence submission). This is a broader scope than that of the decision problem for this appraisal as stated above and is specific to the anticipated marketing authorisation (peri-operative setting). Accordingly, the initial findings of this review were then further restricted to only those studies that specifically reported results of treatment using neoadjuvant and adjuvant pembrolizumab in the indication of interest, and consequently only the KEYNOTE-689 study is of relevance and considered further as part of the clinical effectiveness evidence for this appraisal (as described in Appendix B section B1.2 of the company evidence submission). 

The reason for the exclusion of each of the other 48 studies initially included in the review after full-text screening is that they do not report results of treatment using neoadjuvant and adjuvant pembrolizumab in the indication of interest. 

It was not necessary for the final step to consider for inclusion evidence from studies that did not directly investigate pembrolizumab (for the purposes of e.g. use in indirect treatment

comparison) because no indirect comparisons or mixed treatment comparisons were carried out as the KEYNOTE-689 study provides direct and contemporary evidence for the treatment comparison of relevance to this appraisal (as described in section 2.10 of the company evidence submission, including for both pembrolizumab and the SoC relevant to the UK). Clinical opinion received confirmed that the findings of the KEYNOTE-689 study are generalisable to UK clinical practice, including that the comparator arm of the study is reflective of current UK standard of care. 

**A12.** Appendix B.1.1.2: Study selection: The CS states, ‘ _Two reviewers working independently reviewed all abstracts identified in the literature search. Studies deemed eligible for inclusion by both investigators were advanced to full-text screening_ .’ Please clarify the process in the event that one investigator alone deemed a study eligible for inclusion? Were all such reports excluded? 

## **MSD response:** 

At each screening stage (abstract and full-text), any disagreement between the two primary reviewers was first discussed to reach consensus. If consensus could not be achieved, a third reviewer was consulted to resolve the conflict. Therefore, no study was excluded solely because only one reviewer deemed it eligible.

**A15.** Appendix N, Table 96. Please clarify the numbers of discontinuations in the pembrolizumab arm between surgery and starting adjuvant treatment. Table 96 reports, n=321 completed surgery and n=275 started adjuvant treatment suggesting that 46 discontinued prior to adjuvant treatment (321-275=46), but the text of p.260 states “ _54 were discontinued prior to initiation of adjuvant treatment’_ . Is this 

discrepancy because 8 patients did not have surgery but went on to have treatments that were classified as adjuvant treatments (radiotherapy ± cisplatin ± pembrolizumab)? 

## **MSD response:** 

Yes, that is correct. The discrepancy is indeed due to the 8 patients who did not have surgery but went on to have treatments that were classified as adjuvant treatments. 

**A16.** Appendix N2, p.260 states, ‘ _Among the 321 pembrolizumab participants who completed surgery, 54 were discontinued prior to initiation of adjuvant treatment. The_ 

Clarification questions 




<!-- page 221 -->

Confidential 

_most common reason for discontinuation was progressive disease (27 [50.0%]). Among the 308 SoC participants who completed surgery, 41 were discontinued prior to initiation of adjuvant treatment. The most common reason for discontinuation was adverse event (11 [26.8%])_ ’. Please clarify the reason for the high proportion of patients discontinuing treatment due to progressive disease in the pembrolizumab arm between surgery and starting adjuvant treatment compared with the SoC arm. 

## **MSD response:** 

The higher proportion of patients discontinuing treatment prior to the start of adjuvant therapy is as expected due to the event classification and treatment discontinuation guidelines of earlier versions of the KEYNOTE-689 study protocol prior to Amendment 08 of that protocol (made on 07-SEP-2023). Amendment-08 revised the EFS definition to state that progressions occurring in presurgical phase will be counted as events if there is a preclusion to curative intent surgery. Prior to this amendment, progressions occurring the presurgical phase were counted as events independent of curative intent surgery and these participants subsequently discontinued from study. 

Additionally, per the KEYNOTE-689 schedule of scan activities (described in the response to question A17), in the pembrolizumab group, the first radiographic assessment is the presurgery scan which is required for all participants within 2 weeks prior to the date of surgery. However, in the SoC group, the first radiographic assessment required for all participants is a post-surgery scan (12 weeks after the end of adjuvant RT/CRT treatment). In the SoC group, only if the baseline scans are done more than 2 weeks prior to the date of surgery, the presurgery scan is required. Because of the difference in time of the first radiographic assessment required per protocol between treatment groups, a comparison of the radiographic disease progression pre-surgery is biased in favour of the SoC group with an increased likelihood of capturing more events in the pembrolizumab arm. 

The impact of these differences should be considered when interpreting the discontinuations prior to the start of adjuvant therapy between treatment groups.

**A17.** Please describe the schedule of routine scans to detect recurrence/progression in both arms and highlight any differences in the number or timing of scans required by the study protocol pre- and post- surgery. 

## **MSD response:** 

The schedule of scans (tumour imaging) followed that of the protocol of the KEYNOTE-689 study, described below. 

## Initial tumour imaging prior to randomisation: 

Initial tumour imaging at Screening (contrast enhanced head and neck, chest, and upper abdomen computer tomography [CT] scan or chest CT scan plus head and neck and abdomen magnetic resonance imaging [MRI], and fluorodeoxyglucose-positron emission tomography [FDG-PET or FDG-PET/CT]) must be performed within 28 days prior to the date of randomization. The site study team must review screening images to confirm the participant has evaluable disease per RECIST 1.1 prior to submitting to central imaging vendor. 

The screening images must be submitted to the central imaging vendor for retrospective review. 

Scans performed as part of routine clinical management are acceptable for use as screening tumour imaging if they are of diagnostic quality and performed within 28 days prior to the date of randomization and can be assessed by the central imaging vendor. 

FDG-PET or FDG-PET/CT scans will only be performed at screening to help guide potential SoC neck dissections, if required. Diagnostic quality CT can be acquired on the PET/CT scanner while performing FDG-PET if that is the local standard practice. 

## Tumour imaging during the study: 

The same modality (CT/MRI head and neck, chest, and upper abdomen) used at screening should be used during neoadjuvant and adjuvant treatment and during the post-treatment follow-up visits at the scheduled time points described below. 

For participants in the pembrolizumab arm (Arm A), the first on-study imaging assessment should be performed after completion of 2 cycles of pembrolizumab treatment, at approximately Week 6 (±10 days) from the date of randomization and before surgery. If the presurgery scan shows tumour flare this should not alter the timing or decision to proceed to surgery unless the tumour is unresectable. In the SoC arm (Arm B), the screening imaging will 

Clarification questions 




<!-- page 223 -->

Confidential 

serve as the presurgery imaging. If the presurgery scans for Arm A or baseline scans for Arm B are done > 14 days prior to the date of surgery, then repeat imaging prior to surgery will be required. 

The first post-surgery imaging should be performed 12 weeks (± 7 days) after the end of RT ± cisplatin. Subsequent tumour imaging should then be performed every 3 months (91 ± 7 days), or more frequently if clinically indicated, until the end of Year 3 after randomization, then every 6 months (182 ±14 days) until the end of Year 5. For all postsurgery imaging, the clock will start at the end of RT ± cisplatin (ie, last dose of). All of these visits should stay on track using the last dose of RT ± cisplatin as the starting clock, ie, if one of the imaging visits is late (even the first scan post-surgery), the participants will stay on the original schedule starting with the last dose of RT ± cisplatin for all future visits; do not recalculate. Imaging timing should follow calendar days and should not be adjusted for delays in cycle starts. When the investigator identifies radiographic progression per RECIST 1.1, the site should submit the imaging with verification of progression (VOP) request to the central imaging vendor as soon as possible. Expedited VOP read will be performed by BICR and the results will be communicated to the site and Sponsor via email. If initial site-assessed PD was not verified by BICR, each subsequent imaging must be submitted to central imaging vendor with VOP request until PD has been verified. Treatment should continue until PD has been verified by BICR, initiation of a new anticancer treatment, pregnancy, death, withdrawal of consent, study conclusion or early termination, whichever occurs first. Of note, a participant will only discontinue from study treatment during the neoadjuvant phase if PD precludes surgery. 

## End of treatment and follow-up tumour imaging: 

For participants who discontinue study treatment without a documented event/disease progression, every effort should be made to continue monitoring their disease status by tumour imaging using the same imaging schedule used while on treatment (every 3 months [91 ± 7 days] until the end of Year 3, thereafter every 6 months [182 ± 14 days] until the end of Year 5) to monitor disease status until an event/disease progression, pregnancy, death, withdrawal of consent, or the end of the study, whichever occurs first. For participants who discontinue study treatment due to an event/documented disease progression, this is the final required tumour imaging.

With regard to how any patients who received treatment different from their randomised allocation were handled for the safety analysis, this only occurred in the case of two participants in the SoC group received neoadjuvant pembrolizumab in error (protocol deviations). One received 1 cycle pembrolizumab and was returned to standard-of-care treatment for the remainder of the study (included in the control group for both efficacy and safety analysis); the other received 2 cycles pembrolizumab, underwent surgery, and discontinued study treatment thereafter without adjuvant therapy (included in the control group for efficacy analysis and the pembrolizumab group for safety analysis). 

**A21** Please clarify and define the term ‘clinically meaningful’, e.g. CS, Section B.2, p.37 and multiple instances. 

## **MSD response:** 

“Clinically meaningful” in these instances refers to the results being impactful as it relates to the clinical state or outcome. No specific quantitative thresholds etc. were considered. 

The KN-689 data have been considered clinically meaningful through insights gained at an MSD advisory board, undertaken on 15th May 2025. The data has demonstrated, for the first time in over two decades, a clear peri-operative treatment benefit in patients with resectable locally advanced HNSCC, with significant improvement in event-free survival rates versus standard surgery and adjuvant therapy alone across all biomarker populations. The advisors recognised the neoadjuvant pembrolizumab phase as a key driver of efficacy, enabling early immune activation and reduction in EFS events - which was statistically significant. However, it was also acknowledged that the overall strength of the KN-689 regimen lies in the perioperative design, where continuation of adjuvant pembrolizumab after surgery serves to sustain immune engagement and consolidate the benefit achieved in the neoadjuvant phase, to support long-term disease control in the curative intent setting. 

Clarification questions 




<!-- page 228 -->

Confidential 

This was seen as redefining what could be achieved alongside radiotherapy. Overall, KN-689 was recognised as a pivotal advancement that not only delivers meaningful efficacy but also validates the role of immunotherapy in a new treatment paradigm. 

## **From the MSD advisory board report:** 

- KN-689 was recognised as an important advancement in the treatment of resectable LA HNSCC, with advisors highlighting the significance of the EFS improvement observed in the interim analysis. 

- The neoadjuvant pembrolizumab phase was widely seen as a meaningful contributor to efficacy, with many participants noting the potential for early immune engagement to influence long-term outcomes alongside the adjuvant component. 

- EFS was generally considered an appropriate endpoint for this peri-operative trial. 

- The study was felt to re-establish immunotherapy in the peri-operative setting as a potential option in the curative setting, following previous challenges seen in the adjuvant-only context. 

## **Anonymised advisor quotes from MSD advisory board report:** 

- “The first time we've seen improvement in recurrence rates for this population,” noting the clear benefit over surgery and adjuvant [chemo]radiotherapy alone. 

- The neoadjuvant approach itself was “exciting,” highlighting that previous adjuvant trials with IO had failed to deliver similarly impactful results. 

- The KN-689 study was also described as “the first in over 20 years” to show a clear (neo)adjuvant treatment benefit” 

- Advisors also reflected on the impact of the findings from a radiotherapy (RT) standpoint: “It’s really stretched what we can do alongside RT,” noting the limited impact that current systemic treatments have previously had on survival curves. It was also stated that many clinicians had “lost hope” in IO from negative results of previous trials in the curative setting, but KN-689 reintroduced confidence for IO in the radical treatment setting in a meaningful way. 

- It was also emphasised that KN-689 not only shows efficacy but also corrects some of the uncertainties surrounding IO use, as “it proves we don’t really understand how IO works,”, noting that past trials in the adjuvant setting were difficult to interpret. Advisors 

Clarification questions 




<!-- page 229 -->

Confidential 

also praised the data for showing neoadjuvant IO treatment providing efficacious response in “a new setting for the first time”. 

- It was also suggested that the benefit may derive from prevention of early disease dissemination: “It seems like it does quite a lot in that earlier disease phase, and makes quite a bit of difference in that early period. I feel that it brings IO back to the radical setting, in a way”. 

**A22. PRIORITY** Appendix B.3: Critical appraisal of each study, Table 8: Please clarify the judgement that there were ‘ _No deviations [from the intended intervention(s)] reported’_ . Appendix N2, pp.260-261 states that 2 patients in the comparator arm were exposed to therapy that they should not have received (‘ _In the SoC group, there was no neoadjuvant treatment, however, 2 participants received neoadjuvant treatment mistakenly. One of these 2 participants received 1 cycle of neoadjuvant treatment and was returned to SoC treatment for the remainder of the study, while the other participant received 2 neoadjuvant cycles of pembrolizumab, underwent surgery, and was discontinued from study treatment; this participant did not receive any adjuvant treatment’_ ) and 20 patients in the intervention arm did not receive the planned adjuvant pembrolizumab treatment: ‘ _A total of 255 of the 275 participants received adjuvant pembrolizumab, 36 completed 3 or less cycles of pembrolizumab and 219 completed more than 3 cycles of pembrolizumab while 20 of the 275 participants received RT ± cisplatin only’_ . 

## **MSD response:** 

When assessing this domain, the Cochrane RoB 2 guidance was applied, which considers whether deviations from intended interventions were likely to affect the outcome and whether they occurred because of the trial context. In the KEYNOTE-689 study, clinically important protocol deviations were defined as those that could compromise primary efficacy/safety analyses or participant safety (2). 

Of the two patients in the SoC arm who mistakenly received neoadjuvant pembrolizumab, only one was classified as a clinically important protocol deviation (2). In the pembrolizumab + SoC arm, although 20 participants did not receive adjuvant pembrolizumab, the total number of clinically important protocol deviations in this arm (for any reason) was smaller than 20 (2). This indicates that these cases were not clinically important deviations (due to e.g. acceptable reasons such as medical decisions) and were unlikely to be related to the trial context. 

Clarification questions 




<!-- page 230 -->

Confidential 

It is also noteworthy to mention that the likely direction of bias from both types of deviations (SoC patients receiving pembrolizumab and intervention patients missing adjuvant pembrolizumab) would be toward the null effect, favouring the comparator. Given the small number of clinically important deviations and the use of an intention-to-treat analysis, it was initially judged this domain as “low risk.” However, to address any residual concerns, we can update the judgment to “some concerns” and revised our responses in this domain to explicitly acknowledge these deviations if necessary. 

**A23. PRIORITY** Appendix B.3: Critical appraisal of each study, Table 8: For missing outcome data, please clarify which outcome or outcomes were considered when completing the risk of bias assessment. Please specifically comment on whether any of the judgements would differ for the patient reported outcomes (PROs) versus the outcomes based on BICR/BIPR. 

## **MSD response:** 

The risk of bias assessment for missing outcome data was based on the trial’s primary endpoint, event-free survival (EFS) as assessed by BICR. For patient-reported outcomes (PROs), compliance was high throughout the study. For example, for EORTC QLQ-C30, more than 90% of patients completed the questionnaire at baseline, with over 94% compliance during the neoadjuvant phase at Weeks 4 and 6, and more than 88% compliance in both arms during the post-adjuvant phase at Week 51. Given these high completion and compliance rates, our judgment would not differ for PROs. We would maintain the assessment as “Outcome available for all or nearly all patients,” corresponding to a low risk of bias for this domain. 

**A24. PRIORITY** Appendix B.3: Critical appraisal of each study, Table 8: For measurement of outcome, please clarify the judgement ‘ _Probably no_ t’ in response to the question, ‘ _Could assessment of the outcome have been influenced by knowledge of intervention received_ ?’, given the open-label nature of the trial and the presence of some subjective PROs for quality of life and safety. 

## **MSD response:** 

Although the trial was open-label, the primary endpoint (EFS) and key secondary endpoints (major pathological response and OS) were based on objective measures such as death events and assessments performed by blinded independent central review (BICR) or blinded independent pathologist review (BIPR). Another secondary endpoint, pathological complete 

Clarification questions 




<!-- page 231 -->

Confidential 

response, was also assessed by BICR. These outcomes were therefore unlikely to have been influenced by knowledge of the intervention received. 

However, because some subjective endpoints (e.g., PROs and safety outcomes) could theoretically be affected by the open-label design, we selected “Probably not” rather than “No” in response to this question, even though these endpoints were not part of the hypothesistesting hierarchy.

## **Section B: Clarification on cost-effectiveness data** 

## _**Model structure**_ 

**B1.** CS, Page 121 states, _“The utility value for the IRP state from KEYNOTE-689 may therefore be used as an approximation of utility in the pre-progression IRP substate only.”_ Please clarify how the pre-progression and post-progression Incurable Recurrence/Progression (IRP) sub-states are defined. Please clearly describe the data that are used to determine the transition from pre- to post-progression in the IRP state, and transitions to death from both IRP sub-states. 

The two substates within the IRP health state are not modelled as separate health states, rather they are intended only to allow the costs and HRQoL implications of the IRP state to be more accurately captured. Consequently, transitions to and from the pre- to post-progression IRP substates are not explicitly modelled; the model only considers transitions to and from the IRP state as a whole (in the base case, transitions from IRP to death are estimated based on exponential models fitted to patient-level data from KEYNOTE-689, as described in CS section 3.3.4). 

Once in the IRP state, in each model arm weekly utility and disease management costs for the IRP state are calculated as a weighted average of the weekly utility and costs for the preand post-progression substates, based on the ratio of time spent pre- vs post-progression (Table 18, and ‘Effectiveness’ sheet in model). This is estimated based on the ratio of mean PFS to OS in each arm, determined by the efficacy and mix of first-line treatments applied in the IRP state (as per CS Table 52). Details on the data and assumptions used to calculate the efficacy (i.e. mean PFS and OS) of first-line treatments are provided in CS Appendix J2 (note that the appendix also discusses estimation of the hazard rate for the transition from IRP to 

Clarification questions

## _**Survival curves**_ 

**B2.** PRIORITY: When modelling the transitions from the event free (EF) state, in Approach 1, only the standard parametric model fits are implemented. However, for the transition from the EF state to the IRP state in the SoC arm, the visual comparison to the cumulative incidence curves suggests poor fitting of these models (Appendix J1.2, Figure 8). Please therefore explore the use of more flexible models (spline odds model, spline normal model, spline hazard model) with one, two and three knots within the curve selection process for the EF state. 

## **MSD Response** 

The parametric multistate modelling approach used in this submission represents a different type of flexible parametric model, described in the NICE Decision Support Unit (DSU) Technical Support Document (TSD) 21 as a “poly-hazard model” (3). In a poly-hazard model, the overall hazard function (in this case, the overall hazard of EFS failure) is modelled as the sum of different cause-specific hazards (in this case, the cause-specific hazards of EF → L/SR, EF → IRP, and EF → death), each of which can be modelled using different distributions. The resulting overall hazard function is far more flexible than if standard parametric distributions were fitted to the overall hazard (see Section 3.2.5 of NICE DSU TSD 21). The existing set of candidate distributions resulted in 397 different combinations of 

Clarification questions 




<!-- page 240 -->

Confidential 

parametric distributions for transitions from the EF state, each resulting in unique extrapolation of EFS and of the EF → L/SR, EF → IRP, and EF → death cumulative incidence curves. Nesting additional flexible parametric distributions such as spline models within this flexible parametric modelling approach would have further complicated the base-case curve selection process and potentially led to overfitting. 

As shown in CS Figure 19 (Section 3.3.2), the base-case combination of parametric distributions resulted in close alignment between each predicted versus observed cumulative incidence curve throughout the large majority of the modelled timeframe, including at the tail. In the case of EF → IRP in the SOC arm, there was a slight deviation between the predicted vs. observed cumulative incidence curve during the first ~32 weeks due to a sharp upward bend in the observed curve around weeks 23-30. However, the deviation occurred early on and over a small proportion of the overall trial period and therefore is not expected to appreciably affect the cost-effectiveness results. Moreover, the abrupt increase in the observed hazard of EF → IRP during weeks 23-30 (relative to weeks 0-23) is likely to have been an artifact of the first scheduled CT/MRI at 12 weeks (± 7 days) after the end of radiotherapy ± cisplatin treatment; in this respect, the smoothed hazard of EF → IRP implied by the predicted cumulative incidence may in fact be a more realistic representation of the underlying disease process during the first ~30 weeks after surgery. 

Nevertheless, to assess the impact of this short-term deviation in the EF → IRP cumulative incidence, the model has been updated to include functionality for a scenario analysis in which the transition probabilities from the EF state are based on the _**observed cumulative**_ **incidence curves during the first 32 weeks** , with base-case parametric distributions used in subsequent weeks. The observed versus predicted cumulative incidence curves from this scenario are presented in Figure 4. This approach allows the nuanced curve shape in the early stages of the model to be more accurately captured than if spline models were used, without the need for the additional complexity that inclusion of spline models would introduce. 

This scenario analysis has been presented in Table 19 using the updated company economic model, demonstrating results that are comparable to base case analysis.

**B3.** In Appendix J1.3, Figure 13, the Schoenfeld residual plots are presented to support the assumption of proportional hazards. Please can the company provide further comment on why the proportional hazards (PH) assumption is assumed to hold for the EF→IRP transition, where there appears to be a peak in the residuals. In addition, please report the p-values for all three transitions included in Figure 13. Please also provide the assessment of the PH assumption by assessing the clog-log plots. If indeed the PH assumption is not appropriate for two out of three types of transition, please can the company provide further explanation on why this approach was explored. 

## **MSD Response** 

To clarify, the model does not rely on the proportional hazards assumption as it uses parametric distributions independently fitted to treatment-specific patient level data. The appropriateness of the proportional hazards assumption was assessed as part of the process of determining the most appropriate approach to model survival in each arm, from the three approaches defined _a priori_ (i.e., Approach #1, independently fitted models; Approach #2, jointly fitted proportional hazards models ; Approach #3, time-varying proportional hazards models), as outlined in NICE DSU TSD 14 (4). 

Jointly fitted parametric proportional hazards models with a time-constant treatment effect (i.e., Approach #2) were among the list of candidate distributions that were considered for each transition from the EF state. The combinations of distributions under Approach #2 represented 27 of the 397 candidate combinations of distributions that were considered overall. While the combinations of distributions under Approach #2 were included as candidates a priori, they were excluded from base-case consideration due to rejection of the PH assumption for at least one of the three transitions (EF→L/SR), based on formal statistical testing. The p-values for each transition are presented in Table 20, in addition to the Schoenfeld residual plots presented in CS Appendix J1.3, as further support for the exclusion of the candidate distributions under Approach #2. Log cumulative hazard plots for each cause-specific transition are presented in Figure 5. P- values are considered a more objective assessment than Schoenfeld residual plots or log hazard plots, and therefore these figures should not be assessed in isolation but rather as additional evidence. 

As discussed in CS Section 3.3.2, the PH assumption for the transition EFL/SR was rejected based on formal statistical testing (p-value of 0.0351, see Table 20). For the remaining two 

Clarification questions 




<!-- page 244 -->

Confidential 

transitions, EFIRP and EFdeath, the CS did not conclude that the PH assumption holds, but rather that it could not be formally rejected based on statistical testing (p-value of 0.4414 and 0.0558, respectively). Given that the PH assumption was concluded to **not** hold for at least one of the three transitions from the EF state, combinations of distributions under Approach #2 were excluded from consideration for the base case analysis. Scenario analyses using Approach #2 and Approach #3 were retained in the scenario analysis to demonstrate that these were all explored in the curve selection process, despite not being retained, to show the full range of impact on the cost-effectiveness results. As presented in the CS, after undergoing the full curve selection process, all parametric functions for the 10 finalist combinations used Approach #1 (parametric models fitted individually to each treatment arm, not reliant on the PH assumption) with Gompertz/Gompertz/Generalized gamma selected as the base case.

**B4.** It appears that Approach 3, outlined in Section 3.3.2.1, introduces a time varying treatment effect (before and after 1 year) within a proportional hazards model. From the ‘Parameter Estimates’ sheet in the model this appears to be a piecewise proportional hazard model where a different hazard ratio is applied before and after one year. Please can the company confirm if this is the case, and justify this choice of time point. Can the 

Clarification questions 




<!-- page 245 -->

Confidential 

## company also confirm why this approach was explored as opposed to alternative models which can account for more complex hazard shapes such as spline models? **MSD response:** 

MSD confirms that the above description of Approach #3 is accurate. The allowance of a differing treatment effect during the first year versus following years was specified _a priori_ to reflect the hypothetical possibility of a change in the treatment effect at the approximate end of adjuvant pembrolizumab treatment in the perioperative pembrolizumab + SOC arm. As with Approach #2, the combinations of distributions under Approach #3 represented only 27 of the 397 total candidate combinations of distributions. The 343 combinations of distributions under Approach #1 (parametric models separately fitted to each arm) were considered to account for potentially more complex shapes of the hazard function. However, Approach #3 was considered a useful addition to explore the possibility of an abrupt change in the relative treatment effect beyond the maximum treatment duration. 

As noted in response to question B2, the parametric multi-state modelling approach in and of itself represents a type of flexible parametric modelling (termed as a “poly-hazard model” in NICE DSU TSD 21) (3). Close alignment between predicted vs. observed EFS curves was thus expected to be achievable without nesting additional flexible distributions such as spline models within this flexible modelling approach. 

**B5. PRIORITY** In Section 3.3.2.3 of the CS the company outlines how the base-case parametric models for transitions from the EF state are selected. It is stated that “ _The distribution selection process first selected the distribution for the cause-specific hazards of EF → death, in line with the approach previously taken and accepted in NICE TA1017_ ”. Please can the company provide an explanation as to why this transition was initially chosen to drive the first selection of candidate models in this appraisal. In TA1017 it is stated that this choice of selecting models for EF→Death did not alter the final choice of distribution. Please can the company demonstrate this by selecting an alternative transition in the initial stage of model selection (EF→L/SR or IRP states). Please present the alternative model choices that would be selected following this strategy, along with comment on the base case and the models that would have been chosen as scenario analyses. 

## **MSD response:** 

Clarification questions 




<!-- page 246 -->

Confidential 

The selection process for base-case distributions started with the selection of EF → death distribution as Step 1, rather than starting with the selection of EF → L/SR or EF → IRP distributions, as the summarized MSE results in Step 1 of the distribution selection process provided a clear indication of the most appropriate EF → death distribution under each approach: In both arms, the sets of combinations using generalized gamma under Approach #1, Gompertz under Approach #2, or Gompertz under Approach #3 for EF → death ranked as #1 best-fitting (in terms of both average MSE and minimum MSE) among the various sets of combinations defined by the EF → death distribution. In contrast, EF → L/SR and EF → IRP distributions were less amenable to upfront selection based on the summarized MSE results (i.e., because the ranking of the various sets of combinations differed between the two treatment arms, or because the ranking differed when based on minimum MSE vs. average MSE). This challenge is illustrated in Step 1 of the alternative distribution selection process described below, in which the EF → L/SR distribution is selected first. See response to B8 for further details. 

Regardless, the full curve selection process starting with EF  L/SR is carried out to demonstrate that, as was the case for TA1017, the same base case combination would still be concluded if the process started with the transition that was informed by the fewest number of events. 

Alternative distribution selection process (starting with the distribution selection for EF → L/SR rather than EF → death) 

_Step 1: Initial assessment of statistical fit based on MSE to select the EF→L/SR cause-specific hazards distribution_ 

Table 21, below, presents a summary of fit statistics for different sets of combinations defined by approach and EF → L/SR distribution. As shown, under Approach #1, in the perioperative pembrolizumab + SOC arm the average and minimum of MSEs were lowest for combinations using generalized gamma for EF → L/SR; for the SoC arm, MSEs were lowest for combinations using log-normal for EF → L/SR. Combinations using Gompertz for EF → L/SR under Approach #1 ranked second-best fitting in both arms. 

Thus, unlike with EF → death, the most suitable distribution for EF → L/SR under Approach #1 is less straightforward to select upfront in Step 1. Overall, combinations using Gompertz for EF → L/SR under Approach #1 provide the best balance between statistical fit in the two arms, and we therefore proceed to Step 2 focusing on 67 combinations of distributions using Gompertz under Approach #1, 2, or 3 for EF → L/SR. As seen in the remaining steps below, this upfront selection

ultimately leads to the same base-case combination of distributions as our original selection process; however, due to the upfront exclusion of combinations using generalized gamma or lognormal under Approach #1 for EF → L/SR, this alternative process excludes several combinations that were considered finalists, and presented in scenario analyses, in the original CS selection process. 

## _Step 2: Visual assessment of fit_ 

As illustrated in Figure 6 and Figure 7 below, visual assessment most strongly favoured combinations of distributions using generalized gamma for EF →death and Gompertz for EF→IRP. Combinations using Gompertz for EF →death and/or generalized gamma for EF→IRP also warranted further consideration. Step 3 below therefore focused on the 6 combinations of distributions that used generalized gamma or Gompertz for EF →death and generalized gamma or Gompertz for EF →IRP (including 4 combinations under Approach #1, 1 combination under Approach #2, and 1 combination under Approach #3). 

## _Step 3: Further assessment of statistical fit based on MSE vs. observed EFS_ 

As in the original selection process, combinations of distributions under Approach #2 were excluded due to evidence against the proportional hazards assumption. Therefore, 1 of the 6 remaining combinations after Step 2 was excluded. In both arms, the remaining 5 finalist combinations of distributions (shaded green in Table 22 and Table 23) had excellent MSE ranking among the 67 combinations that remained after Step 2. Because visual assessment most strongly supported combinations of distributions using generalized gamma for EF →death and Gompertz for EF→IRP, the selected base-case combination was Gompertz for EF→LR, Gompertz for EF→IRP, generalized gamma for EF →death under Approach #1, consistent with the original base case. 

Among the other 4 finalist combinations, 1 was also a finalist under the original selection process; the remaining 3 finalist combinations were newly selected under the alternative selection process. The two new finalist combinations that use Approach #1 are presented as a scenario analysis in Table 24, demonstrating cost-effectiveness within the range of the original finalists. The remaining new finalist combination, Approach #3 using Gompertz / Gompertz / Gompertz, was already presented as a scenario in the CS and is included in Appendix B.

**B7.** In Section 3.3.2.3, page 107, it is stated that “ _Of the 9 remaining combinations, the two resulting in the most and least incremental EFS and OS benefit are presented as scenario analyses to demonstrate the range of plausible costeffectiveness.”_ Please can the company clarify how the “most” and “least” incremental EFS was assessed. For instance the Generalized gamma / generalized gamma / generalized gamma has the lowest incremental difference in EFS/OS at year 1, and then the maximum at year 10. Similarly the log-normal / Gompertz / generalized gamma model has the largest incremental difference at year 1 and then the smallest at 10 years (for EFS and OS). 

## **MSD response:** 

The assessment of incremental EFS benefit is based on the timepoint at 10 years. As discussed in the CS Section 3.3.2 curve selection process (page 105), all of the 10 finalist combinations resulted in similar predictions of incremental EFS and OS benefit during the trial period which were also reasonably in line with observed incremental EFS and OS benefit from the KEYNOTE-689 trial (see Table 65 in Appendix J1.5). Therefore, the timepoint at year 10 was used to distinguish long-term incremental EFS benefit between the remaining combinations of distributions.

Please clarify further why selection the process adopted in TA1017 was considered the best approach in this submission.
