## **1 Executive summary** 

This External Assessment Group (EAG) report assesses pembrolizumab before surgery (neoadjuvant) then with radiotherapy after surgery (adjuvant) for the treatment of newly diagnosed resectable, locally advanced (LA), head and neck squamous cell cancer (HNSCC) in adults. The company submission (CS) states that pembrolizumab would be given as neoadjuvant treatment and adjuvant treatment in addition to the current standard of care (SOC) treatment, which it describes as being surgical resection followed by radiotherapy (RT) with or without concomitant platinum-based chemotherapy. The key study informing the CS is the KEYNOTE-689 trial which compares pembrolizumab with SOC to SOC alone. This summary provides a brief overview of the key issues identified by the EAG as being potentially important for decision making. It also includes the EAG’s preferred assumptions and the resulting incremental cost-effectiveness ratios (ICERs). The results presented in the EAG report include the patient access scheme (PAS) price for pembrolizumab but the list prices for comparator technologies and other technologies given as subsequent treatments. For the EAG analyses presented in the confidential appendix to this report, confidential prices have been used that reflect the commercial agreements for pembrolizumab, nivolumab and cetuximab. 

Section 1.1 provides an overview of the key issues. Section 1.2 provides an overview of key model outcomes and the modelling assumptions that have the greatest effect on the ICER. Section 1.3 explains the key issues in more detail. Secondary issues and modelling errors identified by the EAG are explored in Sections 1.4 and 1.5. Background information on the condition, technology and evidence, and nonkey issues are presented in later sections of the EAG report. 

All issues identified represent the EAG’s view, not the opinion of National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE). 

## **1.1 Overview of EAG’s key issues** 

Most of the key issues identified by the EAG relate to the choice of extrapolation models used to estimate transitions from the event-free (EF) health state, which in turn impacts overall survival (OS), and the application of the cure assumption. The choice of models was also dependent on assessing the visual fit of the various model combinations to the data available from KEYNOTE-689, but this was subject to additional uncertainty due to the high degree of censoring in the OS data beyond 3 years. 

3 



<!-- page 399 -->

There was also some uncertainty related to the rate of transitions from the local or salvageable recurrence (L/SR) and incurable recurrence/progression (IRP) states due to low numbers of events informing some of these transitions. The EAG also identified an issue with the company’s estimates of resource use, which used data from the ‘all patients as treated’ (APaT) population instead of the ‘intention to treat’ (ITT) population. 

**Table 1 Summary of key issues** 

|**Table 1**|**Summary of key issues**|||
|---|---|---|---|
|**ID 6477**|**Summary of issue**|**Impact on results**|**Report sections**|
|1|Uncertainty in the long-term extrapolation of<br>OS due to data only being available from the<br>first interim analysis of KEYNOTE-689|Unknown but has<br>the potential to be<br>important based<br>on company<br>scenario analyses.|4.2.6.7|
|2|Company’s choice of extrapolation models to<br>inform event free survival (EFS) and OS|Small|4.2.6.7|
|3|Uncertainty in the application of the cure<br>assumption|Small but varies<br>depending on the<br>models selected|4.2.6.7|
|4|Uncertainty in transitions for patients leaving<br>the L/SR and IRP state|Moderate|4.2.6.7|
|5|Resource use calculated based on the APaT<br>population instead of the ITT population|Moderate|4.2.9.11|



The key differences between the company’s preferred assumptions and the EAG’s preferred assumptions are: 

- an alternative set of curves informing the transitions out of the EF state to avoid using the Gompertz curves which exhibited effective plateaus 

- transitions from the L/SR and IRP states calculated by pooling data across both arms of KEYNOTE689 

- resource use for surgery and adjuvant therapy informed by the ITT population instead of the APaT population from KEYNOTE-689 

- updated prices used for generic drugs 

- corrected intravenous (IV) administration costs for adjuvant pembrolizumab 

- corrected calculation of resource use frequency for the L/SR and IRP health states 

However, the EAG notes that none of these changes individually had a large impact on the ICER. 

4 



<!-- page 400 -->

## **1.2 Overview of key model outcomes** 

NICE technology appraisals compare how much a new technology improves length (overall survival) and quality of life in a quality-adjusted life year (QALY). An ICER is the ratio of the extra cost for every QALY gained. 

Overall, the technology is modelled to affect QALYs by: 

- Increasing OS relative to SOC, with additional years spent in the EF health state which has a higher health-related quality of life (HRQoL) than the post-recurrence/post-progression states 

- Marginally reducing the time spent in post-recurrence/post-progression states 

- Increasing the adverse event burden of adjuvant treatment which has only a small impact on the QALYs 

Overall, the technology is modelled to affect costs by: 

- Increasing drug acquisition costs and administration costs during adjuvant treatment and during neoadjuvant treatment to a lesser extent 

- Reducing drug acquisition costs for subsequent treatments given to patients who have experienced an IRP, and to a lesser extent reducing subsequent treatment costs to those experiencing an L/SR 

- Reducing costs for surgery and adjuvant radiotherapy 

- Increasing disease management costs during additional time spent in the EF state, although these are partially offset by reduced disease management costs for patients who experience a recurrence or progression 

- Increasing costs required for programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1) testing to identify patients with a combined positive score (CPS) of ≥ 1. 

The modelling assumptions that have the greatest effect on the ICER are: 

- Applying the most pessimistic choice of curves to extrapolate EFS and OS from within the 10 finalist curve combinations identified by the company 

- Applying the least pessimistic choice of curves to extrapolate EFS and OS from within the 10 finalist curve combinations identified by the company 

- Applying the alternative censoring for EFS to align with the censoring for OS 

- Using the ITT population to define the proportions having initial surgery, adjuvant radiotherapy and adjuvant cisplatin use 

- Applying transitions from the L/SR and IRP states calculated by pooling data across both arms of KEYNOTE-689 

5 



<!-- page 401 -->

- Whether long-term survival is capped using general population mortality without any adjustment to reflect an increased risk of death for patients with HNSCC 

## **1.3 EAG’s key issues** 

The key issues related to the clinical effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of pembrolizumab with SOC compared to SOC are summarised below as issues 1 to 5. 

**Issue 1 Uncertainty in the long-term extrapolation of OS due to data only being available from** 

**the first interim analysis of KEYNOTE-689**

This therefore results in<br>uncertainty when assessing the visual fit of the OS model<br>estimates to the observed OS data and thus model selection.|

## **1.5 Company’s modelling errors identified by the EAG** 

The EAG identified two errors within the company’s model. The first is related to the calculation of the administration costs for IV pembrolizumab, whereby the company incorrectly calculated the proportion of patients having pembrolizumab with cisplatin, which impacted on the ratio of attendances for IV administration that were costed as simple versus complex IV administration. The second error relates to an incorrect calculation to convert resource use reported in TA490, which used a 4-weekly cycle length, to the estimates required for the weekly cycle length applied in the company’s model. These corrections had minimal impact on the ICER. 

## **1.6 Summary of EAG’s preferred assumptions and resulting ICER** 

Table 2 provides the results from the EAG’s exploratory analyses where each analysis shows the individual changes to the company’s base case ICER. The largest changes in the ICER are seen when adopting the ITT population to calculate resource use in the adjuvant setting and when the same transitions are assumed from the L/SR and IRP states for both arms. 

When including all the changes preferred by the EAG, the deterministic ICER increases to £****** compared to the company’s base case ICER of £****** per QALY gained.

## **2 Background** 

This report critiques the company submission (CS) for pembrolizumab before surgery (neoadjuvant) then with radiotherapy after surgery (adjuvant) for newly diagnosed resectable, locally advanced, squamous cell head and neck cancer. The CS states that pembrolizumab would be given in addition to the current standard of care (SOC) treatment, which it describes as being surgical resection followed by radiotherapy (RT) with or without concomitant platinum-based chemotherapy. 

## **2.1 Critique of the company’s description of underlying health problem** 

Overall, the External Assessment Group (EAG) considers the company’s description of the underlying health problem in the CS to be broadly appropriate,[1] and a brief summary of the underlying health problem is provided here for context. Squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) is the most common form of head and neck cancer making up over 90% of all head and neck cancers.[2] It originates in the squamous cells found in the epithelium of the mucosal lining of the upper aerodigestive tract.[2] The main locations for SCC in the head and neck are therefore the oral cavity, the throat (pharynx), which is divided into the nasopharynx, oropharynx and hypopharynx, and the larynx (voice box).[2] Head and neck cancer occurring in other structures within the head and neck (e.g., the salivary glands, sinuses, muscles or nerves) are much less common than SCC of the head and neck.[2] Risks factors for developing HNSCC include tobacco use, alcohol consumption and infection with the human papillomavirus (HPV).[2] HPV is more commonly associated with oropharyngeal cancer and HPV positive oropharyngeal cancer is associated with more favourable outcomes.[3] The CS reports that head and neck cancer is the 8[th] most common form of cancer in the UK with 9,997 diagnoses of cancers of the oral cavity, oropharynx, larynx, and hypopharynx in 2022.[4] Head and neck cancer is staged using the tumour, node and metastasis (TNM) classification system (see CS, Figure 2).[1, 5] The CS is focused on the population of patients with locally advanced HNSCC.[1] This includes patients with a low grade primary tumour (T1 or T2) but nodal involvement (N>0) and patients with higher grades of tumour (T3 or T4) irrespective of nodal involvement. The locally advanced population is distinct from patients with early-stage disease without nodal involvement (T1/T2 with N0) and patients with metastatic disease (M1). The CS notes that long-term survival depends on both the origin site of the cancer as well as the stage of the disease at diagnosis.[1] The CS states that the survival prognosis for locally advanced HNSCC is 69% at 5 years.[6] It also describes the 10-year survival rate of patients with advanced HNSCC as being as low as 10%, but the EAG notes that study cited is for a cohort with unresectable HNSCC,[7] whereas the focus of the CS if patients with resectable disease.[1] Recurrence for patients with locally advanced disease is described as being common, occurring in around half of patients,[8] with recurrence usually occurring in the first 2 years.[9] Later in the CS, when discussing the extrapolation of trial outcomes (CS, Section 

13 



<!-- page 409 -->

3.3.2.3), the company states that patients who have not experienced disease recurrence 5 years after treatment would be considered functionally cured, based on clinical expert opinion.[1] 

Common symptoms of HNSCC include a lump in the neck or a sore in the mouth or throat that does not heal, a change in the quality of the voice (e.g. hoarseness), or difficultly/pain when swallowing.[10] Severe pain at diagnosis is predictive of lower survival.[11] Both the disease and the treatments offered to manage it can have considerable impact on HRQoL as they can impact on the patient’s ability to speak, swallow, breath, smell and taste.[12] The CS notes that head and neck cancer is associated with a suicide rate that is three times higher than observed in the general population and that is the second highest rate among all cancer types.[13] Fear of recurrence has also been demonstrated to contribute to poor HRQoL, particularly in patients experiencing ongoing pain.[14] 

## **2.2 Critique of the company’s overview of current service provision** 

Overall, the EAG considers the company’s overview of current service provision in the CS to be broadly appropriate,[1] and a brief summary is provided here for context. The company’s summary of the current treatment pathway for resectable LA HNSCC is shown in Figure 1. This figure also indicates the company’s proposed positioning within the current treatment pathway. The CS states that the treatment pathway for LA HNSCC is primarily determined by whether the disease is considered resectable i.e., whether it is suitable for surgery to remove the tumour and lymph node dissection. Given that the proposed indication for pembrolizumab is for patients with resectable LA HNSCC, the company’s description of the current treatment pathway focuses on this population. The CS states that the current standard of care (SOC) treatment is surgery followed by radiotherapy (RT) which may be given with or without concomitant cisplatin. This combination of RT and chemotherapy, in this case cisplatin, is sometimes referred to as chemoradiotherapy (CRT). Figure 1 does not describe any alternative chemotherapy agents being used in combination with radiotherapy as adjuvant treatment in this group. The CS notes TA145 which recommends cetuximab in combination with radiotherapy in patients with LA HNSCC for whom platinum-based chemotherapy is contraindicated. However, the CS describes cetuximab with radiotherapy as being used only for patients with unresectable LA HNSCC in current clinical practice. The EAG’s clinical advisors agreed that cetuximab with radiotherapy is not used as an adjuvant treatment in patients with resectable LA HNSCC in current UK clinical practice. 

14 



<!-- page 410 -->

**Figure 1 The place of perioperative pembrolizumab in the UK treatment pathway for LA HNSCC (reproduced from CS, Figure 3)** 

**==> picture [448 x 251] intentionally omitted <==**

Abbreviations: CPS, combined positive score; CT, chemotherapy. Dotted lines indicated the proposed positioning of perioperative pembrolizumab. 

For patients who experience recurrent / metastatic disease, the CS describes three NICE recommended treatment options. These are: 

- Nivolumab for patients who have progressed within 6 months of having platinum-based chemotherapy (TA736), 

- Cetuximab in combination with platinum-based chemotherapy for patients whose disease started in the oral cavity (TA473), and 

- Pembrolizumab monotherapy for patients who have a programmed death ligand 1 (PD-L1) combined positive score (CPS) of 1 or more (TA661). 

Figure 1 also shows a fourth option of chemotherapy, although no further details are given on the relevant chemotherapy regimens. It is therefore unclear from the CS what treatments are offered to patients who are not eligible for any of the three treatments recommended by NICE for recurrent/metastatic disease. However, the EAG notes that the comparator treatment in TA473 was platinum-based chemotherapy (cisplatin/carboplatin with fluorouracil), and this was considered to 

15 



<!-- page 411 -->

represent the current SOC at the time. The EAG therefore believes that this would remain the SOC for patients with cancer not originating in the oral cavity, who are also ineligible for both pembrolizumab and nivolumab, but who are suitable for platinum-based chemotherapy. In its response to clarification question B34,[15] the company indicates the regimen of cetuximab with cisplatin and docetaxel would be considered as an alternative under TA473, as it combines cetuximab with platinum-based chemotherapy; however, the EAG disagrees as this combination was not appraised within TA473. In TA736, where the relevant population was patients who had progressed on platinum-based chemotherapy, docetaxel was considered the most relevant comparator, with methotrexate used in patients unsuitable for taxanes. The EAG’s clinical experts stated that cetuximab with cisplatin and docetaxel was not part of their standard of care, with single agent docetaxel favoured after failure of platinum-based therapies, due to lower toxicity. Therefore, the EAG considers docetaxel to be most relevant treatment for recurrent/ metastatic HNSCC in patients unsuitable for both platinum-based chemotherapy and immunotherapy. Therefore, the fourth option of chemotherapy shown as ‘CT’ in Figure 1 would be platinum-based chemotherapy or docetaxel in those not eligible for platinum-based chemotherapy. 

The company does not describe second or third-line treatment options for recurrent/metastatic HNSCC within its description of the current treatment pathway (CS, Section 1.3). The EHNS-ESMO-ESTRO Clinical Practice Guidelines state, _“taxanes with or without cetuximab and/or methotrexate are frequently used after platinum failure.”_[16] The Head and Neck Cancer: United Kingdom National Multidisciplinary Guidelines describe carboplatin and paclitaxel as a possible second-line treatment for recurrent/metastatic disease, before going on to state that further options include single-agent cetuximab, taxanes or methotrexate.[17] However, none of these later line options are recommended by NICE. In its response to clarification question B34, the company also highlighted that some of the firstline options could be used second-line in eligible patients. For example nivolumab for those previously progressed on platinum, and cetuximab with platinum-based chemotherapy in those previously progressed on pembrolizumab monotherapy. 

The EAG asked its clinical experts about how earlier treatments lines would affect later treatment choices. They explained that rechallenging patients who had progressed on neoadjuvant/adjuvant pembrolizumab with a later line programmed cell death protein 1 (PD-1) inhibitor immunotherapy (e.g., pembrolizumab/nivolumab) would not be expected to be effective, particularly if the recurrence was within 6 months, and palliative chemotherapy is likely to be favoured over rechallenge. Although they also noted that this judgement was difficult to make in the absence of data on response rates in patients being rechallenged. When asked about rechallenging patients who had progressed after platinum-based adjuvant chemotherapy, they stated that they may rechallenge patients with platinum-based 

16 



<!-- page 412 -->

chemotherapy if recurrence occurred more than 6 months after adjuvant therapy and other options were not available, such as enrolment in a clinical trial of a cancer vaccine. 

## **2.3 Critique of the company’s definition of decision problem** 

A summary of the company’s adherence to the decision problem set out in the NICE scope is provided in Table 3. The EAG’s critique of the company’s deviations from the NICE scope are discussed in Section 2.3. 

## 2.3.1. Population 

The patient population considered in the CS is: “ _Adults with newly diagnosed, nonmetastatic, resectable locally advanced head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (LA HNSCC), ****************_ .” The EAG notes that this population is narrower than the population defined in the NICE scope due to the addition of the requirement for patients to have ***********. The EAG considers this to be a reasonable adjustment as it aligns the population addressed in the CS with the company’s anticipated marketing authorisation. 

The company also provides additional information on eligibility according to tumour location, disease stage and p16 status (positive p16 status indicates the tumour is likely caused by HPV). The EAG notes that these criteria define a population in-keeping with the population recruited to KEYNOTE-689 trial, and therefore specifying these additional criteria aligns the population with the evidence base presented in the submission, as KEYNOTE-689 is the key trial which compares pembrolizumab with SOC to SOC alone. However, it is unclear to the EAG if the marketing authorisation will be restricted in this manner and whether the committee is therefore being asked to consider a population that is narrower than the marketing authorisation. 

In its discussion of relevant comparators, the company states, “ _to be eligible for perioperative pembrolizumab (in the trial and in clinical practice), key criteria are that patients must have a resectable tumour, be planned for surgery, and be fit enough to undergo this surgery followed by adjuvant radiotherapy (RT) ± chemotherapy_ .” Therefore, the population addressed in the CS is further refined to require that patients are considered suitable not only for surgery, but also for adjuvant radiotherapy with or without chemotherapy. 

## 2.3.2. Intervention 

The CS states that the anticipated marketing authorisation for this indication is: ********************************************************************************** 

********************************************************************************** 

17 



<!-- page 413 -->

********************************************************************************** ********************************************************************************** *********** 

The intervention is up to 17 cycles of intravenous (IV) pembrolizumab (200 mg) every 3 weeks (Q3W), which is administered across three distinct phases. The first phase is 2 cycles of neoadjuvant pembrolizumab given prior to surgical resection of the tumour. This is followed by post-operative pembrolizumab given for 3 cycles, concomitantly with either radiotherapy or chemoradiotherapy using cisplatin as the chemotherapy agent. This second phase is started after adequate recovery from surgery. This is then followed by a third stage of up to 12 cycles of pembrolizumab as monotherapy, giving a total maximum of 17 cycles. The second and third phases are referred to as adjuvant treatment, although adjuvant radiotherapy/chemotherapy only occur during phase 2. There is also the possibility for pembrolizumab to be administered as 400 mg every 6 weeks (Q6W) as an alternative to 200 mg Q3W. In the economic modelling this is assumed to occur after the 2 neoadjuvant cycles and the first adjuvant cycle have been administered, such that the remining 14 Q3W adjuvant cycles of pembrolizumab are offered as 7 Q6W cycles of pembrolizumab (see Section 4.2.3). The dosages used in the radiotherapy/ chemoradiotherapy component of treatment reflect those used in the current SOC and are therefore detailed below under comparators. 

In the KEYNOTE-689 trial, pembrolizumab was stopped prior to completion of the 17 cycles if patients experienced confirmed disease progression or unacceptable toxic effects.[18] The total number of cycles for 3-weekly 200 mg pembrolizumab specified in the draft SmPC is ************************************************** .[19] The draft SmPC also specifies ********************************************************************************** ********************************************************************************** ********************************************************************************** **************************************************************************** .[19] The draft SmPC specifies that ********************************************************************************** ********************************************************************************** *****************************************************************[**] *************** ********************************************************************************** ***************************************************************[**] 

## 2.3.3 Comparator 

18 



<!-- page 414 -->

The CS describes the relevant comparator as being, “ _surgical resection followed by radiotherapy with or without concomitant platinum-based chemotherapy_ .” The EAG agrees that this comparator represents established care for this population in the absence of pembrolizumab. Although the company’s description of the comparator in CS, Table 1, does not specify that the platinum-based chemotherapy is cisplatin, the EAG’s clinical advisors stated that other forms of platinum-based chemotherapy (e.g., carboplatin) are not commonly used, and the current SOC consists of radiotherapy with or without concomitant cisplatin. In the KEYNOTE-689 trial, the dosage of cisplatin for those having chemoradiotherapy was 100 mg/m[2] by IV on day 1 of each 3-week cycle for three cycles. In CS, Section 3.2.3.1, it is mentioned that some centres offer weekly cisplatin at a dose of 40 mg/m[2] ; however, the company’s clinical experts advised that many centres offer the Q3W dosing and this was considered generalisable to UK clinical practice. The EAG’s clinical experts advised that many centres use weekly cisplatin due to the shorter administration time, however, 3 weekly cisplatin was also considered a reasonable option as regimens that lower the burden of attendance on the patient are often preferred. Therefore, the Q3W dosing of cisplatin used in the KEYNOTE-689 appears to be reasonably reflective of current clinical practice. 

In the KEYNOTE-689 trial, chemotherapy was only offered to patients classified as high-risk based on the following criteria: “ _the presence of positive margins (<1mm in the primary resection specimen) or positive extranodal extension (ENE; defined as an extension of SCC from within a lymph node through the fibrous capsule and into the surrounding connective tissue).”_ The EAG’s clinical experts were satisfied that these criteria reflect those used in current clinical practice to select patients for chemoradiotherapy instead of radiotherapy alone. However, they noted that some patients who are classified as being high-risk based on pathological criteria would not be considered fit enough to receive chemotherapy and would instead receive radiotherapy alone. 

The dosages of radiotherapy used in the KEYNOTE-689 trial were as follows:  2 Gray (Gy) per day in 30 fractions (total of 60 Gy) for low-risk patients, 33 fractions (total of 66 Gy) for high-risk patients, and 35 fractions (total of 70 Gy) for patients with gross residual disease. The EAG’s clinical experts considered that these dosages were consistent with current clinical practice. 

The CS notes that cetuximab with radiotherapy was also included in the NICE scope as a comparator treatment. However, the company argued that this treatment was only relevant for patients with unresectable disease (see Table 3) and it was therefore excluded as a comparator in the company’s clinical effectiveness review and economic model. The EAG’s clinical advisors agreed that cetuximab with radiotherapy is not used as an adjuvant treatment in current clinical practice, and therefore it is not a relevant comparator in a population with resectable disease. 

19 



<!-- page 415 -->

## 2.3.4 Outcomes 

The CS addresses the majority of the outcomes identified in the NICE scope (see Table 3). The notable omissions were progression-free survival (PFS) and disease-free survival (DFS). However, the company explained that event-free survival (EFS) is the relevant outcome when evaluating a treatment given in a neoadjuvant/adjuvant setting. The EAG agree with this position on the basis that patients are not disease-free in the neoadjuvant setting meaning that this outcome cannot be assessed from the point of randomisation. Similarly, PFS suggests that patients have ongoing disease, and the aim of treatment is to prevent progression. However, patients having surgery may be disease-free following surgery meaning that PFS is not a relevant outcome for all patients post-surgery. The primary trial outcome in KEYNOTE-689 of EFS (see, Table 8) is defined in such a way as to capture both progression events prior to surgery in the neoadjuvant phase, and disease recurrence and/or progression events postsurgery. Overall survival (OS) is included in the CS as it was reported as a key secondary outcome in KEYNOTE-689. 

Response times were included in the NICE scope, but were also not addressed in the CS because this outcome was also not considered relevant in the neoadjuvant/adjuvant setting. The EAG agreed with this and notes that major pathological response (mPR) and pathological complete response (pCR), assessed by blinded independent pathological review (BIPR) of the surgically resected specimens from the primary tumour site and neck lymph nodes (see Table 8) were reported in the CS as key secondary outcomes from KEYNOTE-689. 

HRQoL outcomes addressed in the CS included outcomes from the European Organisation for Research and Treatment of Cancer (EORTC) quality of life questionnaire core-30 (QLQ-C30) and the EuroQol 5-Dimensions 5-Level (EQ-5D-5L) questionnaire. For the EORTC QLQ-C30, the CS reports outcomes for both the global health status and the physical functioning scale. Section 2 of the CS, which reports clinical effectiveness outcomes, only reports outcomes for the VAS component of the EQ-5D-5L. However, utility scores derived from the EQ-5D-5L questionnaire are used to inform the economic analysis. Although not included in the company’s summary of outcomes (CS, Table 1), the CS also reports outcomes for the swallowing scale, speech symptom score and the pain symptom score of the EORTC Quality of Life Questionnaire Head and Neck Module (EORTC QLQ-H&N35). 

Adverse events (AEs) from KEYNOTE-689 were reported in the CS, and further details on adverse events of special interest (AEOSIs) were provided in the company’s clarification response (question A25).[15] AEs were presented for the all-comer population according to treatment received rather than 

20 



<!-- page 416 -->

according to the treatment group allocated at randomisation. This differed from the approach used for effectiveness outcomes whereby patients were analysed according to the treatment allocated at randomisation. 

21 



<!-- page 417 -->

## 2.3.5 Subgroups 

The only subgroup pre-specified in the scope was subgroups based on PD-L1 combined positive score (CPS). However, additional subgroup analyses that were pre-specified in the KEYNOTE-689 protocol are also presented in the CS (see Table 3). 

The EAG notes that the KEYNOTE-689 trial recruited patients irrespective of PD-L1 status. However, the CS focuses on the population with PD-L1 CPS ≥ 1. Although this was a pre-specified population for analysis in the KENOTE-689 trial,  randomisation was not stratified by this specific PD-L1 cut-off and instead PD-L1 tumour proportion score (TPS) (≥ 50% vs. <50%) was used as a stratification factor. The PD-L1 CPS ≥ 1 subgroup comprised 95.5% of the ‘all comer’ overall trial population. For the majority of study outcomes, subgroup analyses are presented within this PD-L1 CPS ≥ 1 subgroup. Results, including subgroup analyses are also presented for the ‘all comer’ overall trial population of KEYNOTE-689 in the appendices to the CS. No subgroup analyses were presented in the economic analysis. 

## 2.3.6 Special considerations 

Although no special considerations related to equity or equality are indicated with the company’s description of the decision problem (CS, Table 1), the company does describe a number of socioeconomic, sex-based, and racial/ethnic disparities in head and neck cancer in the UK in CS, Section 1.4. These are discussed further in Section 5.3.3 of the EAG report.

## **3 Clinical effectiveness** 

This section presents a summary and critique of the clinical effectiveness evidence included in the company’s submission. Section 3.1 focuses on the company’s review of clinical and safety evidence. Sections 3.2 to 3.3 provide a critique of the included studies and clinical-effectiveness analyses. Sections 3.4 to 3.5 critique any indirect comparisons presented by the company. Section 3.6 covers additional work done by the EAG. 

## **3.1 Critique of the methods of review** 

The clinical evidence contained in the CS is comprised of: 

- A systematic literature review (SLR) of clinical evidence on the efficacy and safety of pembrolizumab as neoadjuvant therapy and pembrolizumab in combination with SOC radiotherapy with/without cisplatin as post-surgical adjuvant therapy in treatment-naïve participants with newly diagnosed Stage III/IVA, resectable, LA HNSCC; 

- Summary and results for the KEYNOTE-689 trial. 

In order to identify clinical trials reporting on the efficacy, safety and health-related quality of life outcomes of surgery with neoadjuvant and/or adjuvant treatments in newly diagnosed patients with resectable LA-HNSCC, systematic searches of the following databases were conducted in March 2025: Embase, MEDLINE (including Epub Ahead of Print, In-Process & Other Non-Indexed Citations and Daily) and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL). 

Supplementary search methods included searching the trial registers ClinicalTrials.gov and the European Union Clinical Trials Register (EUCTR). Clarification was sought as to whether the World Health Organisation International Clinical Trials Registry Platform (ICTRP) was also searched. The company stated in response to clarification question A1 that this platform was not searched because ICTRP records largely come from ClinicalTrials.gov and the EUCTR so there is considerable overlap in coverage. The EAG agrees that the risk of missing relevant trial records is minimal, although it is not zero. 

Conference proceedings of relevant organisations from 2021 to 2025 were also searched, along with the Northern Light database of Northern Light Life Sciences Conference Abstracts between 2010 to 2025. Additionally, the bibliographies of identified SLRs and network meta-analyses were searched. This process was not clearly reported in the CS, but the company’s response to clarification question A3 confirmed that hand searching was performed of the bibliographies of 

32 



<!-- page 428 -->

relevant systematic reviews and meta-analyses that had been identified at the abstract screening stage. 

The overall strategy is an acceptable balance of specificity and sensitivity. The population has been quite narrowly defined, increasing specificity, but the search only includes two concepts overall (population and study design). Interventions and comparators have not been searched for, resulting in a more sensitive search (reflected in the high number of results that were retrieved and screened) that is adequate in retrieving relevant studies to meet the objectives of the clinical SLR. 

The EAG had no major concerns regarding the conduct of the clinical effectiveness review. CS Appendix B.1.1.2[1] reports that, for all citations, both the title/abstract and full-text screening stages of study selection were undertaken independently by two reviewers, but it was unclear whether the selection of an item by a single reviewer made it eligible for consideration at full-text stage. However, this was clarified in response to a question by the EAG which confirmed that any discrepancies were resolved by discussion or by a third independent reviewer, if necessary (clarification response, A12).[15] The EAG considers independent study selection by two or more reviewers, as conducted here, to be best practice in systematic reviewing. The results of the study selection process were detailed, as required, by a Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) flowchart (CS Appendix B, Figure 1).[1] 

The clinical effectiveness review presented in the CS identified for inclusion 85 reports covering 49 studies (CS, Appendix B, p.14, Figure 1 and Table 7).[1] However, only evidence from one trial was presented in the clinical effectiveness section of the CS: KEYNOTE-689. Following a request for clarification from the EAG, the company confirmed that the SLR and search were conducted using a _“broader scope than that of the decision problem’ and that these results (n=49) were then ‘further restricted to only those studies that specifically reported results of treatment using neoadjuvant and adjuvant pembrolizumab in the indication of interest.”_ As a result, 48 studies were excluded for the following reasons: that they did not specifically report results of treatment using neoadjuvant and adjuvant pembrolizumab in the indication of interest; and the CS did not conduct an indirect treatment comparison (clarification response, A11).[15] The EAG believes that no relevant published Phase III trials of neoadjuvant and adjuvant pembrolizumab in HNSCC patients have been omitted from the CS that could have provided additional data on safety and efficacy. 

KEYNOTE-689 is an international Phase III, multi-centre, active-controlled, open-label study randomised controlled trial (RCT). One unpublished clinical study report (CSR)[24] and 1 conference abstract[25] relating to this trial were identified by the SLR (CS, Appendix B, Table 7).[1] The principal 

33 



<!-- page 429 -->

publication for the trial[18] was cited in the CS only in relation to the treatment pathway (CS, Section 1.3.2., p.35).[1] The EAG requested clarification from the company regarding the omission of the key publication from the clinical effectiveness review (but cited elsewhere in the submission). The company confirmed that the paper was published (July 2025) after the searches were conducted (31[st] March 2025) and that the company submission occurred within 6 months of these search and so inclusion of more recent publications was not required, and that it did not contain any data different from the CSR. As a result, there was _“no need”_ for its inclusion (clarification response A9).[15] A published protocol was also available but not cited in the CS (NCT03765918).[26] In the absence of referencing, the EAG requested clarification on the source of clinical data reported in the CS; the company confirmed that all data reported in the CS for KEYNOTE-689 were extracted exclusively from the CSR[24] (clarification response A10).[15] 

Data extracted from the included studies are presented in Sections 2.2-2.8 of the CS.[1] Details of the data extraction process are reported in CS Appendix B.1.1.3.[1] The process was undertaken independently by two reviewers, and any discrepancies were resolved by consensus or by discussion with by a third independent reviewer, if necessary. The EAG considers complete independent data extraction by two or more reviewers, as conducted here, to be best practice in systematic reviewing. 

CS Appendix B.1.14[1] reports that the quality assessment process was undertaken independently by two reviewers, and any discrepancies were resolved by consensus or by discussion with by a third independent reviewer, if necessary. The EAG considers independent risk of bias/quality assessment by two or more reviewers, with referral to a third if necessary, as conducted here, to be best practice in systematic reviewing. However, differences between the company and EAG in the quality assessment of the principal included trial are reported in Section 3.2.4. 

The EAG agrees with the CS (Section 2.9)[1] that a meta-analysis is not appropriate given that only a single relevant trial was identified (KEYNOTE-689), and no other relevant trial has been missed. The KEYNOTE-689 trial is ongoing and is estimated to complete in September 2026. The CS argues that an indirect treatment comparison comparing pembrolizumab with therapies other than SOC (radiotherapy ± cisplatin) is not necessary because KEYNOTE-689 provided direct evidence for the treatment comparison of relevance to this appraisal (CS, Section 2.10).[1] This assessment is discussed in detail in Section 3.5. 

34

## **3.2 Critique of the methods of KEYNOTE-689** 

## 3.2.1 Characteristics and study design of the KEYNOTE-689 trial 

KEYNOTE-689 an international Phase III, multi-centre, active-controlled, open-label study RCT with an unspecified planned follow-up period. The trial was conducted in 192 centres across North and South America, Europe and Asia. There were six UK centres (patients n=19, CS, Appendix L4, p.235[1] ) (NCT03765918[26] ). Details of study location, treatments, trial inclusion and exclusion criteria, permitted and prohibited concomitant medications and relevant outcomes are reported in Table 4. The primary completion date was 25[th] July 2024, and the estimated completion date is listed as 10[th] September 2026 (NCT03765918). The full eligibility criteria of the KEYNOTE-689 study are listed in Table 4. The KEYNOTE-689 trial enrolled patients aged ≥18 years with a new clinical diagnosis of non-metastatic, resectable LA HNSCC. Eligible patients also had to have tumour stage III or IVA/B and an Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group Performance Status (ECOG PS) 0 or 1. Patients were randomly assigned in a 1:1 ratio. The intervention arm treatment consisted of pembrolizumab (200 mg intravenously [IV] every three weeks [Q3W] for two cycles) as neoadjuvant therapy prior to surgery, followed by either pembrolizumab (200 mg IV Q3W for 15 cycles) plus SOC radiotherapy (RT) with cisplatin (100 mg/m[2] IV Q3W for three cycles) as adjuvant therapy following surgery for high-risk patients, or pembrolizumab (200 mg IV Q3W for 15 cycles) plus SOC RT without cisplatin as adjuvant therapy following surgery for low-risk patients. The comparator arm treatment consisted of SOC RT with cisplatin (100 mg/m[2] IV Q3W for three cycles) as adjuvant therapy following surgery for high-risk patients, or SOC RT without cisplatin as adjuvant therapy following surgery for low-risk patients. The criteria for post-surgery risk categorisation are described in Table 4.

## 3.2.2 Participant flow and analysis populations: KEYNOTE-689 

In KEYNOTE-689, overall, 1044 patients with a new clinical diagnosis of nonmetastatic, resectable LA HNSCC were enrolled, and 714 patients satisfied the eligibility criteria and were randomised: 363 were allocated to pembrolizumab and 351 to SOC. The disposition and flow of participants is detailed in Figure 3 (‘all comer’ population). In the pembrolizumab arm (n=363), three patients received no treatment; 341 completed neoadjuvant treatment; 321 completed surgery, *** started adjuvant treatment and 155 completed adjuvant treatment. In the SOC arm (n=351), 315 patients received treatment (‘All patients as Treated’ [APaT]); 308 completed surgery; *** of the ‘all comer’ population started adjuvant treatment, and 261 completed adjuvant treatment. The CS (Section 2.6.1.1 and Table 11[1] ) reported  that the median actual follow-up was ******************************************** in the pembrolizumab arm and ******************************************** in the SOC arm.

In response to a request from the EAG, the company clarified that a possible reason for this disparity was the greater frequency of scans in the pembrolizumab + SOC arm compared with the SOC arm, which led to ‘an increased likelihood of capturing more events in the pembrolizumab arm’ (clarification response, questions A16 and A17).[15]

## 3.2.3 Baseline characteristics, endpoints and analysis sets 

## **Baseline characteristics: KEYNOTE-689** 

The demographic and baseline characteristics of those patients randomised in KEYNOTE-689 and satisfying the PD-L1 CPS>1 criterion are presented in Table 6. The two arms were generally wellbalanced at baseline across most variables, including prognostic factors such as age, tumour site and stage, HPV status and race.[16, 17, 27, 28] The median age was 60 years (range 29-82 years) in the pembrolizumab arm and 61 years (22–87 years) in the SOC arm. Most participants were male and white. Most participants across both groups had an overall cancer staging at baseline of IVA (74.6% in the pembrolizumab arm vs 73.4% in the SOC arm), with the primary tumour site being the oral cavity (60.5% vs 61.2%, respectively). The pembrolizumab arm had more patients with an ECOG PS score of 1 (rather than 0) compared with the SOC arm (46.1% vs 40.0%). Clinical advice to the EAG confirmed that the characteristics of the trial participants in KEYNOTE-689 were largely similar to the population in clinical practice in England, with the exception that there might be more patients in clinical practice who were HPV positive, and fewer patients with oropharynx as the primary site as most of these patients would be considered inoperable and treated with definitive CRT. Baseline data for the ‘all comer’ population were provided in the CS, Appendix Section N.[1]

## 3.2.4 Quality assessment of the KEYNOTE-689 trial 

The CS reported risk of bias assessments in Appendix B.3 (Table 8).[1] The appraisal of the quality of relevant clinical trials was conducted using the Cochrane Risk of Bias tool (Version 2).[29] The EAG confirms that this is an acceptable tool for risk of bias assessment. The assessments of both the company and the EAG are based on information in the CSR and protocol. 

The CS and EAG judgements for the KEYNOTE-689 trial are presented in Table 10. The CS judged the KEYNOTE-689 trial to be at low risk of bias (CS, Appendix B.3).[1] The EAG agreed with the company’s judgements of ‘Low risk of bias’ regarding the randomisation process, management of 

50 



<!-- page 446 -->

missing data (and the application of an appropriate ITT analysis) and the absence of selective reporting. 

However, the EAG questioned the company’s judgement regarding deviations and the measurement of some outcomes (which also affected the ‘missing outcome data’). The company confirmed that, while the recorded deviations were unlikely to be clinically important, the judgement could be revised to ‘Some concerns’ ‘to explicitly acknowledge these deviations if necessary’ (clarification response, question A22).[15] 

The appraisal did not specify which outcomes were being assessed (e.g., primary and/or key secondary endpoints only). In its clarification response to question A24, the company confirmed that, as a result of the open-label nature of the trial, ‘some subjective endpoints (e.g., PROs and safety outcomes) could theoretically be affected by the open-label design’, but judged that this had ‘probably not’ affected ‘the outcome’ because these were not ‘part of the hypothesis-testing hierarchy.’[15] However, the EAG judged this item to have ‘Some concerns’ because the appraisal was not only limited to outcomes that used objective measures. 

The overall risk of bias was therefore assessed by the EAG to be ‘Some concerns’, given that at two of the five categories were judged to have ‘Some concerns’.

## **3.3 Critique of the results of the trials of the technology of interest** 

The CS reports the latest available results from the KEYNOTE-689 study from the first interim analysis (IA1) with a database cut-off date of 25th July 2024.[1] The interim analysis was planned after 207 events of disease progression, disease recurrence, or death in the CPS-10 population and 9 months after the last participant underwent randomisation.[18] The clinical efficacy sections of the CS (Section 2.2 to 2.8[1] ) only reported the results for the subgroup of participants with PD-L1 CPS ≥1; the efficacy results for the entire “all comer” overall KEYNOTE-689 participant population were reported in the CS, Appendix N, but are not reported here. PD-L1 status, measured using tumour proportion score (TPS), was a stratification factor at randomisation to ensure that the treatment groups were balanced with respect to this potential effect modifier. The CS reported safety results for the ‘all comer’ APaT (All Participants as Treated) population (Section 2.11).[1] 

## 3.3.1  Primary endpoint: Event free survival (EFS) in KEYNOTE-689 

The primary efficacy endpoint was EFS by Blinded Independent Central Review (BICR). The definition of EFS assessed by RECIST 1.1 was described in Table 8 and the findings for the primary efficacy endpoint are reported in Table 11. The CS reports a statistically significant improvement in EFS per RECIST 1.1 as assessed by BICR for participants in the pembrolizumab + SOC arm compared with the SOC arm (Hazard Ration [HR]: 0.70; 95% Confidence Interval [CI]: 0.55, 0.89; _p_ =0.00140). This represents a 30% reduction in the risk of an EFS event in the pembrolizumab + SOC group versus the SOC group. Median EFS was reported to be 59.7 months in the pembrolizumab + SOC group compared with 29.6 months in the SOC group. The CS (Section 2.6.1.2[1] ) also reports that this improvement was ‘clinically meaningful’, but no definition of what constituted ‘clinically meaningful’ was given. The EAG therefore requested clarification of this terminology. The company responded that ‘“Clinically meaningful” in these instances refers to ‘the results being impactful as it relates to the clinical state or outcome. No specific quantitative thresholds etc. were considered’ (clarification response A21).[15] The EAG therefore notes that this term is not based on a validated threshold, such as a Minimally Clinically Important Difference (MCID). The EAG notes that the incidence of local progressive disease (PD)/recurrence was 10.7% in the pembrolizumab + SOC group vs 11.0% in the SOC group, while distant PD was 6.9% in the pembrolizumab + SOC group vs 15.2% in the SOC group.

## **3.3.2 Secondary endpoints** 

## **Overall Survival (OS)** 

The CS reported a number of secondary endpoints from the KEYNOTE-689 trial. OS was a secondary outcome in the KEYNOTE-689 trial. Clinical advice to the EAG indicated that OS was the most important clinical outcome. The findings for the secondary efficacy endpoint of OS in patients with baseline PD-L1 CPS ≥1 are reported in Table 12 and Figure 5 based on the IA1 data cut-off of 25th July 2024. The CS (Section 2.6.1.3) reports that, as per the prespecified multiplicity strategy, OS was not 63 



<!-- page 459 -->

formally tested in the CPS≥1 population at IA1 due to the lack of statistical significance of OS within the CPS≥10 population.[1] The median actual follow-up time was 117.4 weeks, and the OS HR estimate statistically significantly favoured pembrolizumab + SOC group versus SoC (HR:0.72; 95% CI: 0.56, 0.94; nominal p=0.00666). Median OS was not reached in the pembrolizumab + SOC group compared with a median OS of 61.8 months in the SOC group.

## **Major Pathological Response (mPR)** 

The secondary efficacy endpoint mPR was assessed by Blinded Independent Pathologist Review (BIPR). The EAG notes that the original protocol listed mPR and EFS as the primary efficacy endpoints (original protocol, Section 10.4.1.1, p.130[18] ), but this was changed in September 2023 and mPR was demoted to a secondary endpoint (final protocol, p.3[18] ). The definition of mPR was described Table 8 

65 



<!-- page 461 -->

and the findings for this secondary efficacy endpoint are reported in Table 13. The CS reports a statistically significant improvement in mPR as assessed by BIPR for participants in the pembrolizumab + SOC group (9.8%) compared with the SOC group (0%) with a difference in response rates of 9.8% (95% CI: 7.0%, 13.3%; p<0.00001). The CS also states that this finding was below a p-value boundary of 0.0005.[1]

## **3.3.4 Safety** 

The incidence and types of AEs for the ‘all comer’ APaT population (n=361 in the pembrolizumab + SOC group and n=315 in the SOC group) in KEYNOTE-689 are reported in Table 15. ## **3.7 Conclusions of the clinical-effectiveness section** 

The EAG had no major concerns regarding the conduct of the clinical effectiveness review. The pivotal trial evidence was provided by KEYNOTE-689, which is an international Phase III, multicentre, active-controlled, open-label study RCT. The trial was conducted in 192 centres across North and South America, Europe and Asia. There were six UK centres (patients n=19). KEYNOTE-689 is ongoing and is estimated to complete in September 2026. The EAG accepts that no other relevant trial evidence was missed. 

The EAG notes that, while the KEYNOTE-689 trial included all adult patients with a new clinical diagnosis of nonmetastatic, resectable LA HNSCC, in accordance with the NICE decision problem, 

73 



<!-- page 469 -->

the CS focuses on a narrower population of participants with PD-L1 CPS>1, 

****************************************************************************** 

************* The EAG considers that this was a reasonable adjustment. Participants with CPS ≥1 comprised 95.5% of the ‘all comer’ overall KEYNOTE-689 population and the proportion of patients with CPS ≥1 was balanced between the two trial arms (95.6% in the pembrolizumab + SOC arm and 95.4% in the SOC arm). Clinical advice to the EAG confirmed that the characteristics of the trial participants in KEYNOTE-689 were largely similar to the population in clinical practice in England, with the exception that there might be more patients in clinical practice who were HPV positive, and fewer patients with oropharynx as the primary site as most of these patients would be considered inoperable and treated with definitive CRT. 

The primary endpoint was event-free survival (EFS) per RECIST 1.1 as assessed by BICR. The secondary endpoints were OS, and mPR and pCR as assessed by BIPR. The CS reports a statistically significant improvement in EFS for participants in the pembrolizumab + SOC arm compared with the SOC arm (HR: 0.70; 95% CI: 0.55, 0.89; _p_ =0.00140). Median EFS was reported to be 59.7 months in the pembrolizumab + SOC group compared with 29.6 months in the SOC group. For OS, HR estimate statistically significantly favoured pembrolizumab + SOC group versus SOC (HR:0.72; 95% CI: 0.56, 0.94; nominal _p_ =0.00666). Median OS was not reached in the pembrolizumab + SOC group compared with a median OS of 61.8 months in the SOC group. The CS reports a statistically significant improvement in mPR for participants in the pembrolizumab + SOC group (9.8%) compared with the SOC group (0%) with a difference in response rates of 9.8% (95% CI: 7.0%, 13.3%; _p_ <0.00001), and a statistically significant improvement in pCR for participants in the pembrolizumab + SOC group (3.2%) compared with the SOC group (0%) with a difference in response rates of 3.1% (95% CI: 1.6%, 5.6%; _*_ *******).Following clinical advice, the EAG accepts that these represent reasonable clinical endpoints (with OS being the most relevant endpoint). 

The benefits of pembrolizumab + SOC over SOC for all primary and secondary endpoints appears to be consistent across all prespecified subgroups and efficacy endpoints, although small sample sizes in some subgroups (principally primary tumour site: hypopharynx) resulted in wide CIs; the results of those analyses should therefore be interpreted with caution. 

The incidence of AEs overall, including drug-related AEs, AEs leading to death, and Grade 3 to 5 AEs in the pembrolizumab + SOC group were similar to the SOC group. However, the incidence of the following types of AE were higher in the pembrolizumab + SOC group than the SOC group: SAEs; drug-related SAEs; drug discontinuation due to an AE; and drug discontinuation due to the following: a drug-related AEs, SAEs or drug-related SAEs. The EAG notes that the AE profile is likely to be affected by longer treatment duration in the pembrolizumab + SOC group. 

74 



<!-- page 470 -->

The EAG judged the overall risk of bias of KEYNOTE-689 to have ‘Some concerns’. This was because the trial was judged to be at low risk of bias for the categories of randomisation, missing outcome data and data selection, but judged to have ‘Some concerns’ for the two categories covering deviations and the measurement of some outcomes (which also affected the ‘missing outcome data’). 

The EAG agrees with the company that an indirect treatment comparison comparing pembrolizumab with therapies other than SOC (radiotherapy ± cisplatin) was not necessary because KEYNOTE-689 provided direct evidence for the treatment comparison of most relevance to this appraisal.

## **4 Cost effectiveness** 

## **4.1 Critique of the review of cost-effectiveness evidence** 

## 4.1.1 Search strategy 

The search strategies for the economic evaluation SLRs were performed in April 2025. Publications related to cost-effectiveness and cost and healthcare resource use were searched for using one set of search strings (reported in CS Appendix E) and then screened for inclusion in the relevant review. HRQoL studies and health state utility values studies were searched for separately (reported in CS Appendix F). 

The eligibility criteria reported in CS Appendix E1.2 indicates that a broader population was searched for (locally advanced HNSCC patients with unresectable status or unknown resectability status), although a core scope (to match the population of the KEYNOTE-689 trial, including the requirement for patients to have resected/resectable disease) was prioritised during screening. If no studies from the core scope were identified, then studies matching the broader scope were included. 

A comprehensive range of databases were searched: Embase; MEDLINE, including MEDLINE In Process; and EconLit. Although the CS reports that NHS EED, DARE, International HTA database and Tufts CEA registry were also searched, search strategies were not reported. The company’s response to clarification question A8 provided these, along with updated PRISMA diagrams incorporating the number of search results from these databases. Database searching was supplemented by searching a comprehensive set of relevant conference proceedings and HTA websites for the years 2021-2025 to retrieve relevant results not indexed by Embase. 

The search reported in Appendix E, Table 22 was a simultaneous search of MEDLINE and Embase conducted on Embase.com. During the clarification round, the EAG queried this approach because it may be subject to potential issues with the platform mapping the two distinct controlled vocabularies used for MEDLINE and Embase in an unpredictable manner. The company’s response to clarification question A4 that the Embase.com platform does effectively handle mapping MeSH terms from imported MEDLINE records to the Emtree subject headings used for Embase. The EAG is unable to access Embase.com to assess this more fully, although it accepts that the risk of missing studies through imperfect subject heading mapping is low. 

CS Appendix, E Section E1.1 and Appendix F, Section F1.1.mention that filters were used to ensure the search matched the relevant review question. The company’s response to clarification question A6 confirms that the sources for these filters were the Scottish Intercollegiate Guideline Network (SIGN) 

76 



<!-- page 472 -->

and Canada’s Drug Agency (CDA-AMC), and that they had been modified for use in the searches to align with the objective of the SLRs. The EAG considers it best practice to use validated search filters without modification for most reliable results, and to justify reasonable modifications where they have been made. 

Overall, the searches for the economic evaluation SLRs have been effectively conducted to identify relevant studies of cost-effectiveness, HRQoL, health state utility valuation studies and cost and healthcare resource use. 

## 4.1.2 Identified studies 

CS Appendix E reports the results of the economic SLR. Three studies were identified for the core scope (including only resectable patients with LA HNSCC), and a further 10 studies were identified for the broader scope (including LA HNSCC patients regardless of resectability). 

None of the three ‘core scope’ studies were conducted in the UK, whereas three ‘broader scope’ studies were UK-specific. Out of the three UK studies, two studies relate to the appraisal of cetuximab in addition to radiotherapy versus radiotherapy alone for LA HNSCC in NICE and SMC,[21, 30] whereas the third was a cost-utility analysis of docetaxel as induction chemotherapy followed by chemoradiation.[31] 

## 4.1.3 Interpretation of the review 

None of the included studies in either scope were UK studies relevant to the current decision problem, thus the company developed a _de novo_ economic model (outlined in Section 4.2.2). 

## **4.2 Critique of the submitted economic evaluation** 

Section 4.2 provides a summary and critique of the methods of the economic evaluation submitted by the company, with results summarised in Section 5.1. Unless otherwise stated, it reflects the version submitted following the clarification request. The EAG’s exploratory analyses to explore areas of uncertainty identified in the company’s analysis are summarised in Section 5.2.

## 4.2.2 Population 

The modelled population considered by the company for this STA is adults with untreated, newly diagnosed, resectable, LA HNSCC who have PD-L1 CPS≥1. This is **************************************************** . 

The modelled population is narrower than the NICE final scope, which includes people with PD-L1 CPS≥1 only as a subgroup but the EAG does not consider this to be unreasonable as the pre-specified analysis of KEYNOTE-689 and clinical data used in the economic model used to estimate cost‐ effectiveness reflect this subgroup. 

Baseline characteristics of the modelled population are reflective of the ‘all comer’ cohort of KEYNOTE‐689, which is the key trial used for this STA. Table 24 of the CS presents these characteristics including BSA, and glomerular filtration rate (GFR). BSA was used for calculating the doses of cisplatin, 5-FU, cetuximab, gemcitabine, paclitaxel, pemetrexed, and methotrexate, whereas GFR was used to calculate the dose of carboplatin. 

## 4.2.3 Interventions and comparators 

The intervention considered for the economic analysis is perioperative pembrolizumab in addition to SOC. Pembrolizumab, which is an IV infusion, is delivered as a monotherapy 200 mg every three weeks (Q3W) in the neoadjuvant setting for a maximum of two cycles. Conditional on eligibility, this is followed by surgical resection which is the first step of the SOC arm. 

79 



<!-- page 475 -->

After surgery, patients receive pembrolizumab in addition to SOC, which comprises radiotherapy with or without cisplatin. In KEYNOTE-689, pembrolizumab 200 mg IV was given for a maximum of 15 three-week cycles postoperatively. Cisplatin 100 mg/m[2] is given to patients with high-risk pathological features following surgery for a maximum of three three-week cycles, whereas radiotherapy is given to patients regardless of the patient’s classification as having high or low risk pathological features. 

In the adjuvant setting, pembrolizumab can be given as a 400 mg IV Q6W as an alternative to the Q3W dosing schedule. Of note, the CS base case uses the three-week regimen only for the first cycle adjuvant cycle which is followed by seven cycles of 400 mg Q6W. This was assumed due to service capacity constraints, where the initial two doses were spaced at three weeks to reflect “ _closer patient monitoring as they reinitiate treatment with pembrolizumab after surgery, and to prevent delivering a higher total dose of pembrolizumab over the full treatment schedule than is specified in the protocol_ .” The dosing regimen assumed in the model provides a total dose which is in line with the total pembrolizumab dose received in KEYNOTE-689. The EAG’s clinical experts agreed that the six weekly pembrolizumab dosing is preferred in clinical practice. 

Radiotherapy dosing depended on the patient’s risk level. Low-risk patients received 2 Gy per day in 30 fractions (total of 60 Gy) compared to 33 fractions (total of 66 Gy) for high-risk patients, and 35 fractions (total of 70 Gy) for patients with gross residual disease. 

## 4.2.4 Model structure 

A _de novo_ state transition model was developed in Microsoft Excel[®] to assess the cost‐effectiveness of perioperative pembrolizumab + SOC compared with SOC alone. The model structure developed by the company aims to simulate the disease pathway after diagnosis of resectable stage III-IVa LA HNSCC, in that patients can remain event‐free, experience either a local/salvageable or incurable recurrence or die. Thus, the health states included in the model are event-free (EF), local or salvageable recurrence (L/SR), incurable recurrence/progression (IRP) and death. Figure 10 presents the model schematic. Although the company describes it’s submitted as a Markov model, time-varying transition probabilities are allowed for transitions out of the EF state. However, the Markovian assumption of constant hazards over time is applied to transitions from the intermediate states (L/SR and IRP). 

80 



<!-- page 476 -->

**Figure 10 Model structure (reproduced from CS, Figure 17)** 

**==> picture [397 x 268] intentionally omitted <==**

All patients enter the model in the EF health state following diagnosis and remain in this state until recurrence of disease or death. Recurrence of disease in the model is defined as either local or salvageable recurrence (where subsequent treatment, if any, is given with curative intent) or incurable recurrence (whereby cancer has spread to a distant organ/site and treatment is given with palliative intent). Transitions from the EF health state to the L/SR state, IRP state and death are informed by analyses of individual patient data (IPD) from KEYNOTE‐689 (as discussed in Section 4.2.6). 

In the L/SR health state, a proportion of patients receive salvage surgery or radiotherapy and remain in this health state if their disease does not progress further, or they die (transition to the death state). If the disease progresses, patients transition to the IRP health state. Transitions from the L/SR health state to the IRP health state and death are informed by analyses of IPD from KEYNOTE‐689 (as discussed in Section 4.2.6. 

Patients who transition to the IRP health state remain in this state until death. The IRP state consists of two sub-states which the CS does not explicitly mention: pre-progression IRP and post-progression IRP. This structure enables the costs and HRQoL implications of metastatic HNSCC to be more accurately captured and is reflective of the health states that would typically be included in metastatic oncology modelling; however, these sub-states were not independently modelled (i.e., using separate transition probabilities). 

81 



<!-- page 477 -->

The pre-progression IRP state represents patients who have a confirmed IRP recurrence; all patients who transition to the IRP health state enter the pre-progression sub-state and a proportion of patients are assumed to receive first-line systemic therapy for metastatic HNSCC. The post-progression IRP state represents patients who have progressed on first-line therapy; a proportion of these patients are assumed to receive second-line systemic therapy for metastatic HNSCC. 

The expected proportion of time spent pre- versus post-progression within the IRP state was estimated using the ratio of mean PFS and OS of first-line treatments for recurrent/metastatic HNSCC. This is based on the treatments received in the pembrolizumab + SOC and SOC arms in the KEYNOTE-689 trial, which are provided in Table 52 of the CS and the details of the approach are outlined in CS Appendix J2. The mean PFS and OS (in weeks) were determined according to the following steps for each arm: 

- 1) A reference treatment, cetuximab + platinum + 5-FU (the comparator from KEYNOTE-048, a Phase 3 RCT of pembrolizumab ± chemotherapy versus cetuximab + chemotherapy in patients with incurable untreated R/M HNSCC) was chosen and the weekly exponential rates of OS and PFS were evaluated for the CPS≥1, untreated population using the reported median survival. 

- 2) For the other first-line treatments, HRs identified from a SLR for recurrent/metastatic HNSCC with CPS≥1 were synthesised and HRs corresponding to the treatment versus the reference treatment were estimated within a fixed effect NMA (see Appendix J4 and Table 67 of CS Appendix J2). Two treatment regimens, gemcitabine + paclitaxel and cisplatin + pemetrexed, could not be connected within the NMA and thus the exponential rates were evaluated directly as a function of the reported median OS and PFS without applying HRs, see Table 66 in CS Appendix J2. The treatments 5-FU monotherapy, methotrexate monotherapy and cisplatin + paclitaxel did not have OS or PFS data available for synthesis and instead the efficacy was assumed to be equal to that of similar chemotherapy regimens (for e.g., cisplatin + paclitaxel was assumed the same as cisplatin monotherapy). 

- 3) The estimated HRs for each treatment regimen were applied to the OS and PFS exponential rates of the reference treatment, and the subsequent mean OS and PFS evaluated for that treatment regimen. 

- 4) The overall mean OS and PFS (averaging over all first-line treatments) was calculated as a weighted average, according to the market shares of first-line treatments for recurrent/metastatic HNSCC (see Table 52 of the CS). 

- 5) The ratio of the overall mean PFS and overall mean OS was subsequently evaluated. The ratio of PFS:OS therefore represents the proportion of time within the IRP state that a patient spends in the pre-progression IRP sub-state, while 1 - (PFS/OS) represents the remaining proportion of time spent in the post-progression IRP sub-state. 

82 



<!-- page 478 -->

The ratio of mean PFS:OS was then calculated for each model arm, and this ratio was used to determine the relative weight given to the pre-progression IRP versus post-progression IRP values for utility values (Section 4.2.8) and disease management costs (Section 4.2.9) as these factors differ between the two sub-states. In the company’s base case analysis, these estimated PFS and OS ratios do not inform the estimated time to death for the IRP state, which is instead based on parametric survival models fitted to the KEYNOTE-689 trial (Section 4.2.6.4). 

The company assumed a model cycle length of one week with half‐cycle correction applied. The model time horizon was set to 40.1 years (lifetime), as the mean age in KEYNOTE‐689 at baseline was 59.9 years. The perspective of the analysis was based on the UK NHS, with costs and benefits discounted using a rate of 3.5%, as per the NICE reference case. 

## 4.2.4.1 EAG Critique of the model structure 

The EAG considers the company’s model structure to be generally appropriate. However, some concerns were identified regarding how the health states were defined and parameterised. The distinction between L/SR and IRP states seems subjective and dependant on the investigator’s notes. Moreover, the presence of such two intermediary states within a transition-based model made it challenging to apply a time-varying hazard of transitioning out of these two states. The company stated that including the potential for time-varying hazards of transitioning out of the intermediate L/SR and IRP states using either tunnel states or visual basic coding would increase complexity and reduce transparency in the model compared with assuming an exponential distribution (clarification response, B11). Hence, the company chose to apply a Markovian assumption for these states and explored only exponential fits for these transitions (see Section 4.2.6). 

The EAG notes that there are some limitations to the approach underpinning the estimate of the preversus post-progression time ratio within the IRP state. Firstly, the NMAs used within the estimation of the ratio of mean PFS and OS for first-line treatments of recurrent/metastatic HNSCC were reliant on the proportional hazards (PH) assumption. The PH assumption was tested using log cumulative hazard plots and there was suggestion that the PH assumption did not hold for all studies within the network. In response to clarification question B13, the company provided Schoenfeld residual plots and applied Grambsch-Therneau tests to assess the PH assumption. The company states that there may have been potential violations of the PH assumption for both OS and PFS in the KEYNOTE-048 trial,[33] for PFS in Burtness _et al_ .,[34] and for OS in Friesland _et al_ .[35] 

Secondly, although the population within the NMAs was restricted to CPS≥1, no additional effect modifiers were discussed or included within the NMAs which may result in biased estimates within the evaluation of the mean PFS and OS. 

83 



<!-- page 479 -->

Thirdly, the reference treatment to which the synthesised HRs are applied was approximated via an exponential fit which assumes constant hazards and is potentially a large simplification of the true observed behaviour and projection of PFS and OS for this treatment. However, the EAG acknowledges that this approach is pragmatic and allows for the incorporation of data from multiple sources in the instance that this ratio could not be estimated using the KEYNOTE-689 data alone.

The company used IPD from KEYNOTE-689 to estimate transitions from the EF, L/SR and IRP states for both the pembrolizumab + SOC and SOC arms.

## 4.2.6.1 Censoring rules applied in the estimation of transition probabilities 

The primary censoring rules for EFS and OS differed in the KEYNOTE-689 analyses. Censoring for EFS was such that patients were censored at the date of last assessment, whereas for OS, patients were censored at the date they were last known to be alive. Therefore, the censoring times under the OS rule were consistently greater than or equal to those in the primary censoring case. According to the primary censoring criteria of KEYNOTE-689, *** and *** patients in the all-comer population were censored in the 25-Jul-2024 DCO Kaplan-Meier analysis of OS and EFS respectively. On average, the date of last disease assessment was *** days before the last date the patient was known to be alive. 

Due to the structural linking of EFS and OS within the company’s model, the censoring of EFS and OS needed to be aligned. In the company’s base case, the censoring according to EFS was employed, and thus OS was re-censored to align with this. OS therefore was censored according to the last disease assessment for patients who are censored according to both EFS and OS, and the last date known alive 

86 



<!-- page 482 -->

for patients who are only censored according to OS. The impact of re-censoring EFS and OS to align the censoring rules is shown in Figure 11 and Figure 12. 

The company selected to use the EFS censoring regime within their base case as EFS was the primary outcome of KEYNOTE-689 and this reflects how patients are followed up in clinical practice.

## 4.2.6.2 Transitions from the EF state 

Within the company’s submitted model, there are three transitions from the EF state (EFàL/SR, EFàIRP and EFàDeath). Transition probabilities were estimated according to a parametric multistate modelling approach described by Williams _et al._[36, 37] using individual patient data from the KEYNOTE-689 trial. Standard parametric models independently fitted to each treatment arm, PH models with a “timeconstant treatment effect” and PH models with a “time-varying treatment effect” were used to estimate cause-specific hazards for each transition for the pembrolizumab + SOC and SOC arms. The transition probabilities within each weekly cycle were evaluated as a function of the three cause-specific hazards by calculating the proportion of the joint hazard of any EFS event attributing to each event type and then converting onto the probability scale, as outlined in the following section. 

## _Estimation of cause-specific hazards and transition probabilities_ 

To calculate the cause-specific hazards with respect to time for each failure type, the individual patient data were first re-censored to account for the competing event types. For each failure type, the two competing failure types were considered censoring events.[38] For example if re-censoring the IPD for EFàL/SR, the competing failure types (EFàIRP and EFàDeath) were treated as censoring events. Parametric models were fit to each of the re-censored datasets. The model fitting was performed using the _flexsurvreg_ package in R.[39] 

For each transition type, thirteen models, were fit to the re-censored data. These models spanned three approaches and included: 

- Approach 1: Independently fitting standard parametric survival models (exponential, Weibull, Gompertz, log-logistic, log-normal, gamma, and generalised gamma distributions) to the pembrolizumab + SOC and SOC arms. The same model choice for both arms was assumed. 

- Approach 2: Jointly fitting PH models with a time-constant treatment effect. This was restricted to the exponential, Weibull and Gompertz models within the PH class. For this approach, a single, constant HR was assumed to apply indefinitely. 

- Approach 3: Jointly fitting PH models with a time-varying treatment effect. As in Approach 2, the three PH models were fitted. Instead of assuming a single constant HR, two HRs were assumed within the model, one corresponding to the model at times less than 1 year, and another for the period from 1 year onwards. The 1-year cut-point was chosen as it corresponds with the maximum duration of adjuvant pembrolizumab. 

88 



<!-- page 484 -->

When implementing Approaches 2 and 3, the PH assumption was initially assessed through the statistical assessment of Schoenfeld residual plots, but following the clarification response, cumulative log-hazard plots were also provided. In the CS the company stated that the PH assumption did not hold for EFàL/SR ( _p_ =0.0351) and that this was supported by the residuals displaying a non-horizontal trend. The PH assumption could not be formally rejected for EFàIRP ( _p_ =0.4414) and EFàDeath ( _p_ =0.0558). The company clarified that because the PH assumption did not hold for one of the three transitions, combinations of models under Approach 2 were excluded; however, the models under Approach 2 were retained for scenario analyses to ensure completeness. 

As both Approach 2 and Approach 3 are reliant on the PH assumption within regions of the data set, and this was demonstrated not to hold for all transitions, the EAG does not expand on these methods further; results for these approaches can be found in Section 3.3 of the CS and CS Appendix J. Additionally, the final 10 candidate models (see Section 4.2.6.5) identified by the company included only models using Approach 1 and thus the EAG considers it is appropriate to focus on this approach within this report.

1. For each cause of failure, denoted 𝑘𝑘, the average cause-specific hazard from week 𝑡𝑡−1 to week 𝑡𝑡, (ℎ𝑘𝑘[(t)][), was calculated as  ]

Where 𝐻𝐻𝑘𝑘(𝑡𝑡) is the cumulative hazard of cause 𝑘𝑘 from the parametric model fitted to the recensored individual patient data for cause 𝑘𝑘 at time 𝑡𝑡.
