To account for background mortality, the transition probability from EFàDeath was constrained to be the maximum value of the model-derived probability of transition to death and the age- and sex-matched background mortality for that cycle. Background mortality rates were derived from the Office for National Statistics (ONS) United Kingdom life tables 2021-2023.[41] A standardised mortality rate (SMR) of 1.0 was assumed. 

The model selection for each transition type from the EF state is further discussed in Section 4.2.6.5. 

## 4.2.6.3 Transitions from the L/SR state 

The cost-effectiveness model is a Markov model and therefore transition probabilities from intermediate states cannot, by design, be dependent on the amount of time spent in the intermediate state. Therefore, exponential models, with constant hazards, were chosen to model the cause-specific hazards of the L/SRàIRP and L/SRàDeath transitions. This choice appears to have been made based on the selection of the Markov structure as opposed to clinical input regarding the plausibility of constant hazards of event within intermediate states. 

As for the transitions from the EF state, IPD from the KEYNOTE-689 trial were used. The PD-L1 CPS≥1 population was used and there were ** patients (** in the pembrolizumab + SOC arm, ** in the SOC arm) who experienced L/SR as their first EFS failure event. 

There were ** (* in the pembrolizumab + SOC arm and * in the SOC arm) patients who first experienced L/SR and subsequently IRP as a recurrence event. To estimate the cause-specific hazards for the L/SRàIRP transition, patients were censored at the earliest of the death date, or date last known to be alive, and an exponential model fit to the re-censored individual patient data. The cumulative incidences predicted by the model and the observed data are shown in Figure 13.

## 4.2.6.4 Transitions from the IRP states 

Following the approach used to model transitions from the L/SR intermediate health state (Section 4.2.6.3), exponential models were fit to the KEYNOTE-689 IPD and were used to estimate the causespecific hazard of the IRPàdeath transition. 

There were *** patients (** in the perioperative pembrolizumab + SOC arm and ** in the SOC arm) who experienced IRP as their first EFS failure event and ** patients (* in the perioperative pembrolizumab + SOC arm and * in the SOC arm) who experienced L/SR followed by IRP as a subsequent recurrence event. Of the patients who experienced IRP as their first EFS failure event, ** patients (** in the perioperative pembrolizumab + SOC arm and ** in the SOC arm) experienced death as a subsequent event. Of the patients who experienced IRP as their second EFS failure event, * patients (* in the perioperative pembrolizumab + SOC arm and * in the SOC arm) experienced death as a subsequent event. These data, from patients who experienced L/SR followed by IRP and those who experience IRP as their first event, were pooled and exponential models were fit to the time from IRP health state entry to death or censoring (due to end of data or loss of follow-up) for each arm. The transition probabilities were subsequently derived from the exponential model rates. As for the EFàDeath and L/SRàDeath transitions, the probability of IRPàDeath was constrained as the maximum of the model-derived probability of transition to death or the age- and sex-matched background mortality for that cycle. ## 4.2.6.5 Selection of base case models 

The CS states that assessing model fit is more challenging in the context of a multistate model as opposed to the context of simpler partitioned survival models. The proportions of individuals experiencing an event are determined by combinations of survival models as opposed to a single survival model.[38] Thus there is a significantly higher number of potential model combinations that must be assessed. 

As exponential models were chosen to model events from intermediate states (L/SRàIRP, L/SRàDeath and IRPàDeath), only the combination of models for EFàL/SR, EFàIRP and EFàDeath needed to be considered during model selection. In accordance with TSD 14, the company chose to the use the same functions for the pembrolizumab + SOC and SOC arms.[42] Under the three approaches outlined in Section 4.2.6.2, with 13 (7 + 3 + 3) candidate model choices for each transition, there was a total of 397 possible combinations of models for the transitions from the EF state. Of these, 343 (7×7×7) combinations corresponded to the models fitted according to Approach 1. 

The choice of models was informed by the following criteria: 

- Statistical fit via the mean squared error (MSE) of the model EFS prediction relative to the 

## observed EFS 

The company states that the Akaike Information Criteria (AIC) “ _is not a suitable measure of fit with observed data when modelling competing risks”_ as per Williams _et al_ ..[36] The MSE of EFS was therefore used as an alternative measure to assess the fit of the predicted EFS curves from different combinations of models with the observed EFS curve. The MSE of EFS was calculated by evaluating the difference between the observed and modelled EFS at weekly intervals and weighted according to the numbers of patients at risk for each combination of models. 

## • Visual assessment of predicted EFS and observed EFS 

Predicted EFS curves from different combinations of models for EFàL/SR, EFàIRP and EFàDeath were compared visually to the observed EFS Kaplan-Meier curve as per the approach by Williams _et al_ .[36] In addition, cumulative incidence curves for each of the individual transitions were compared with the observed cumulative incidence curves from KEYNOTE689. 

93 



<!-- page 489 -->

• Clinical plausibility and external validity of model long-term EFS and OS extrapolations. 

The company conducted a targeted literature review to identify real-world studies reporting long-term EFS and OS outcomes to inform clinical plausibility of the fitted models. The company did not identify any previous studies which implemented treatment strategies including neoadjuvant or perioperative treatment for resectable LA HNSCC. As a result, any identified studies reported DFS as opposed to EFS. There was therefore a discrepancy between the time of randomisation and thus the time for which patients are considered at risk. The company therefore did not identify any studies with comparable EFS data for external validation of the model extrapolations. The company also highlighted significant differences in trial populations, especially with regards to the anatomical site which can be a strong prognostic factor within LA HNSCC. Despite this, the company did use external studies with longerfollow up (with potential caveats) to assess the predicted OS extrapolations for the SOC arm (see CS Appendix J1.4 for full details of studies). The company also sought expert opinion relating to the possibility of long-term trends in EFS such as an observed plateau. The company did not use expert-derived survival estimates to inform the model selection process. The company concluded that the follow-up period of the KEYNOTE-689 trial (approximately 5 years), was sufficient to allow for robust internal validation of candidate models via comparison of the EFS and OS model predictions and observed Kaplan-Meier curves from KEYNOTE689. 

Consideration of the hazard plots for the model combinations was primarily considered when assessing the applicability of the cure assumption (see Section 4.2.6.6) and not during the curve selection process. 

## **Curve selection step 1: Priority transition model choice** 

The company’s model selection process first aimed to prioritise the choice of model for the EFàDeath transition. For each choice of model for the EFàDeath transition, the minimum and average MSE was calculated across all other combinations of models for EFàL/SR and EFàIRP. To evaluate the minimum and average MSE for each model set, the following was performed. 

1. Evaluate the MSE for each individual model combination (i.e., evaluate the MSE for all 397 model combinations). 

2. Group the model combinations according to the choice of distribution for the EFàDeath transition. This results in 13 sets of models corresponding to the use of the exponential, Gompertz, Weibull, log-logistic, log-normal, generalised gamma, and gamma under Approach 1, the 3 time-constant PH models under Approach 2, and the 3 time-varying PH models under Approach 3. 

94 



<!-- page 490 -->

3. For each set according to the choice of model for the EFàDeath transition, evaluate the minimum and average MSE of the set. This corresponded to the minimum/average MSE of 49 model combinations under Approach 1 for each EFàDeath model choice, three sets of 9 model combinations under Approach 2, and three sets of 9 model combinations under Approach 3. 

4. Identify the model set with the lowest minimum and average MSE values to select the model for EFàDeath. 

The company chose to prioritise the EFàDeath transition to initially refine the list of candidate models as assessment of the minimum and average MSEs for each model set resulted in a clearer choice of best distribution for the EFàDeath transition in both arms compared to the other two transitions. According to both the minimum and average MSE for each set, presented in Table 56 of CS Appendix J the generalised gamma distribution for the EFàDeath transition provided the best fit to EFS for both the pembrolizumab + SOC arm and SOC arm. 

As highlighted in Section 4.2.6.2, the PH assumption was shown not to hold for the EFàIRP transition and thus the best fitting models for EFàDeath under Approaches 2 and 3 are not summarised within this report, though the company did explore these to fully assess the potential impact of these approaches on the cost-effectiveness estimates. The EAG does not believe the models under Approaches 2 and 3 are appropriate and therefore focuses on the candidate models under Approach 1 only. 

## **Curve selection step 2: Selection of distributions for remaining transitions** 

Having selected the generalised gamma distribution for the EFàDeath transition, there were 49 candidate model combinations to consider for the remaining two transitions. The visual fit of predicted versus observed cumulative incidence curves was assessed for each candidate combination (see Figure 16, Figure 17 and Figure 18). 

Within Figure 16, the colour family corresponds to one model fitted to the EFàL/SR cause-specific hazards, and the different shades correspond to the different models for EFàIRP (i.e., the red colour family corresponds to the seven models where the EFàL/SR transition is modelled by the exponential, and the different shades of red correspond to combinations where EFàIRP is modelled via the exponential, Weibull, Gompertz, log-logistic, log-normal, generalised gamma and gamma distributions). Therefore, for each colour, there are seven curves corresponding to the different combinations of models under that choice of the EFàL/SR model. In Figure 17 and Figure 18, each colour family instead corresponds to the model choice for the EFàIRP state, and the different shades correspond to the different model choices for the EFàL/SR state (i.e., the red colour family corresponds 

95 



<!-- page 491 -->

to the seven models where the EFàIRP transition is modelled by the exponential, and the different shades of red correspond to combinations where EFàL/SR is modelled via the exponential, Weibull, Gompertz, log-logistic, log-normal, generalised gamma and gamma distributions). 

For both arms, all combinations of models, except models which applied the exponential model to the EFàL/SR state, showed good visual fit of the cumulative incidence of EFàL/SR (see Figure 16). As shown in Figure 17, it was evident that models applying the Gompertz distribution for EFàIRP tended to produce the best visual fit of predicted versus observed cumulative incidence for EFàIRP. The company also identified the generalised gamma distribution as a candidate model choice for EFàIRP. There was little difference between the predicted and observed EFàDeath cumulative incidence under the candidate models; however, there was variability in the long-term projections of cumulative incidence between the models. 

Following these visual assessments, the company identified 12 candidate models under Approach 1, which applied either the Gompertz or generalised gamma distribution for EFàIRP, the generalised gamma distribution for EFàDeath and excluded the exponential distribution for EFàL/SR.

## **Curve selection step 3: Statistical assessment of candidate models** 

All model combinations following selection of the generalised gamma distribution for the EFàDeath transition were ranked according to their MSE of EFS for each arm. The MSE for each of the 12 candidate models all resided in the top half of the rankings for best statistical fit according to MSE (Table 58 and Table 61 in the CS Appendix J). 

It was noted that the MSE for the SOC arm was generally higher than the MSE for the pembrolizumab + SOC arm, indicating a poorer fit, therefore the choice of model combination was driven by the ranking according to the SOC arm. 

Two model combinations from the 12 candidate models (Weibull/ Gompertz/ generalised gamma and gamma/ Gompertz/ generalised gamma given as EFàL/SR / EFàIRP / EFàDeath respectively) were excluded from further analysis as they did not appear in the top 10 MSE ranked distributions in the SOC arm. 

## **Curve selection step 4: Comparison of predicted versus observed EFS and OS** 

All 10 candidate model combinations provided good agreement to the observed OS from KEYNOTE689 for the pembrolizumab + SOC and SOC arms, as presented in Figure 19 and Figure 20, respectively. In addition to the candidate model extrapolations for the SOC arm, longer-term data from three external studies are displayed. These three studies are not directly comparable to KEYNOTE-689, due to differences in population and thus present a large variability in long-term survival. The study reported by Leeman _et al_ . predominantly included patients with oropharyngeal disease.[43] Of these patients 48% were HPV-positive which is associated with a better prognosis than HPV-independent disease. Burbure _et al_ . and Chen _et al_ . both report survival for hypopharyngeal patients who historically have worse outcomes compared with other tumour sites.[44, 45] However, the company highlight in Section 3.3.2.3 of the CS that the candidate model projections fall within the range of these external studies which supports their selection as candidate models.

## **Curve selection step 5: Assessment of incremental EFS and OS benefit at 10 years** 

Finally, the incremental benefits between the pembrolizumab + SOC and SOC arms for EFS and OS were evaluated at 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 10 years, see Table 19. The incremental benefits at 1 to 5 years could be compared with the observed incremental benefits observed within the KEYNOTE-689 trial. All 10 candidate models resulted in close predictions of the observed incremental benefits for both EFS and OS, see Table 19. 

At 10 years, the log-normal/Gompertz/generalised gamma distribution resulted in incremental benefits of 6.7 and 6.8 percentage points for EFS and OS respectively, which appeared to be an outlier compared to the 9 remaining distributions. It was highlighted by the company’s clinical experts that patients who remain event-free at 5 years would be considered cured in both arms and a plateau in the EFS would be expected after 5 years. The log-normal/Gompertz/Generalised model choice does not show this behaviour, however, the company retained this distribution for use as a pessimistic scenario, as outlined in Section 4.2.6.6. 

The company identified the generalised gamma/generalised gamma/generalised gamma  model combination as having the largest incremental EFS benefit at 10-years and also retained this for a scenario analysis.

## **Selected base case model** 

Following the approach outlined in the previous sections, the company selected the Gompertz/Gompertz/generalised gamma model combination as their base case. This model choice was deemed to be the best-fitting model according to the assessment of MSE of EFS, visual assessment of cumulative incidence curves, comparison of observed versus predicted EFS and OS (see Figure 27 and Figure 28), a mid-range predicted incremental EFS and OS among the ten candidate models, and consistency with expert opinion regarding long-term plateauing of the EFS curve. Further to this, this combination of models ranked first for the SOC arm MSE analysis, see Table 61, CS Appendix J. 

The selected base case model combination resulted in the capping of the EFàDeath, and L/SRàDeath transition probabilities to that of the background population (derived from age- and sex-matched lifetables) due to the model estimated transition probabilities dropping below the corresponding background probabilities. In the company’s base case, the capping for EFàDeath at weeks 628 and 471 for pembrolizumab + SOC and SOC respectively, and for L/SRàDeath at week 2036 for the pembrolizumab + SOC arm only. Following these time points, the probability of death for the age-, sexmatched background population was used with an SMR=1.0.

## 4.2.6.6 Selection of scenario analyses 

## **Alternative model choice for transitions from the EF state** 

As highlighted in the Section 4.2.6.5, out of the 10 candidate models the lognormal/Gompertz/generalised gamma model combination was selected as a pessimistic scenario as this model predicts the lowest incremental EFS and OS benefits at 10-years (Scenario SA2, CS, Table 61). 

The generalised gamma/generalised gamma/generalised Gamma model provided the largest incremental benefit out of the 10 candidate models and was chosen as a complementary scenario analysis (Scenario SA1, CS, Table 61). 

Additional model combinations under Approaches 2 and 3 were also included in scenario analyses conducted by the company (Scenarios SA5 and SA6 in CS, Table 61); however, these are not presented within this report due to the aforementioned reasons relating to the applicability of the PH assumption. 

## **Alternative choice of priority transition in curve selection step 1** 

During the clarification stage, the EAG asked the company to conduct the curve selection process using a different priority transition within the first step of the curve selection process (see clarification response, question B5). The company stated that when EFàL/SR or EFàIRP was prioritised, different best fitting models for the priority transition were identified for the two arms. 

However, the company did explore the selection of EFàL/SR as the priority transition, as discussed in the response to clarification question B5. The prioritisation of this transition followed the approach in 

110 



<!-- page 506 -->

TA1017 where the transition with the fewest numbers of events was chosen as the candidate distribution.[46] 

The Gompertz distribution was selected as the most appropriate model for the EFàL/SR transition as this was ranked second best fitting according to minimum and average MSE for both the pembrolizumab + SOC and SOC arms (Table 21 of the clarification response). The best-fitting model differed for the pembrolizumab + SOC and SOC arms (generalised gamma and log-normal respectively); this is explored further in Section 4.2.6.7. The selection of the Gompertz model therefore reflected a pragmatic approach to balance the accuracy of the fit according to EFS and ensuring the same model was selected for both arms. 

Despite prioritising EFàL/SR, the company resulted in the selection of the same base case scenario. Two additional candidate combinations were identified and explored in SA24 and SA25 in the clarification response. 

## **Use of observed cumulative incidence curves up to 32 weeks** 

Despite the highly flexible nature of the employed approach, the EAG noted that the company’s base case model combination provides a relatively poor fit to the cumulative incidence curve for the EFàIRP transition for the SOC arm (Figure 17). During the clarification stage the EAG requested the trial of more flexible models such as spline models in order to improve the fit for the cumulative incidence comparison (see clarification response, question B2). 

In its response, the company stated that the inclusion of spline models within the curve selection process would have further complicated the selection of the base case. Additionally, the company stated that the inclusion of spline models could have led to over-fitting due to the approach currently employed already being flexible due to the combination of three model types. 

The company also highlighted that the sharp increase observed in the cumulative incidence of EFàIRP in the SOC arm is likely to be an artefact due to the scheduling of the first CT/MRI of these patients at 12 weeks (±7 days), (see Figure 17). 

Despite the deviation between the observed and predicted cumulative incidence only occurring for a short period within the follow-up, the company provided a scenario whereby the observed cumulative incidence was used for all transitions up to 32 weeks, and the base case parametric distributions used thereafter. This approach therefore aimed to capture behaviours relating to the more nuanced shape of the EFàIRP cumulative incidence for the SOC arm. This scenario did however still utilise parametric 

111 



<!-- page 507 -->

fits in the tail region which were derived from the entirety of the observed data, see SA23 in the clarification response for further details. 

## **Consideration of cure** 

The company was advised by its clinical experts that the majority of recurrences within this population were likely to occur within the first two years. Any patients remaining event-free at 5 years following treatment would be considered functionally cured and discharged. It was highlighted that the risk of recurrence would not be zero. This was believed to apply to both the pembrolizumab + SOC and SOC arms. 

The selected base case model choice appears to capture this plateau in EFS for both arms and also has low hazard rates for both arms implying a low risk of recurrence, thus reflecting the clinical expert opinion, see Figure 25. The company therefore believes that the potential for cure has already been captured by the base case model and concluded that including a further structural cure assumption in the base case model would potentially “overestimate and potentially double count” the likelihood of cure within the population. 

The company did however also present a scenario analysis whereby a structural cure assumption was applied to the base case, with an instantaneous application of the cure assumption at 5 years applying a 95% risk reduction in the predicted probability of recurrence or death from the EF state (Scenario SA7, CS, Table 61). 

In its response to clarification question B9, the company highlighted that the application of the cure assumption should be considered on a curve-specific basis, in that the behaviour of the EFS extrapolations at 5 years should be considered, as well as the hazard rates. Therefore, some distribution choices for the transitions from the EF state may result in models whereby the clinical expert opinion is not captured fully, and thus the cure assumption could be applied in these cases without the risk of overestimating the likelihood of the cure. 

The company highlighted that for the pessimistic scenario analysis, whereby the incremental EFS and OS benefits are shown to be the least out of the 10 candidate models (log-normal/Gompertz/generalised gamma), the EFS hazard of both arms steeply decline, as expected, but then cross which lacks face validity (Figure 25). The application of the cure assumption mitigates this effect of hazards crossing and is explored as an additional scenario analysis (Scenario SA4, CS, Table 61). 

112 



<!-- page 508 -->

For the optimistic scenario analysis (generalised Gamma/generalised gamma/generalised gamma), the hazard rates appear to be approximately twice the magnitude of those observed in the base case which may not reflect the clinical expert opinion received by the company (Figure 25). This combination of models also does not capture the plateau in EFS. Therefore, the company further explored the application of the cure assumption to this scenario as an additional analysis (Scenario SA3, CS, Table 61). 

## **Alternative transition probability for IRPà Death** 

The company also presented a scenario analysis (Scenario SA10, CS, Table 61) where efficacy data from subsequent treatments used within the IRP state were used to estimate transitions from IRPà death instead of data from KEYNOTE-689 (details provided in Section 4.2.2 and CS Appendix J2). 

The weekly hazard rate was evaluated by dividing 1 by the mean OS (evaluated as the weighted average according to market shares) for each arm independently. The alternative exponential hazard rates for the pembrolizumab + SOC and SOC arms used in the scenario analysis are presented in Table 68, CS Appendix J. 

## **Alternative censoring** 

The primary censoring rules for EFS and OS differed in the KEYNOTE-689 analyses. As EFS and OS are structurally linked within the model, the impact of censoring according to the OS censoring regime, as opposed to that employed for EFS as in the base case, was assessed in a scenario analysis (Scenarios SA8 and SA9, CS, Table 61). 

The EFS data were re-censored according to the OS censoring rule and the same approach to fit parametric models to each of the transitions from the EF state was applied, as outlined in CS Appendix J3. Models for each of the competing events were chosen using the same model selection process and transition probabilities for each of the transitions evaluated using the approaches outlined in Section 4.2.6.2. 

The Gompertz distribution for EFàL/SR and EFàIRP and the generalised gamma distribution for EFàdeath were selected as the most clinically plausible combination of models for both arms. This, as for the base case, was based on evaluation of the MSE, visual fit of cumulative incidence functions, clinical plausibility assessed via incremental EFS and OS, and visual fit to EFS and OS curves (according to the alternative censoring regime) from KEYNOTE-689. Seven other finalist combinations of models were identified under the alternative censoring rule and were tested as scenario analyses, though only the results for the scenario analysis corresponding to the use of the Gompertz model for EFàL/SR and the generalised gamma for EFàIRP and EFàDeath were presented. 

113 



<!-- page 509 -->

## 4.2.6.7 Critique of approach to include treatment effectiveness 

The EAG believes that the overall approach to the selection of models within this multistate approach is pragmatic and captures a representative range of scenarios that reflect the potential uncertainty in long-term clinical effectiveness regarding EFS and OS given the current data available (IA1) and the restriction to the standard parametric models. There is uncertainty in the survival outcomes of this patient group within the KEYNOTE-689 trial due to the high degree of censoring at approximately 3 years. This therefore results in uncertainty when  assessing the visual fit of the OS model estimates to the observed OS data and thus model selection. 

The base case model combination selected by the company reflects clinical opinion from the EAG clinical experts including that: (i) it is not expected for OS to converge between 10-15 years; (ii) relapses following 5 years are rare and (iii) the majority of transitions from the EF state are to death as opposed to L/SR or IRP. Clinical experts also suggested that the observation that EFàIRP is lower in the pembrolizumab + SOC arm compared to the SOC is plausible due to the potential mechanism of action of the neoadjuvant and adjuvant use of pembrolizumab. 

Additionally, from the EAG’s own analyses, it is evident that the combination of models for the transitions from the EF state is highly multi-modal, with many model combinations presenting similar overall fits to the observed EFS and OS. However, the EAG notes some potential limitations to the methods employed. 

Whilst the EAG appreciates that it may not be appropriate to use the AIC and BIC when selecting the individual models for each of the transition types, as per Williams _et al._ ,[36] the use of the MSE to identify the best fitting combination of models for EFS is not necessarily validated within the literature. Therefore, this approach may have limitations and may not robustly identify the most applicable models. The EAG is generally content with the approach adopted but highlights that there may be limitations in this approach. 

In curve selection step 1, the company uses the aggregate minimum and average MSE evaluated across all model combinations within each set to select the optimum model choice for the EFàDeath transition (Section 4.2.6.5). The EAG notes that by adopting this approach and considering the minimum and average MSE to select the model for the EFàDeath transition, some model combinations which provide adequate fits to the EFS and OS may have been excluded early within the curve selection process and thus not considered later in subsequent analyses. The full plausible range of model extrapolations may therefore not have been captured within the scenario analyses adopted by the company. 

114 



<!-- page 510 -->

Within TSD 14 and TSD21 it is recommended that the hazard trend of candidate models should be considered when selecting a base case and scenario analyses.[42, 47] The overall predicted hazards for EFS and OS should have been compared to the observed empirical hazards for EFS and OS and factored into the model selection process. On clarification, the company did provide the necessary figures to facilitate this comparison, but the figures provided by the company appeared to have been subject to heavy smoothing and the methods to produce the plots were unclear. However it was noted that all ten candidate models demonstrated ********************************* in the EFS hazard (Figure 25), but this behaviour was not evident in the smoothed EFS hazard (Figure 23). This, however, may be an artefact of the smoothing approach employed by the company, but as mentioned previously, the approach to generate the hazard plots was not described in sufficient detail. Despite this, the overall trend in the hazard, ignoring the **************************************, appears to align with the model predicted hazard trend. 

The approach employed by the company relies on the assumption that there is no strong reason to assume different curve selections across the two arms. However, the two treatment arms do differ, for instance in the inclusion of a neoadjuvant component of the treatment regimen versus no neoadjuvant treatment, and a prolongation of the adjuvant treatment period, and thus there could be rationale for different models across the two arms, but this was not considered. Additionally, the selected base case and scenario analyses appear to provide a generally poorer fit to the observed data in the SOC arm which could reflect the need for different model choices for the two arms. However, both the clinical experts to the company and to the EAG supported the argument that if patients remained event-free until 5 years, they could be considered functionally cured, and thus the projected long-term EFS and OS behaviour is likely to be consistent across both arms. Additionally, the EAG highlights that the consideration of differing models across the arms would result in a greater number of potential model combinations to consider which would require more complex approaches for curve selection in order to retain robustness and clarity of the selection process. 

More fundamentally, the use of the exponential model for transitions from the intermediate states is a limitation of this approach. The EAG highlights that alternative models could have better captured transitions from the intermediate states, though this would necessitate a semi-Markov model structure, allowing for time-varying hazards of transitioning out of the intermediate states. Further to this, there are very few events informing the L/SRàIRP transition, particularly in the SOC arm (Section 4.2.6.3). This low number of events could therefore lead to high uncertainty in the fit of the exponential providing unstable estimates of the exponential rate parameter. In response to the classification request (B10), the company explored the impact of pooling data across arms when estimating the rates for transitions out 

115 



<!-- page 511 -->

of the L/SR state in a scenario analysis. The EAG preferred to incorporate these pooled estimates for transitions out of the L/SR state in its base case (see Section 5.2.2 and 5.2.3). 

When the transition probabilities from IRPàDeath were evaluated using the efficacy and market shares for treatments for relapsed/metastatic disease, the risk of death from the IRP state was found to be higher for the pembrolizumab + SOC arm, whereas in the company base case, where KEYNOTE-689 data was used, the risk of death from the IRP state was higher in the SOC arm. Clinical experts to the EAG stated that the case in which the risk of death from IRP is highest in the pembrolizumab + SOC arm could reflect the potentially reduced treatment options within this arm, but that there are little data to inform this. They also noted that it would be clinically plausible for pembrolizumab to improve survival for patients experiencing disease progression if the treatment results in recurrent disease that is less extensive. However, further long-term follow-up would be needed to demonstrate any such benefit. The company also highlighted that in the scenario analysis, a conservative approach is assumed whereby there is no ongoing benefit from perioperative pembrolizumab +SOC relative to SOC in the IRP state. Whereas, in the base case, where the transition probabilities were estimated using the KEYNOTE-689 trial data, these benefits would be captured. The company stated that this ongoing benefit could counteract the lack of available immunotherapy treatment options available to these patients at this later stage. The EAG therefore believes this to be an uncertain area of the model. To address this uncertainty the EAG explored the impact of pooling events across arms for transitions out of the IRP state. It combined this with pooling events out of the L/SR state in its EAG exploratory analyses (See Section 5.2.2) and incorporated this change in it base case (see Section 5.2.3). However, as it considered this to be an area of uncertainty, the EAG also explored removing this from its base case in its scenario analyses (see Section 5.2.4) 

The company surmises that due to the shapes and magnitudes of the observed EFS hazard in the base case, the cure assumption should not be applied but should be considered for the two scenario curve combinations. The company states that the appropriateness of applying the cure assumption for a particular set of curves should be considered on a case-by-case basis. The EAG agrees with this but highlights that the company has not provided a set of definitive rules for making this judgement. Therefore, choice of whether to apply the cure assumption remains potentially subjective. The company also did not comment on the behaviour of the fitted Gompertz distributions which exhibit effective plateauing behaviour for EFàL/SR and EFàIRP for both arms. The EAG believes that any cure-like behaviour should be captured via an intentional structural assumption (i.e., via the cure assumption) as opposed to the use of these Gompertz distributions with effective plateauing behaviours. Therefore, the EAG’s adoption of a base case model without explicit use of the Gompertz, further explores the 

116 



<!-- page 512 -->

potential implications of this (see Section 4.2.6.8 for discussion of the EAG’s preferred alternative model, with the impact on the cost-effectiveness results presented in Section 5.2.2). 

The application of the cure assumption in the company’s model occurs instantaneously at 5 years and imposes a risk reduction of 95% to the transitions from the EF state. Though the EAG’s clinical advisors agree with this timepoint for a potential cure, this approach is somewhat simplistic and results in a discontinuous hazard for EFS and OS in both SA1 and SA2. The EAG notes that if cure was believed to be plausible within this population, approaches including dedicated cure methods could have been explored, for instance by fitting parametric mixture-cure models to the EFS IPD and assessing whether a non-zero cure fraction is consistently predicted across different models, the EAG has further explored this in Section 4.2.6.8, with the impact on the cost-effectiveness results presented in Section 5.2.2. 

Additionally, a SMR equal to 1.0 is assumed within the model meaning no excess mortality was applied to the general population mortality to model background mortality for this appraisal’s population. The EAG notes that the choice of this value does not appear to have been explored, nor does this choice appear to have been validated by clinical experts. Clinical experts highlighted that this population may be subject to other comorbidities following longer survival, and thus the impact of a non-unity SMR should have been explored. The EAG also explores this further in Section 4.2.6.8, with the impact on the cost-effectiveness results presented in Section 5.2.2. 

Within the company’s base case and the majority of scenario analyses, the EFS censoring regime was chosen. The EAG agrees with this decision, as the alternative censoring regime (used for OS within KEYNOTE-689) would result in the assumption that between the time of last-assessment and last known date alive, any patient who has not had a recurrence/progression at their last assessment, must remain progression-free until the date they are known to be alive. In some cases, this period between the last assessment and the last date known alive was considerable, hence this assumption may not hold. This is a fundamental feature and challenge associated with the KEYNOTE-689 trial design. The EAG is however content with the primary use of the EFS censoring rules and the subsequent exploration of the impact of censoring according to the OS censoring rules. 

Finally, whilst the EFS data appears to have sufficient follow-up and events to enable some meaningful comparison of estimated EFS and observed EFS, the OS data is subject to a large degree of censoring beyond 3 years and is comparatively immature. Therefore, when comparing the estimated OS with the observed OS, there is a potentially high degree of uncertainty. The current data and analyses correspond to IA1 and the company states in the Section 2 summary of the CS that the KEYNOTE-689 trial is ongoing and may provide additional evidence in the next 12 months. Additional follow-up may impact 

117 



<!-- page 513 -->

the final choices of model combinations for transitions from the EF state, though the EAG notes that the OS data is only used for visual assessment of estimated model fits to the observed data, unlike the EFS which is used when assessing the statistical fit of the curves. The high degree of censoring in the OS data, means that there is uncertainty regarding the survival outcomes of this patient group within the KEYNOTE-689 trial, and thus also a source of uncertainty within the cost-effectiveness assessment. 

## 4.2.6.8 Additional work conducted by the EAG 

To further supplement the evidence provided by the company and explore some areas of uncertainty in the modelling of the treatment efficacy, the EAG conducted several additional analyses which are outlined in the following sections. 

## _EAG base case model combination_ 

The Gompertz distributions used to model EF  L/SR and EF  IRP exhibited effective plateaus for both the pembrolizumab + SOC and SOC arms, as discussed in 4.2.6.7. Following this, and as per Section 4.2.6.7, the EAG believes that any cure-like behaviour should be captured via an inherent structural assumption which implements cure within the model. The EAG has therefore identified an alternative combination of models for transitions from the EF state. 

The EAG has selected the model combination which did not use a Gompertz model for either EF  L/SR or EF  IRP, with the lowest EFS MSE for the SOC arm from Table 61 of the CS, Appendix J. The SOC arm was prioritised when identifying this model combination due to the generally poorer fits observed for the SOC arm compared to the pembrolizumab + SOC arm. The log-normal/generalised gamma/generalised gamma was ranked first out of all model combinations under Approach 1 for the SOC arm and ranked fifth for the pembrolizumab + SOC arm (Table 58, CS Appendix J). This model combination was also identified in the company’s initial identification of the 10 candidate models, as discussed in Section 4.2.6.5. 

The predicted model fits to the EFS and OS appear to be plausible (see Figure 29 and Figure 30) and provide similar visual fits to the company base case model and the remaining 8 candidate models identified by the company (see Section 4.2.6.5). The fits to the cumulative incidences also appear to be adequate, though the poorer fitting for the SOC arm is noted for the EF  IRP state, as was the case in the company base case due to the artefacts introduced by the scheduling of patient follow-up following initial treatment, see Figure 31. Finaly, the hazard plots for this alternative model combination exhibit the same behaviour of an initial increase, see Figure 26, followed by a decrease until background mortality is used to inform the death transitions due to the capping. The times at which the capping is applied for this combination of models, is the same as the company base case, outlined in Section 4.2.6.5.

_Alternative curve selection for transitions from the EF state_ 

Due to the large number of possible model combinations for transitions from the EF state and the possibility of missing additional plausible model combinations, the EAG explored alternative combinations of models for the three transitions. Firstly, the EAG considered the approach in the clarification response to questions B5/B8 where instead of prioritising EFàDeath, EFàL/SR was prioritised during the initial step of the curve selection process. Within its response, the company chose the Gompertz model for EFàL/SR as a pragmatic approach to balance statistical fit with selection of the same model for both arms. The generalised gamma distribution for EFàL/SR was ranked best for the pembrolizumab + SOC arm and the log-normal distribution ranked best for the SOC arm. These model choices were thus explored. 

Following the company’s approach for curve selection, the visual fits to the cumulative incidence curves when choosing the generalised gamma distribution for EFàL/SR for both arms were assessed. All models where the exponential was chosen for either EFàIRP or EFàDeath resulted in poor fits to the cumulative incidences and thus these were excluded, leaving 36 candidate combinations. From further visual assessment of the cumulative incidence curves for EFS and OS (under the primary EFS censoring regime), the EAG identified four additional potentially viable model combinations (in addition to those already previously identified by the company) whereby the Gompertz distribution was selected for EFàIRP and then the Weibull, Gompertz, log-normal and log-logistic models were chosen for EFàDeath. 

This process was then repeated but instead using the log-normal distribution for EFàL/SR for both arms. This process resulted in an additional four candidate combinations which applied the Gompertz distribution for EFàIRP and the Weibull, Gompertz, log-normal, and log-logistic distributions for EFàDeath. 

However, all eight of these alternative model combinations were reliant on EFàIRP being modelled via a Gompertz distribution exhibiting plateau-like behaviours (see Section 4.2.6.7).  Therefore, these alternative model combinations were not explored further in the EAG’s scenario analyses. 

## _Consideration of the statistical plausibility of cure_ 

The plausibility of cure was supported by both the company clinical experts and the EAG’s clinical advisors. Both sources supported the notion that at 5 years there would likely be fewer recurrences and progressions of individual who remained event-free until this stage. To explore this further and the plausibility of the cure assumption, the EAG utilised the EFS KM estimates from the company model and re-constructed IPD for the pembrolizumab + SOC and SOC arms using the Guyot algorithm.[48] Mixture-cure models, using the seven parametric models (exponential, Weibull, Gompertz, log-logistic, 

122 



<!-- page 518 -->

log-normal, gamma and generalised gamma), were fitted independently for the two arms using the _flexsurvcure_ package in R which builds on the _flexsurv_ package.[39] The estimated cure fractions are presented in Table 20, and the model fits for the pembrolizumab + SOC and SOC arms shown in Figure 32 and Figure 33 respectively. 

Most mixture-cure models predicted similar cure fractions, though the Gompertz and generalised gamma mixture-cure models displayed highly uncertain estimates for the pembrolizumab + SOC arm. The cure fraction is mostly stable in these statistical estimates and therefore the EAG believes this may support the plausibility of cure-like behaviour within the EFS data as discussed by clinical experts to the company. The EAG has explored the impact of applying the cure assumption to the EAG’s preferred base case scenario in its scenario analyses (see Section 5.2.4).

## _SMR applied to background mortality_ 

The CS presents no evidence that the background mortality for adults with untreated, newly diagnosed, resectable, LA HNSCC who have PD-L1 CPS≥1 would be the same as general population mortality in patients who survive long enough for the general population mortality rates to apply. The EAG could not conduct a formal SLR to search for evidence on SMRs for this population, however it conducted hand searches on causes of mortality for long-term survivors of HNSCC. The EAG found considerable literature indicating that this population has significant burden due to baseline cardiovascular risk 

125 



<!-- page 521 -->

factors in addition to a higher incidence of second primary malignancy.[49-51] Most notably of the identified articles was Du _et al._ which is a prospective cohort study where cases surviving five years post diagnosis were compared to age-matched, noncancer controls.[52] Ten-year survival was examined by site, stage, p16, and treatment using Kaplan-Meier and Cox proportional hazard models with analyses adjusted for race, sex, age, insurance, and smoking status. Though this study does not explicitly report SMR values, hazard ratios (HR) for death versus general population controls were reported for the several subgroups which broadly represented the majority of the population of the KEYNOTE-689 RCT. These included patients who had radiation and surgery (HR=1.6), surgery and chemoradiotherapy (HR=1.9), stage III disease (HR=2.4), stage IV disease (HR=2.5), oral cavity tumour (HR=2.7), and larynx tumour (HR=2.0). Although a higher HR was identified for patients having hypopharynx tumour (HR=3.6) these were a small minority of patients in both the KEYNOTE-689 RCT and in the cohort study by Du et _al._ making the estimate from Du et _al._ both uncertain and less relevant to the KEYNOTE689 population. Therefore, the EAG considered that the HR relevant to the KEYNOTE-689 population would likely lie in the range of 1.6 to 2.7. In the absence of better data sources to inform the most appropriate SMR value, the EAG conducted scenario analysis using these HR bounds as proxies for SMR values and applied it to the EAG preferred base case as discussed in Section 5.2.4. 

## 4.2.7 Adverse events 

The CS includes all-cause treatment-emergent adverse events (TEAE) of Grade 3 or higher that were reported by at least 5% of patients in either treatment arm of KEYNOTE‐689 as presented in CS, Table 32. This was obtained from the all comer APaT population. The mean duration, mean number of episodes per patient, and percent resulting in hospitalisations for each AE was obtained via pooling across both trial arms of KEYNOTE‐689. These data are used to estimate the QALY loss and costs associated with AEs per each treatment arm as explained in Section 4.2.8.2 and Section 4.2.9.4 respectively. 

In response to clarification question B25, the company provided a table of Grade 2+ AEs occurring in ≥10% of the trial population. There were some differences among the two arms (e.g., hypothyroidism occurred in 19.4% versus 3.2% of the pembrolizumab + SOC versus SOC arm). Clinical advice received by the EAG highlighted some of these AEs to be of significance on HRQoL; however, the EAG agrees with the company that the impact on cost-effectiveness estimates would be minimal. 

126 



<!-- page 522 -->

## 4.2.8 Health-related quality of life 

The company used data from KEYNOTE-689 and performed an SLR to identify external studies which reported appropriate health state utilities, the SLR is described in CS Appendix F. The identified studies are discussed in Section 4.2.8.3. 

## 4.2.8.1 HRQoL data from KEYNOTE-689 

Health state utility values are derived from EQ‐5D‐5L data from KEYNOTE‐689 for the EF, L/SR, and pre-progression IRP health states, while such data were collected from few patients and were too limited to inform the post-progression IRP state as the company implies that this happened beyond the available follow-up data for most patients. 

In KEYNOTE‐689, EQ‐5D‐5L data were reported for the PRO FAS population (see Table 8 for definition). Data were collected both pre- and post-surgery. However, the baseline PRO visit was defined differently between the two treatment arms; for pembrolizumab +SOC it occurred on day 1 of the first cycle of neoadjuvant pembrolizumab whereas for SOC it was the last PRO assessment prior to surgery. This led to a higher proportion of patients being classified as ‘missing by design’ for baseline EQ-5D in the SOC arm as local implementation sometimes meant this pre-surgical PRO visit was not scheduled (see response to clarification question B19). Pre-surgical assessment of EQ-5D was scheduled to occur at weeks 1, 4 and 6 for the pembrolizumab + SOC arm. After surgery, EQ‐5D‐5L questionnaires coincided with radiotherapy ± cisplatin treatment prior to treatment administration on weeks 1 and 4 in both arms. Thirty days after completion of adjuvant radiotherapy ± cisplatin treatment, questionnaires were administered once, and then every three months up to end of year 3, and then annually in years 4 and 5 (CS, Section 3.4.1.1). As reported in CS Appendix K, compliance with the EQ‐5D‐5L questionnaires (defined as the proportion of patients expected to complete the questionnaire in any given visit, excluding those missing by design) exceeded **% in both treatment arms at all visits up to week 129. It is notable that missing by design includes death, disease progression, other discontinuations (reasons may include unacceptable AEs, withdrawal of consent, intercurrent illness that prevents further administration of treatment, investigator's decision to discontinue the participant, non-compliance with study treatment or procedure requirements or administrative reasons requiring cessation of treatment, and unavailable translation). The EAG’s understanding based on the company’s response to clarification question B21 is that patients who had discontinued treatment were classified as missing by design, with the reason for treatment discontinuation reported for contextual information, and those who had not discontinued from treatment but who had not had PRO data reported in the expected time frame were also reported as missing by design with ‘completed treatment’ reported for context. The company’s response to clarification question B20 further clarifies that whilst these patients could be marked as “missing by design” according to the trial protocol if PROs were not obtained, their 

127 



<!-- page 523 -->

discontinuation did not automatically imply that PROs were not solicited or analysed; hence, estimates for the progressed state and the EF state with Grade 3+ AEs could be obtained. However, the EAG is concerned that excluding patients who were ‘missing by design’ from the calculation of compliance has the potential to overestimate data completeness. 

The company base case uses descriptive utility values which were evaluated without explicitly accounting for repeated measures. Utilities were estimated by pooling across both arms as the company deemed that there was no clinically meaningful HRQoL difference between the two arms (see CS, Sections 2.6.1.6 and 2.6.1.7). Baseline measurements were excluded from the analysis. In clarification response B22, the company highlighted that the descriptive means could be viewed “ _as if coming from a generalised estimating (GEE) regression model with an independence working correlation matrix_ ”. Although the company did not provide the GEE derived estimates at the clarification stage, they later provided these within their factual accuracy check and confidential information check response. When these estimates were compared with those used in the company base case, the point estimates were identical, but the standard error (SE) was larger in those derived using the GEE approach. 

In accordance with NICE’s updated manual for health technology assessment, patient responses to the EQ-5D-5L questionnaire were mapped onto the UK EQ-5D-3L values set using the approach developed by Hernández Alava _et al._[32] 

The estimated utilities are presented in Table 33 of the CS. In response to clarification question B22, the company also presented a mixed-effects regression for the pooled sample, and for each treatment arm separately (see clarification response, Table 30). The estimated utilities differed slightly between the two methods. The mixed-effects approach however does not produce marginal estimates (i.e., reflecting the population average rather than being subject-specific) of the utility for each health state and thus the company highlighted that its original approach should be used within the decision-making context. 

## 4.2.8.2 Adverse event related disutilities 

AE‐related disutilities were applied as a one‐time QALY decrement in the first model cycle, calculated based on the proportion of patients in each treatment arm who experienced each AE, the mean duration of each AE, the mean number of episodes as mentioned in Section 4.2.7, and the mean estimated disutility for a Grade 3+ AE (******). Mean disutility is calculated as the difference between the mean utility across patient-visits in the EF state with any Grade 3+ AE minus the mean utility in the EF state with no Grade 3+ AE. The resultant QALY decrements applied to each treatment arm in the CS base case are ***** and ***** for the perioperative pembrolizumab + SOC and SOC arms respectively. 

128 



<!-- page 524 -->

## 4.2.8.3 HRQoL data from external sources 

A SLR was conducted to identify alternative, external sources of utility values for the L/SR and IRP states. Details pertaining to the SLR are presented in CS Appendix F. 

## **HRQoL data from external sources relevant to progressed/recurrent HNSCC** 

As explained in Section 4.2.8.1, EQ-5D data from KEYNOTE-689 could not inform the HRQoL associated with the post-progression IRP state; hence, external literature was consulted. Five utility estimates were identified within the SLR, which are summarised in Table 34 of the CS. Four of the identified sources were concluded by the company not to be appropriate due to the following reasons. 

Utilities for the post-progression IRP state estimated in KEYNOTE-048, which were available to the company, appeared to be greater than those estimated for the IRP pre-progression state using KEYNOTE-689 (**************). Clinical experts consulted by the company believed that they would ordinarily expect the utility of patients to decrease on progression; however, in this specific case the observation is plausible as patients with _de novo_ metastatic disease are likely to have better HRQoL versus patients who have progressed from LA disease. However, due to the reduction in utility between pre- and post-progression, this study was not deemed to be informative for this health state. 

Singh _et al._ report a patient preference study; however, this study was not specific to the postprogression status and limited description of the patient characteristics was provided.[53] Therefore, this study was not deemed useful. 

The M-TAG utility study which informed TA145 was also identified, but these values were obtained from oncology nursing staff rather than HNSCC patients and thus are not aligned with the NICE reference case.[54] Additionally, the reported utility for post-progression was 0.129 which was described by the company as being “remarkably low” and may be considered to lack face validity. 

An additional study, TAX-323/EORTC-24971 (Parthan _et al._[31] ), reported utility values collected via EORTC-QLQ-C30 which were mapped to the EQ-5D. However, the study population was patients with unresectable LA HNSCC. Therefore, the utility values for progressed disease from this study reflected patients who had progressed from LA HNSCC and therefore were not specific to patients who had progressed on treatment for incurable/metastatic disease.[31] 

The company chose the EXTREME trial used to inform the utility values in NICE TA172 and its revision (TA473).[55] That appraisal assessed cetuximab for treating recurrent or metastatic HNSCC, where EQ-5D-3L utility values were obtained by mapping EORTC QLQ-C30 data collected from patients in the EXTREME trial. This study reported a value of 0.52 for the post-progression state. The 

129 



<!-- page 525 -->

company concluded that this utility value was logically consistent with the utility data from KEYNOTE689 and captures the limited treatment effect expected within this stage of the treatment pathway, so it is selected for the CS base case.

The EQ-5D-5L measurements collected in KEYNOTE-689 for the EF, L/SR, and pre-progression IRP were mapped back to the EQ-5D-3L version of the tool using the NICE DSU algorithm.[32] A summary of the utility values used in the company’s base case model is presented in Table 21.

The utility value derived from the EXTREME trial was used for the IRP post-progression state in the base case and the company explored the impact of this choice by applying the same utility for both IRP 

130

sub-states using the value derived for the pre-progression state using the KEYNOTE-689 data (Scenario SA11, CS, Table 61). 

As the model does not explicitly track the occupancy of the pre-and post-progression IRP states separately, the utility for the IRP state was evaluated as a weighted average of the IRP pre- and postprogression utility values derived from KEYNOTE-689 and the EXTREME trial respectively. This average was weighted according to the expected proportion of time spent pre- versus post-progression, as summarised in Section 4.2.2 and CS Appendix J2. 

4.2.8.5 Critique of approaches used to estimate utilities within the model Overall, the EAG is fairly satisfied with the utility values used in the model, although it has some concerns regarding the proportion of HRQoL observations which were categorised as ‘missing by design’ and the potential impact of this on the trial-based utility estimates. 

The point estimates of the descriptive utility values used within the base case, which do not explicitly account for repeated measures, are identical to those estimated via the GEE regression model. However, the SE of the utilities is smaller than when calculated using the GEE regression model which accounts for repeated measures. Therefore, there would be no impact to the deterministic base case if the alternative utility values were used, but the EAG notes that there is an underestimation of uncertainty in the probabilistic analyses. The EAG therefore considers the utilities used for the EF without Grade 3+ AEs, EF with Grade 3+ AEs, L/SR and IRP pre-progression states, using the KEYNOTE-689 to be appropriate but highlights that there may be an underestimation of uncertainty within the probabilistic analyses. However, the EAG notes that no methodological details of the GEE method used were provided. Additionally it does not appear that baseline utility or other covariates were included within the analysis. 

The EAG also notes that, as discussed in the company’s response to clarification question B20, there are some states which may be affected by PROs being “missing by design” due to progression or AEs. However, the company highlighted that under the assumption progressed patients with poorer HRQoL are less likely to complete the PRO surveys, the company’s base case utility estimates for the progressed states would likely be overestimates, and thus the company base case provides a conservative estimate of cost-effectiveness. 

Similarly, the company stated in its response to clarification question B20 that under the assumption that patients who are event-free who have more severe AEs are less likely to complete PRO surveys, 

131 



<!-- page 527 -->

the utility associated with the EF with Grade 3+ AEs state is likely to be an overestimate. This may result in a higher QALY loss than is currently estimated, though the company noted that in the deterministic scenario analysis (DSA) the effect of changing the utility for this state appeared to have negligible impact on the ICER. 

Additionally, when evaluating the utility values using the KEYNOTE-689 data, baseline values were excluded. The EAG highlights that there is therefore no adjustment for baseline utility within the analysis, though it is also apparent that due to the asymmetric treatment schedules, there were considerably more missing HRQoL assessments at baseline for the SOC arm versus the pembrolizumab + SOC arm, which may have presented a challenge have baseline utility been included within the utility analysis. 

Due to the inability to evaluate the utility value for the IRP post-progression state using KEYNOTE689, as discussed in Section 4.2.8.1, external data sources were explored to inform the choice of utility value. Ultimately the company chose to use utility data from the EXTREME trial reported in TA172/TA473. The EAG however notes some concerns and limitations with this approach as the methods employed to inform the evaluation of the utility value using the HRQoL data from the EXTREME trial are not reported and are not available to the company, making it harder for the EAG to assess the robustness of this estimate. 

The EAG asked the company to clarify why external sources were not considered as an alternative to the estimates from KEYNOTE-689 for the pre-progression IRP state, given that these were also based on a low number of observations. The company responded that the values from the literature available from the Parthan study (0.67) and the EXTREME trial (0.67) were consistent with the values obtained from KEYNOTE-689 (*****) (clarification response B17). The value from Singh _et al._ was lower (0.57) but details regarding the methodology employed in this study were sparse. The company did not comment on the values from KEYNOTE-048 (*****) which were higher than the value from KEYNOTE-689 (*****), but the potential reasons for this discrepancy have been previously described for the post-progression IRP utility values. Given the consistency between the value from KEYNOTE689 and two alternative published sources, and the fact that the KEYNOTE-689 trial provides a direct measure of utility in the population of interest, the EAG is satisfied with the company’s rationale for not using alternative sources from the literature for the pre-progression IRP state. 

## 4.2.9 Resources and costs 

The company performed an SLR of cost and HCRU studies, and these were reported in Appendix G. This resulted in 10 publications reporting costs and 23 publications reporting HCRU. Resources used 

132 



<!-- page 528 -->

mainly rely on data from KEYNOTE-689, expert elicitation, and published literature. Costs were obtained from publicly available sources which primarily included the British National Formulary (BNF) and NHS Cost Collection.[57, 58] 

The costs included in the economic model consist of drug acquisition costs, administration costs, initial surgery and adjuvant radiotherapy costs, disease management costs by health state including subsequent treatment costs, costs for managing AEs, PD-L1 testing costs, and terminal care costs incurred at the end of life. The details of each are given in the following subsections. All cost data were sourced from recent literature of the current cost year (such as NHS Cost Collection) except for terminal care costs which are inflated to 2024 prices using the ONS Health Consumer Price Index.[59] Typically, NHS Cost inflation indices from PSSRU are preferred, however the impact here would be negligible. 

Vial sharing is assumed for all included IV treatments, and weight- and BSA- dependant dosing is calculated based on the average weight or BSA rather than method of moments. 

There are no relevant confidential prices for comparator treatments; however, several treatments used as subsequent-line therapies have confidential prices, and these are discussed further in Section 5.4. 

4.2.9.1 Drug acquisition costs in the neoadjuvant/adjuvant settings Neoadjuvant pembrolizumab is given as a fixed 200 mg dose administered by IV infusion every three weeks (Q3W) for up to two cycles. In KEYNOTE-689, pembrolizumab was given after surgery as 200 mg every 3 weeks for 15 cycles. However, in the economic analysis, the company assumes that the patient receives one 200 mg dose at the start of adjuvant treatment, and then three weeks later, the patient is switched to 6-weekly treatment with 400 mg for 7 cycles to manage capacity. ***** of the perioperative pembrolizumab + SOC arm received adjuvant pembrolizumab reflecting *** patients from the pembrolizumab arm with PD-L1 CPS≥1 (N = 345) of KEYNOTE-689. 

Both arms were able to receive adjuvant 100 mg/m[2] cisplatin administered by IV infusion Q3W for up to three cycles if the patient was classified as high risk. This is equivalent to a 180 mg dose based on a mean BSA of 1.8 as per KEYNOTE-689. Of the patients who received any study treatment, ***** (**/345) versus ***** (***/300) received adjuvant cisplatin from the pembrolizumab + SOC versus SOC arms of KEYNOTE-689 respectively. 

A relative dose intensity of 100% is assumed for all treatments and the model uses the Kaplan-Meier estimates to capture time on treatment for each regimen as described in Section 4.2.9.3. Table 38 of the CS presents the unit drug costs for all regimens including subsequent therapies used in later stages. All 

133 



<!-- page 529 -->

costs were sourced either from electronic Market Information Tool (eMIT) or the British National Formulary (BNF).[57, 60] 

The list price per 100 mg vial of pembrolizumab is £2,630.00. There is currently a Patient Access Scheme (PAS) discount in place for pembrolizumab which is accounted for the economic model. The NICE Committee should refer to Table 54 in Appendix I of the company submission for more information. 

## 4.2.9.2 Drug administration costs 

In response to clarification question B26, administration unit costs were updated to reflect the relative activity for outpatient versus day case chemotherapy. Administration costs for neoadjuvant pembrolizumab were based on the simple parenteral chemotherapy at first attendance cost code (SB12Z) from NHS Cost Collection 2023‐2024,[58] which is £372 as the weighted average between an outpatient procedure and day case. For adjuvant pembrolizumab, the first two cycles involved adjuvant cisplatin for ***** of the pembrolizumab + SOC arm as mentioned in Section 4.2.9.2, which was costed based on the more complex parenteral chemotherapy at first attendance (SB13Z) of £470; while patients not receiving concomitant cisplatin accrued the same administration costs as with neoadjuvant chemotherapy. 

The third cycle of cisplatin in the pembrolizumab + SOC arm does not coincide with pembrolizumab administration and therefore is costed as a simple parenteral chemotherapy (£372). This is applied in the economic model by allocating one third of this cost (£124) for each cisplatin cycle.. For the SOC arm, the full cost (£372) was assigned for each cisplatin cycle. 

## 4.2.9.3 Time on treatment 

As explained in Section 4.2.9.1, perioperative pembrolizumab and adjuvant cisplatin both have a maximum number of cycles before discontinuation. Therefore, fully mature time‐on‐treatment (ToT) Kaplan-Meier estimates from KEYNOTE‐689 were used directly in the model to estimate the proportion of the patient cohort for whom perioperative pembrolizumab and adjuvant cisplatin acquisition and administration costs are applicable. These are presented in Table 40 of the CS and replicated in Figure 34.

## 4.2.9.4 Adverse event management costs 

The unit costs of treating AEs are given in Table 54 of the CS. Unit costs were derived from NHS Cost Collection 2023‐2024.[58] AE management costs are applied as a single cost in the first model cycle, calculated based on the proportion of patients in each treatment arm who experienced each AE, as described in Section 4.2.7. 

All AEs not requiring hospitalisation are assumed to have the same cost per episode (£159.94 which is the cost of an outpatient visit), whereas the other costs were AE-specific if it resulted in hospitalisation. The calculated total costs associated with AEs are £192.31 for the perioperative pembrolizumab + SOC arm versus £227.57 for the SOC arm. 

## 4.2.9.5 Initial surgery and adjuvant radiotherapy costs 

Surgery costs were sourced from NHS Cost Collection 2023-2024 code CA93A (£8,051.66).[58] In KEYNOTE-689, ****% (***/345) versus ****% (***/300) proceeded to surgery from the pembrolizumab + SOC versus SOC arms, respectively, and these estimates inform the costs for surgery in the model. This cost was applied in the pembrolizumab + SOC arm six weeks after entry into the model to account for time on neoadjuvant pembrolizumab, whereas for the SOC arm, this cost was applied upon model entry. 

135 



<!-- page 531 -->

Radiotherapy costs comprise two parts; preparation one-off cost equal to £2,460 (NHS Cost Collection 2023-2024 code SC41Z), and costs of delivered radiotherapy fractions. As observed in KEYNOTE689, the model uses five fractions/week for a mean of 6.4 weeks and the cost per fraction is £238 (NHS Cost Collection 2023-2024 code SC23Z). Therefore, estimated total radiotherapy cost is £10,095.39 and was applied after seven weeks from initial surgery. In KEYNOTE-689, ****% (***/345) versus ****% (***/300) received radiotherapy from the pembrolizumab + SOC versus SOC arms respectively - these figures inform the radiotherapy costs in the model. 

## 4.2.9.6 Disease management costs 

Disease management costs were applied in the model for each health state based on the estimated healthcare resource use in each state, and the unit costs associated with each resource. Unit costs and healthcare resource use frequencies for each health state were applied equally to the pembrolizumab + SOC and SOC arms. The unit costs of healthcare resources considered in the model are provided in CS, Table 43. 

The company’s estimates of the frequency of resource use and the proportion of patients incurring these resource are provided in Tables 44 and 45 of the CS. The weekly frequencies for the resources used in the EF state are informed by the company’s clinical experts (N = 5) and included: consultant visits; clinical nurse specialist visits; blood tests and computed tomography (CT) scans. These differed by treatment arm to capture the additional resource use associated with delivering perioperative pembrolizumab. Other resources such as consultations with dieticians and speech and language therapists were not included as these were assumed equal between both arms. Frequencies are assumed the highest in the first year, then lower from year 2 to year 5, after which no resources are assumed, and the patient is discharged. 

The resource use for disease management (i.e. excluding subsequent treatments described in Sections 4.2.9.7 and 4.2.9.8) is assumed to be the same for the L/SR and pre-progression IRP health states based on the company’s clinical experts. These, together with resources for post-progression IRP, were sourced from TA490.[61] TA490 based the resources used and the proportion of patients who received each resource item on Nash Smyth _et al._ ; this is a UK study which reported treatment patterns and resource use in patients with repeatedly-treated metastatic HNSCC.[62] In the absence of specific data, TA490 assumed for simplicity that each resource item was used once per cycle. Because the cycle length used in TA490 was four weeks, the current CS converts all the 4-week proportions of patients from TA490 to weekly proportions using the following equation:

## 4.2.9.7 Subsequent treatment costs following L/SR 

Following L/SR, subsequent treatment costs include radiotherapy, salvage surgery or systemic therapies, and are applied as one-time costs once patients enter the state, as per the proportions of patients who received each of these therapies in the KEYNOTE-689 trial. 

Unit costs for salvage surgery and radiotherapy are assumed to be the same as with initial surgery and adjuvant radiotherapy, except that the duration of radiotherapy was assumed half that of the adjuvant radiotherapy (i.e., 3.2 weeks) to account for increased morbidity following recurrence. Clinical advice received by the EAG indicates that the duration of retreatment radiotherapy is indeed shorter, however remains “very difficult” to quantify due to the variety of different regimens used in the UK. 

Therefore, total costs for surgery and radiotherapy are estimated to be £8,051.66 and £6,277.62, respectively. These costs for surgery and radiotherapy are applied to ***** (out of ** patients from both arms who experienced L/SR as their first EFS event, ** had surgery) and ***** (out of ** patients 

137 



<!-- page 533 -->

from both arms who experienced L/SR as their first EFS event, ** had radiotherapy), respectively, in both modelled treatment arms. 

Subsequent systemic therapies include: pembrolizumab monotherapy; nivolumab; cisplatin + 5-FU; cetuximab + cisplatin + docetaxel; cisplatin + paclitaxel, cetuximab + cisplatin and cisplatin alone. Data on mean ToT and proportions of patients receiving each treatment regimen were available from KEYNOTE-689 (CS, Table 47 and Table 48, respectively). Dosing schedules for L/SR were assumed the same as in the first-line IRP setting (CS, Table 49 and clarification response, question B31). Mean ToT and dosing schedules are used to calculate the total acquisition and administration costs per each treatment regimen. Pembrolizumab plus chemotherapy is not recommended by NICE; hence, the proportions of patients who had this treatment combination were redistributed among the other included regimens based on the market share of each. 

Only ***** and **** patients received systemic therapies with curative intent in the perioperative pembrolizumab + SOC and SOC arms of KEYNOTE-689, respectively, therefore ***** and ***** are assumed to receive no active treatment. The resultant total acquisition and administration costs for systemic therapy are provided in Table 22.
