4.2.9.8 Subsequent treatment costs following IRP 

The company included subsequent treatment costs associated with the IRP state, in first-line (preprogression) and second-line (post-progression) settings, as a single cost on entry to the IRP health state. The dosing schedule for the first- and second-line treatment regimens with the relative dose intensity and sources for these data are provided in CS, Table 49. Drug acquisition costs for all subsequent treatments (CS, Table 38) were sourced from the BNF and eMIT.[57, 60] 

Updated administration costs (clarification response, Table 34) were sourced from NHS Cost Collection 2023‐2024.[58] Activity codes SB12Z, SB13Z, SB14Z, SB15Z, or SB11Z were used dependent on the complexity, duration, and means of administration, IV or oral, of each subsequent treatment. 

First‐line subsequent treatment was assumed to continue until progression based on exponential PFS curves estimated for each first‐line treatment regimen. These PFS curves were estimated based on an 

138 



<!-- page 534 -->

exponential curve fit to median PFS estimated from the NMA conducted by the company and reported in Appendix J4. Table 50 of the CS provides the discontinuation rates for the three reference treatments of the NMA, with the HR used to calculate the rates for the rest of regimens. Some regimens or components of a regimen had a maximum treatment duration and could be stopped earlier. Mean ToT for second-line therapies was sourced from KEYNOTE-048 and provided in CS, Table 51. 

In the company’s base case, a two‐stage discounting approach was adopted for first‐line subsequent treatment costs. For the first stage, a total cost for a full course of first‐line treatment was discounted as if it were initiated in cycle 0, this cost was then applied in the model on entry to the IRP health state and then in the second stage was discounted again to account for the delayed initiation (relative to cycle zero). Second-line treatment costs were only discounted via the second stage. The market share estimates applied in the CS base case, for both the pembrolizumab + SOC and SOC arms, are provided in Table 52 and 53 for the first- and second-line therapies, respectively. These were based on regimens used in KEYNOTE-689, including the following adjustments: 

- The first-line treatment mix includes options that met three criteria: a) had relevant PFS and OS inputs available, (b) that are recommended by EHNS–ESMO–ESTRO clinical guidelines, and (c) may be used in the UK. 

- The share of excluded options based on the above criteria was redistributed among the selected regimens in proportion to their observed usage as patients' first systemic treatment in the IRP state. 

- Because pembrolizumab plus chemotherapy is not recommended by NICE, the proportion of patients who received this regimen were redistributed among the other included regimens based on the market share of each. 

- Patients in the pembrolizumab + SOC arm were divided into two subgroups based on whether they would be eligible for rechallenge with an anti-PD-1 immunotherapy (i.e., pembrolizumab or nivolumab). Those who recurred within the first 18 months of model entry were assumed ineligible for further anti-PD-1 immunotherapies. The shares of these immunotherapies were redistributed among the selected regimens in proportion to their observed usage for the immunotherapy-ineligible population. 

A weighted average of administration and acquisition costs, for a full course of each first- and second‐ line subsequent therapy, is applied on entry to the IRP health state. These costs are provided in Table 24.

## 4.2.9.9 PD-L1 testing costs 

PD-L1 testing costs are sourced from NHS Cost Collection 2023-2024 code PATH02 (£36.20).[58] These are applied once in the economic model upon entry in the EF and IRP states. In the EF state, this is only applied to the pembrolizumab + SOC arm and the cost of 1.05 tests is used to reflect the expected number of PD-L1 tests needed to identify one patient with PD-L1 CPS ≥1 (i.e., 1.05 = 1 / 95.5%). In the IRP state, the cost of one test is applied to both arms upon entry to the state. The requirement for a repeat test even in patients were previously tested for PD-L1 at first-line is justified by the company on the basis of advice from clinical experts that it is possible for the disease pathology of recurrent tumours to differ to the primary tumour. 

## 4.2.9.10 Terminal care costs 

The CS includes a one-off end‐of‐life cost, applied upon transition to the death health state. This cost reflects the management costs associated with terminal care. A cost of £6,207.60 was sourced from Georghiou and Bardsley 2014[63] and inflated to its 2024 value (£8,498.27). 

## 4.2.9.11 EAG critique 

NICE informed the EAG of eMIT price updates for 5-FU, carboplatin, cisplatin, docetaxel, gemcitabine, methotrexate, paclitaxel, pemetrexed. These are reflected in the EAG cost-effectiveness analysis reported in Section 5.2. 

The company’s base case model uses the APaT population to inform all model resource use inputs sourced from KEYNOTE-689. This limits the sample size to patients who started neoadjuvant pembrolizumab in the pembrolizumab + SOC arm and patients who underwent surgery in the SOC arm. In response to clarification question B41, the company justified this approach over using the ITT 

140 



<!-- page 536 -->

population (i.e., all patients randomised regardless of whether treatment was received) in order to account for, _“the open-label nature of the KEYNOTE-689 trial and better reflect expected outcomes of patients receiving the respective treatment regimens”_ . 

The EAG notes that in the pembrolizumab + SOC arm, number of patients is similar between the ITT and APaT PD-L1 CPS ≥1 populations (*** versus *** respectively). This contrasts with the SOC arm where the APaT population comprises only *** patients compared to *** in the ITT population. The EAG considers that more patients would have been captured in the APaT population of the SOC arm had they had neoadjuvant therapy which is part of the positioning of pembrolizumab in the current appraisal. The population used makes a difference in the estimated proportions of patients undergoing initial surgery, adjuvant radiotherapy, and adjuvant cisplatin as shown in Table 25. This critique point is subsequently explored in the EAG’s exploratory analyses in Section 5.2.2, when the EAG has changed the company’s base case assumption from using the ITT instead of the APaT population. This change has also been included in the EAG’s preferred base case scenario (see Section 5.2.3).

The EAG identified two calculation/implementation errors in the model. The first concerned administration costs assigned to adjuvant pembrolizumab. Based on *** receiving adjuvant cisplatin in the pembrolizumab + SOC arm, the model assigns to *** (1-***) of patients starting adjuvant pembrolizumab the administration cost of simple IV chemotherapy, whereas the rest would be assigned the cost of delivering IV complex chemotherapy owing to the delivery of two chemotherapy regimens. However, the *** is reported as part of the whole arm population and not only those who received pembrolizumab. Hence, the breakdown should be *** (*** minus ***) receiving pembrolizumab alone versus *** receiving pembrolizumab with cisplatin. This equates to a ratio for simple IV delivery to complex IV delivery of ***:*** complex IV delivery instead of the ratio in the company’s base case of ***:***. 

The second error was related to the frequency of resource use for the L/SR and IRP health states sourced from TA490. The EAG does not believe such a rate/probability conversion is necessary as these 

141 



<!-- page 537 -->

resources are not one-off events. The EAG prefers simply to divide the resource use by the ratio of cycle lengths between the current appraisal and TA490 (i.e., if one resource was used once every 4 weeks in TA490, then this means its weekly use is 0.25). Both errors are subsequently explored in the EAG’s exploratory analyses in Section 5.2.2. 

Regarding the dosing schedule for adjuvant pembrolizumab, the EAG notes that this does not coincide with the SmPC for using pembrolizumab in this setting. The EAG considered it more likely that pembrolizumab 200 mg Q3W would be given alongside cisplatin for three cycles (instead of the first two in the CS base case), and then the 400 mg Q6W schedule would take over after this. However, the EAG found a negligible impact of this change on the cost-effectiveness estimates and has therefore not included it formally in its exploratory analyses. 

The EAG considers that there is uncertainty regarding whether patients having pembrolizumab as neoadjuvant/adjuvant treatment would be rechallenged with an immunotherapy if they experience an IRP occurring at least 6 months after completing treatment with pembrolizumab. The company has provided two scenario analyses exploring this. The first scenario (company scenario 16) explores a higher usage of immunotherapy, matching that used in the SOC arm, which they argue may better reflect immunotherapy usage for later recurrences, which they claim may not be adequately captured in the KEYNOTE-689 follow-up. The second scenario (company scenario 27), provided in response to the clarification request (B33) explored a situation in which no rechallenge with immunotherapy was offered to patients having neoadjuvant/adjuvant pembrolizumab. Although both scenario analyses had minimal impact on the ICER, the EAG notes that these scenario analyses only impact the costs of subsequent treatments in the pembrolizumab with SOC arm. Therefore, they do not capture the full uncertainty, which includes whether rechallenge would be more or less successful than the mix of subsequent treatments offered in KEYNOTE-689, in which only small proportion of patients in the pembrolizumab with SOC arm received immunotherapy after IRP (***% pembrolizumab for first-line treatment of IRP and ***% nivolumab for second-line treatment of IRP). The EAG has explored the impact of assuming no immunotherapy rechallenge in its scenario analyses, presented in Section 5.2.4, although it notes the limitation that this only impacts subsequent treatment costs. 

Finally, subsequent treatments used in the company’s model included options not mentioned in clinical practice guidelines. In response to clarification question B34, the company provided a scenario analysis where methotrexate was excluded from first-line treatments given in the IRP health state, and cetuximab monotherapy and cisplatin monotherapy were excluded from second-line treatments in the IRP state. The EAG replicated applied these changes to the EAG’s preferred base case as a scenario analysis, as described in Section 5.2.4. 

142

## 4.2.10 Model validation steps taken by the company 

The company reports using quality control procedures to verify the model programming. It also reports performing internal validation of EFS and OS by comparing outcomes predicted by the model to the KEYNOTE-689 data which was used to inform the model. However, it notes that this comparison was complicated by the use of different censoring rules for the EFS and OS survival analyses. It also reports using published OS estimates from other cohorts to perform external validation. However, it notes that there were several limitations with the external validation process.[43-45] Firstly, the studies that were identified reported DFS for adjuvant treatments rather than EFS which is the relevant outcome for neoadjuvant treatments, as reported in KEYNOTE-689. Secondly, the external studies reporting OS varied in terms of the patient characteristics in their cohorts, with particular concerns regarding the distribution of anatomical sites for HNSCC,[44, 45] and the proportion of HPV-positive HNSCC (see Section 4.2.6).[43] These studies were also adjuvant treatment studies meaning that OS was reported from the time of surgery, reflecting a different period of risk from KEYNOTE-689 where OS was reported from randomisation with a potential delay in surgery for the pembrolizumab arm to accommodate neoadjuvant treatment.

## 5.1.2.2 Deterministic sensitivity analysis 

The company conducted one‐way sensitivity analyses (OWSAs) to access the impact, on the ICER, of varying specific parameters in isolation and to identify the main model drivers. The results are illustrated using the tornado diagram in Figure 37. The ICER was most sensitive to the exponential hazard of transitions from L/SR to IRP, followed by the utility value for the post-progression IRP health state. In order of importance, unit costs of IV administration and initial surgery/adjuvant radiotherapy, and EF state management costs also had an impact. Across all the DSAs, the ICER ranges from £****** to £****** per QALY gained.

## 5.1.2.3 Scenario analysis 

The company undertook a series of scenario analyses to assess the impact of applying alternative assumptions to key model parameters. These scenarios are presented in Table 29. The largest change in ICER occurred when alternative survival distributions were selected to model the transitions from the EF to L/SR and IRP health states. The ICER increased to £****** per QALY when independently fit (Company’s approach 1, detailed in Section 4.2.6.1) log-normal and Gompertz distributions were used for the EF to L/SR and IRP transitions, respectively. This was in contrast to when generalised gamma distributions were selected for both transitions where the ICER decreased to £***** per QALY. Applying the cure assumption at five years moved both ICERs closer to the company’s base case ICER. 

Other scenarios of impact were: using the alternative censoring rule for EFS events where last known date alive is used instead of last disease assessment (ICER increased to £******), limiting the model time horizon to 20 years (ICER increased to £******), using the ITT instead of APaT population to 

148 



<!-- page 544 -->

estimate costs of adjuvant treatments (ICER increased to £******), and using a discount rate of 1.5% (ICER decreased to £******). Applying the mix of subsequent treatments observed for recurrences classed as IRP to recurrences classed as L/SR decreased the ICER to £******, but changing the assumptions regarding rechallenge with immunotherapy had minimal impact on the ICER. The scenarios exploring alternative utility values had a fairly small impact on the ICER suggesting the costeffectiveness is not particularly sensitive to the utility value applied post progression for IRP, or the use of alternative  utilities based on a mixed-effects model. Assuming 3 weekly dosing of pembrolizumab throughout the adjuvant treatment phase also had minimal impact on the ICERs.

## **5.2 EAG’s additional analyses** 

## **5.2.1 Model validation and face validity checks conducted by the EAG** 

The EAG performed cell checks and conducted face validity checks on the impact of cost effectiveness outcomes when inputs are varied. The EAG could not detect any logical inconsistencies or suspicious model behaviour, and it believes that the company’s model is reliable for decision-making. 

## **5.2.2 EAG’s exploratory analyses using company’s base case** 

The prices used in the company’s model for 5-FU, carboplatin, cisplatin, docetaxel, gemcitabine, methotrexate, paclitaxel, pemetrexed (as stated in CS, Appendix I) were not up to date with the latest published prices provided to the EAG by NICE from the electronic Market Information Tool (eMIT) database (accessed in November 2025). As mentioned in Section 4.2.9.11, the EAG corrected two implementation errors. The first is related to the ratio of IV simple to complex administration costs for people receiving adjuvant pembrolizumab, whereas the second concerns how resource use frequency for the L/SR and IRP states were derived from TA490. The EAG corrected these errors in EAG exploratory analyses 2 and 3 and included these changes in its preferred base case. 

The EAG preferred using the log-normal / generalised gamma / generalised gamma combination for extrapolating EFS and explored adding the cure assumption as a scenario analysis as discussed in Section 4.2.6.6. The EAG’s preferred combination of models was applied in EAG exploratory analysis 

155 



<!-- page 551 -->

4 and incorporated into the EAG’s base case (see Section 5.2.3). The addition of the cure assumption to the EAG’s base case was examined in EAG scenario analysis 1 (see Section 5.2.4). 

Additionally, the EAG prefers the use of the ITT population to inform all model resource use inputs sourced from KEYNOTE-689 (Section 4.2.9.11). This was applied in EAG exploratory analysis 5 and included in its preferred base case. 

In addition, the EAG preferred to use time-to-event data pooled from the two treatment arms to estimate transitions from the L/SR and IRP states as the treatment-specific data were too few and uncertain to be used for the L/SR state and there was uncertainty regarding whether pembrolizumab with SOC reduced or increased the risk of death from the IRP state. The model included the functionality to use pooled data for transitions from the L/SR state, however, this was not an available option for the transitions from the IRP state. The EAG added the option to use pooled data for transitions from the IRP state and death assuming an average of mortality rates from IRP from both arms in EAG exploratory analysis 6. This change was included in the EAG’s preferred base case (see Section 5.2.3), but the EAG also presented a scenario analysis excluding this change (see Section 5.2.4). 

Table 31 summarises the EAG’s exploratory analysis using the company’s base case model, whereas Table 32 reports the results for each individual analysis. The biggest impact on ICER was when the ITT population was used in place of the APaT population to inform proportions on adjuvant treatment where the ICER increased from £****** to £****** per QALY gained. The remaining analysis only varied the ICER between £****** and £****** per QALY gained.

## **5.3 Decision modifiers** 

## 5.3.1 QALY weighting for severity 

The company states in CS, Section 3.6 that it considers that pembrolizumab does not qualify for an additional severity modifier in this indication as the expected QALY loss for SOC versus the general population does not meet any severity modifier threshold. Although the company does not present its severity modifier calculation in the CS, the EAG has examined the company’s QALY shortfall calculation within its submitted model and it agrees with the company’s conclusion based on their calculation. The EAG has also corroborated their findings by using a published online QALY Shortfall Calculator,[64] and it is satisfied that the population does not meet the criteria, based on the information presented in Table 36. 

The CS later goes on to state, in Section 3.13, that all other STAs for inoperable or metastatic HNSCC (i.e., TA661, TA736) were appraised under the previous End of Life guidance and approved under the end-of-life criteria. The EAG notes that firstly, this guidance no longer applies under current STA processes and secondly, the assessment of whether a severity modifier should apply should be based on QALY shortfall for patients at the point in the care pathway that the treatment is indicated for, which in this case is locally advanced resectable disease and not inoperable or metastatic disease.

## 5.3.2 Uncaptured benefits 

In CS, Section 3.13, the company describes several areas where it believes there are benefits which are not captured in the QALY calculations. These include the provision of a treatment that provides EFS and OS benefits in a disease that has seen few advancements over the last 20 years and where there are limited treatment options, especially for recurrent disease. However, the EAG considers that these aspects of the current care pathway and the potential benefits of pembrolizumab on EFS and OS are captured within the QALY calculation. The CS also describes the psychological distress associated with HNSCC and the broader impact on the patient and their family including social isolation from having a visible disability which impacts on basic functions such as speaking and swallowing. The company proposes that the opportunity to use an effective treatment prior to surgery has the potential to allow surgery to be de-escalated to be more organ-sparing due to tumour downstaging. It argues this potential benefit could not be captured in the trial as de-escalation of surgery was not permitted by the trial protocol. The EAG considers that further research would be required to provide evidence to support the claim that neoadjuvant pembrolizumab has the potential to provide better HRQoL through this mechanism, and also to confirm that the recurrence and mortality risk would not be adversely affected by de-escalation. The company also proposes that there are uncaptured benefits from the lower usage of cisplatin in the pembrolizumab with SOC arm, which is likely to have a positive impact on HRQoL 

162 



<!-- page 558 -->

due to reduced toxicity. It claims this benefit is not captured in the model due to the application of pooled utilities across treatment arms. However, it notes that the study was not formally powered to ascertain differences in cisplatin usage across trial arms. The company argues that a reduction in recurrences would impact patients and careers in terms of work productivity, employment, finances and increases in out-of-pocket expenditure. The EAG considers that any impact of reduced recurrences on patient QALYs or NHS/PSS costs should be captured in the economic model and the other aspects mentioned by the company fall outside of the NICE reference case. The company notes that patients with HNSCC experience a higher rate of suicide and that the impact of bereavement from suicide is not factored into the economic analysis. The EAG agrees that QALY losses related to bereavement falling on both carers and other family members are not captured in the company’s economic analysis. However, QALY losses related to bereavement are not usually included in NICE appraisals. 

## 5.3.3 Health inequalities 

No special considerations related to equity or equality are indicated with the company’s description of the decision problem (CS, Table 1). However, the company describes a number of socioeconomic, sexbased, and racial/ethnic disparities in head and neck cancer in the UK in CS, Section 1.4. These are discussed further in Section 5.3.3. Firstly, there were disparities highlighted with regard to incidence. These related to a higher incidence in males than females, a higher incidence for females in the Asian ethnic group versus females in the White ethnic group, but lower incidences overall for people of Asian, Black or mixed/multiple ethnicity, compared with those of White ethnicity, and a higher incidence for people living in the most deprived areas. People living in the most deprived areas were also likely to be diagnosed with disease at a later stage and were noted to have a higher mortality rate that those living in the least deprived areas. However, the EAG considers that these disparities are unlikely to be impacted by whether this technology is reimbursed for this indication as they mostly relate to disease incidence or delayed diagnosis. The EAG also notes that the company states in the box at the start of CS, Section 1, that “ _Use of this technology is not anticipated to raise any equity or equality considerations_ .” 

## **5.4 Confidential comparator and subsequent treatment prices** 

The PAS discount is applied to pembrolizumab within the model regardless of whether it is used firstline or as a subsequent treatment. For the EAG analyses presented in the confidential appendix to this report, confidential prices have been used that reflect the commercial agreements for pembrolizumab, nivolumab and cetuximab. 

163 



<!-- page 559 -->

## **5.5 Conclusions of the cost-effectiveness section** 

The EAG was satisfied that the company’s model was generally well programmed and suitable for decision making, although it noted two errors which it corrected in its EAG exploratory analyses. In addition, the EAG noted that the company’s model structure did not allow for time-varying transition probabilities for patients leaving the intermediate health states. The EAG considered this to be a significant limitation, although the EAG accepted that incorporating time-varying transition probabilities for the two intermediate health states would add significant complexity to the company’s model and any impact on the cost-effectiveness results was uncertain. The probabilistic version of the company’s base case model provides an expected ICER of £****** per QALY gained, which was similar to the deterministic ICER (£******). The company’s deterministic scenario analyses provided ICERs ranging from £***** to £******* with the choice of distributions used to model transitions from the EF state being the factor associated with the most variation in the ICERs. 

Most of the EAG’s exploratory analyses had minimal impact on the ICER and the ICER for the EAG’s preferred base case was similar to that provided by the company’s base case (£****** and £****** for the probabilistic and deterministic ICERs respectively). However, the EAG’s critique of the company’s model identified several key uncertainties that could not be fully addressed within the EAG’s exploratory analyses. The first key uncertainty relates to the choice of extrapolation models used to estimate transitions from the EFS and OS health states. Whilst the ICER when using the EAG’s preferred choice of models is similar to that obtained in the company’s base case, the company’s most pessimistic and least pessimistic model selections, explored in the company scenario analyses, demonstrate the sensitivity of the ICER to this uncertainty. The EAG also notes that whilst there was some evidence to support the plausibility of a cure assumption, the decision regarding whether to apply a cure assumption remains uncertain and the company’s preferred structural implementation of the cure assumption is somewhat simplistic. 

The EAG notes that there is uncertainty in the long-term efficacy of pembrolizumab in combination with SOC because the CS is based on data from the first interim analysis (IA1) of KEYNOTE-689. The CS states that the overall survival data from KEYNOTE-689 beyond year 3 is subject to a high degree of censoring and should be treated with caution. However, the choice of models for the transitions from the EF state, which are subsequently used to generate EFS and OS predictions, relies on assessing the visual fit of the various model combinations to the data available from IA1. This means that there may be uncertainty in the model selection due to the high degree of censoring in OS. If longer-term data from KEYNOTE-689 were to become available, such as data from the second interim analysis (IA2), then this would reduce the censoring in the data set, reducing the uncertainty in the OS estimates beyond 3 years. Within the CS, the company states that the KEYNOTE-689 study is ongoing and thus may 

164 



<!-- page 560 -->

provide additional evidence in the next 12 months. The later data cut-off may therefore result in a different combination of models being selected for the transitions from the EF state which could impact the predicted efficacy of pembrolizumab with SOC, the predicted efficacy of SOC and the decision regarding the application of the cure assumption. 

The EAG notes that the impact of the company’s decision to employ a state-transition model structure which restricted transitions from the intermediate states to be time-invariant (i.e. employing an exponential extrapolation model with fixed hazards over time) cannot be tested within scenario analyses. It also notes that the exponential models fitted to the observed transitions from the L/SR and IRP states provide limited fits to the data, due to the constraint of a constant hazard imposed by the exponential, and that there is considerable uncertainty in the transition from the L/SR state due to the low number of events reported in KEYNOTE-689 that are available to inform this transition. The EAG partially addressed the issue of low event numbers from the L/SR state in its scenario analysis by pooling the data across arms for transitions out of these later states. The EAG also notes the uncertainty in the IRPàDeath transition, with contradicting transition rates for the individual arms dependent on the method used to estimate them. The EAG addressed this issue by pooling the data across arms for the IRPàDeath transition. However, it still considers the use of the exponential models to extrapolate transitions out of these states to be a limitation of the company’s chosen model structure. 

The EAG also considers that there is some uncertainty regarding whether rechallenge with immunotherapy agents would be offered in clinical practice to patients who have experienced a recurrence/progression after receiving neoadjuvant/adjuvant pembrolizumab. Although it is noted that the impact on the ICER of assuming no rechallenge is fairly limited, this scenario analysis does not capture the full uncertainty, which includes whether rechallenge would be more or less successful than the mix of subsequent treatments offered in KEYNOTE-689, in which only small proportion of patients in the pembrolizumab with SOC arm received immunotherapy after IRP. 

Finally, the company’s model assumes that mortality for adults with untreated, newly diagnosed, resectable, LA HNSCC who have PD-L1 CPS≥1 would be the same as general population mortality in patients who survive long enough for the general population mortality rates to apply within the model. However, the company provides no evidence to support this assumption, meaning the validity of this assumption is uncertain. The EAG exploratory analyses demonstrate that applying a SMR to the general population mortality rates, to reflect the potential for a higher risk of death in long-term survivors of LA HNSCC, has the potential to increase the ICER. However, the EAG considers that uncertainty remains regarding the most appropriate SMR and this could be reduced by a more comprehensive review of the literature.

## **Addendum: Health state utilities using Generalised Estimating Equations (GEE)** 

Health state utilities values using the Generalised Estimating Equations (GEE) approach to account for repeated measures is presented in **Table 1** below. The summary statistics presented are calculated using multiple records per participant, treating each record as independent while employing GEE with an independent working correlation structure. A robust sandwich variance estimator is utilised to compute standard errors. 

**- Table 1. Health state utility values derived from KEYNOTE 689 using GEE**

|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
|||||**Value**|||**SE**||

|EF (with grade 3+ AEs)|***||*****||*****||*****||
|L/SR|**||**||*****||*****||
|IRP|**||**||*****||*****||



Abbreviations: AE: Adverse events; EF, event-free; IRP, incurable recurrence/progression; L/SR, local or salvageable recurrence; SE, standard error. N = Number of participants with non-missing EQ-5D score 

M = Number of records with non0missing EQ-5D score 

With Grade 3+AE is referring to the duration of a single AE episode that started as or worsened into grade 3 or worse during that episode regardless of the starting and ending severity grade within the BICR-free health state 

Database Cutoff Date: 25JUL2024
